list 2 of 3Will ICE agents play a role in the 2026 US midterm elections?

list 3 of 3Dying in ICE custody: Inside one family’s story of heartbreak

end of list

The letter accused FlokiNET of violating its terms of service by publishing a “stolen” employee dataset and asked it to “remove or disable” the information.

“The content is live and places more than 40,000 identifiable individuals at risk of harassment, stalking, and physical harm,” the letter said.

FlokiNET said the letter concerned one domain, icepi.cx, which has compiled information about employees from a range of DHS agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

Those agencies have come under intense scrutiny since the start of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign in 2025.

But the Trump administration has often refused to identify DHS agents involved in specific operations, citing safety risks.

Though FlokiNET said it refused to comply with DHS’s request, it noted that the website’s registrar ultimately suspended the domain. The employee information has since moved to a different domain.

In a statement posted online, FlokiNET defended its decision not to remove the site.

“Federal officers carrying out an enforcement programme are not private individuals while they are carrying it out,” the company said. “The public has a legitimate interest in knowing who is doing that work, under whose authority, and in which office.”

The database was first posted online on Wednesday by Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), a group that showcases leaked government data.

In the past, DDoSecrets has released emails from convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, as well as information from the Israeli Ministry of Justice and police departments in the US.

A hacker group calling itself the “Department of Peace” has claimed responsibility for obtaining and sharing the DHS data.

Since the database was first published, other groups have spread the information elsewhere, including on sites like icepi.cx. As a result, the information is unlikely to be entirely scrubbed from the internet.

The Trump administration, however, has taken an aggressive approach to online platforms purporting to contain information about ICE employees and other agents involved in immigration operations.

Last year, for instance, the US Department of Justice pressured tech giants like Apple to remove apps that track ICE agents, including one called ICEBlock.

The move sparked backlash from Democrats and free-speech advocates, who argued that the public has a right to report on ICE’s movements.

“Blocking access to these apps at the request of the federal government raises the distinct possibility that Apple is working with government to violate its customers’ First Amendment right to record and report on the activities of their government,” Democratic Representative Jamie Raskin wrote in a letter last year, asking Apple to review its decision.

Immigration agents, meanwhile, have taken several steps to conceal their identities during operations, including wearing face masks or street clothes.

That lack of transparency has spurred criticism from human rights groups and immigration advocates, who argue that they have little recourse to pursue allegations of excessive force or impropriety during ICE raids.

Since Trump was sworn in for a second term, at least 25 people have faced gunfire from immigration agents. Six of the shootings have resulted in deaths.

Other cases have involved alleged violations of civil liberties – including unlawful arrests and racial profiling – as well as controversial tactics like car ramming and tackling.

The City of Santa Maria is providing an update on an incident involving a Santa Maria High School student who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents while walking to school.

KSBY community reporter Arly Lara previously reported that the student was detained Oct. 21 about half a mile from campus and later released.

In an update Wednesday, the city said the incident happened in the area of South Broadway and Enos. The student was reportedly injured during the encounter.

Santa Maria police assisted by calling an ambulance for the student. Police Chief Christopher Williams also contacted the District Attorney’s Office, California Attorney General’s Office and ICE’s Los Angeles office. The city said Williams remains in communication with the agencies as they investigate the incident.

The city said Santa Maria police do not enforce federal immigration laws or ask people about their immigration status. Its public safety policies comply with Senate Bill 54, the California Values Act.

“Public safety depends on trust, and we encourage all residents, regardless of immigration status, to contact the Police Department when they need help."

The city said it remains committed to communicating residents’ rights and strengthening community partnerships.

title: Republicans face Latino backlash over ICE arrests as Texans turn to Democrats
description:
He's the second person to be killed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in Texas this year.
Four months on, Lorenzo Jr wants America's Latino population to do just one thing to remember his father: vote.
ICE has arrested people in the car park of the market, says Rosa Martinez, who sells shoes and clothing.

text:
As he prepared to leave his home in Houston, Lorenzo Salgado Sr had just over an hour to live.

The construction worker started July 7 the same way he had for the past 30 years. He woke up, grabbed his lunch and a coffee and left the house before 6am to put in another hard day's work.

On the way, he was followed by unmarked vehicles. By 7am, he was fatally shot.

He's the second person to be killed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in Texas this year.

Salgado Sr was an undocumented Houston construction worker who had lived in the US for 30 years. His sons say being arrested by ICE was his biggest fear.

Instead, they killed him.

CCTV shows an unmarked vehicle pursuing Lorenzo's van, but there is no footage of the actual shooting. The agent who shot him through the passenger side window was not wearing a body camera.

Authorities claimed that Lorenzo drove towards an ICE agent.

"That doesn't sound like our dad," Lorenzo Jr says.

"Our dad had a great respect for the law.

Ronaldo Salgado thinks his father thought he was being robbed.

"I imagine him being scared of someone trying to steal his van, his tools, that morning, and I am fairly confident that some of his last thoughts were about us, because he cared a lot about us.

"He cared a lot about his wife, our mum, and I know he worried about him leaving us alone."

Four months on, Lorenzo Jr wants America's Latino population to do just one thing to remember his father: vote.

"Voting is voluntary, so at least in some of the lower-income neighbourhoods that are accustomed to not being heard, they feel that their votes don't matter," he tells 7.30.

"I think voter turnout is going to make the difference."

At the 2024 US presidential election America's Latino community was split between Donald Trump and Kamala Harris.

But at the midterms, polls suggest Latinos will heavily favour the Democratic Party, largely because of a backlash against widespread immigration arrests and the deaths of at least nine people by ICE operations since Mr Trump was elected to a second term in the White House.

Living in fear

The arrests and killings have up-ended America's Latino communities.

In Texas alone, more than 100,000 people have been detained by ICE agents in the past two years. Many of those arrested have been deported.

In south Texas, the prospect of being targeted by ICE has left many in the Latino community frightened.

At the sprawling Mercadome Flea Market in Alamo, near the Mexico border, customers are staying away.

ICE has arrested people in the car park of the market, says Rosa Martinez, who sells shoes and clothing.

"It's very slow.The sales have gone down, I think maybe 70 per cent," Ms Martinez tells 7.30.

And nobody seems immune from immigration arrests — even Sister Letty Ugboaja, a nun from Nigeria who was arrested on her way to the Our Lady of Sorrows church in McAllen, Texas.

After a flurry of phone calls, Sister Letty was eventually released. Most of those detained are not so fortunate.

Parents have been arrested after dropping their children at school.

The church now asks parents to fill in a form allowing someone else to collect their children, just in case they are arrested after drop-off before eventually being deported.

"We don't call them illegal, we call them undocumented," says Father Jorge Gomez, the rector of the Basilica of Our Lady of San Juan del Valle.

"Mothers are afraid that the husband is not going to come back home after his job because there are a lot of raids, taking people, deporting people, mostly men, when they get out of work, a restaurant or a construction site or a store.

"We have a lot of mothers left behind with two or three kids that are in need because the breadwinner has been deported or is in the process of being deported."

The evaporation of a workforce

As well as exacting a human toll, the arrests have had a significant impact on the construction industry in south Texas.

Local builder Mario Guerrero has lost much of his workforce. A construction project in Phar, Texas, is taking years longer than it should.

"We should have been done in year one because it doesn't take much to build these apartments," Mr Guerrero says.

"It's taking long to build because we don't have the proper labour force right now."

His skilled workforce, hired through sub-contractors, has evaporated.

He says ICE detains everyone on a job site, legal or not, and releases them only when they can prove they're in America legally.

Mr Guerrero voted for Mr Trump two years ago partly because he vowed to stop the wave of refugees and migrants coming across the southern border. However, he says the wave of arrests will drive people to vote for the Democrats.

"[Former US president Joe] Biden was a failure," Mr Guerrero says.

"He opened our borders. Nobody wanted that. Nobody wants open borders. So when Trump was like, 'We're gonna stop that. We're gonna close that. We're gonna send them all back,' [we were pleased]. Of course we want them to go back, but we never thought that he was gonna terrorise people that were here already working and and providing a better living for their families."

'Make quinceaneras great again'

Now the blue wave appears to be surging.

Three Texas congressional districts may fall to the Democrats, including some that were gerrymandered to favour Republican candidates.

In the Fifteenth Congressional District, the party is pinning its hopes on a former teen idol, Tejano singer Bobby Pulido.

Early in the campaign, Mr Pulido was mocked by his Republican rival as not worthy of being a congressman because he was merely "a quinceanera act". Quinceaneras are coming-of-age celebrations for 15-year-old girls.

Mr Pulido embraced the jibe and performs at quinceaneras most weekends as part of his campaign.

"That's when he said, "Well, let's make quinceaneras great again,'" says Sandra Riviera, wearing a hat with the same slogan.

Mr Pulido estimates he's since performed at 80 quinceaneras.

At a recent Saturday night rally in south Texas, he had a plea for his supporters.

"This election is so important for everybody to get out and vote," he tells them.

"Everybody comes up to me, 'Yeah, you got this in the bag.' No, we don't.

"We do not have this in the bag if we don't show up and vote with an urgency. That [is what] we really truly need to go out and do."

'Real change' putting an end to 'lies'

The rise of Mr Pulido and the south Texas Democrats is music to the ears of Julio Garcia, a committed Democratic supporter who has spent much of the past two years engaged in a peaceful, albeit noisy, protest against Mr Trump.

He rides high through local streets in his truck decorated with anti-Trump signs and has had an air-horn retrofitted to the vehicle so he can respond loudly whenever someone gives him a wave or a honk.

"There's a lot of Latinos who voted for Trump," Mr Garcia says.

He says that is no longer the case, judging by how often he's sounding his horn as the election gets closer.

"They are frightened of ICE because ICE has done such terrible things," he says.

"ICE has gone up … to people's homes and workplaces, and they've taken innocent people."

Father Gomez is careful not to criticise Mr Trump or his policies but he is unhappy with the way his laws are being enforced, which he says has been "inhuman".

"Some people are being killed when they're [immigration enforcement] just trying to go and get them," he says.

"Some of them haven't been running."

Back in Houston, the Salgado brothers regularly visit a roadside memorial for their father.

They've been buoyed by the public reaction. Every day there are are more flowers and tributes to their father left at the site where he was shot and killed.

"I hope that we've done enough to encourage enough people to vote, at least here in our communities," Ronaldo Salgado says.

text:
WASHINGTON, DC – Marking 100 days since the conclusion of the 2026 FIFA World Cup this week, Congressmember Nellie Pou (D-NJ-09), the Ranking Member of the House Homeland Security Task Force on Special Events, today released a new official report detailing how the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement policies and mishandling of federal security money created unnecessary security risks before and during the tournament.

The report, issued by minority members of the Task Force, examines shortcomings in federal security coordination and the botched distribution of $625 million in congressionally appropriated security money. Those delays threatened World Cup match permits in Massachusetts, a major fan festival in Miami, and security operations in Kansas City.

The report is also signed by fellow Task Force members Congresswoman LaMonica McIver (D-NJ-10) and Congressman Al Green (D-TX-09).

“The World Cup was an extraordinary success, including in New Jersey where we proudly hosted the historic championship final. I again commend our local, state, and federal law enforcement officers whose careful work kept millions of fans and visitors safe,” said Congresswoman Pou. “But that success should not prevent us from examining what could have gone better. Our new report identifies several avoidable problems with immigration enforcement, security coordination, and delays in federal money that complicated preparations for the tournament.”

Pou concluded: “With the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics fast approaching, we have an opportunity and a responsibility to learn from our experiences in the 2026 World Cup. I hope our findings will help strengthen security preparations for the Olympics and other major events America will host in the years ahead.”

Key Report Findings

Immigration Enforcement: ICE’s expanded operations and refusal to rule out civil immigration enforcement at World Cup events created uncertainty for fans and host communities.

Security Coordination: Conflicting guidance about ICE’s role complicated local security planning, while congressional requests for information were ignored.

Tourism and Local Economies: Immigration enforcement fears and threats to withdraw airport customs personnel needlessly risked discouraging visitors and harming local businesses.

Federal Funding Delays: DHS missed its own deadline for awarding $625 million in World Cup security funding by nearly seven weeks, jeopardizing local security preparations.

FEMA Cuts and Mismanagement: DHS carried out mass firings, encouraged resignations, and diverted personnel from their primary responsibilities to support ICE and CBP operations. President Trump repeatedly called for eliminating FEMA, even as the agency administered World Cup security money.

With Congress already providing $1 billion for security at the 2028 Olympics, the Task Force report urges DHS to set transparent funding rules and ensure FEMA has the manpower needed to deliver those resources on time.

As the top Democrat on the Task Force, Ranking Member Pou helped lead congressional oversight of World Cup security, including hearings examining human trafficking prevention and coordination among local, state, and federal law enforcement.

At a February 2026 oversight hearing, then-ICE Director Todd Lyons refused to rule out civil immigration enforcement at the World Cup when directly questioned by Pou. Pou subsequently led Democratic Task Force members in demanding an emergency hearing on the Trump administration’s immigration plans. The hearing was never held by the majority, and written questions to ICE and CBP went unanswered. In March 2026, Pou introduced the Save the World Cup Act (H.R. 7986(link is external)) to ban civil immigration enforcement at World Cup matches and fan festivals.

Pou also repeatedly pressed DHS to release the $625 million Congress appropriated specifically for World Cup security. Following pressure from Pou and other committee members, DHS finally announced grant awards on March 18, 2026, nearly seven weeks after its own deadline. The report today documents how the delays threatened security preparations in several host cities and calls for reforms to prevent similar problems ahead of the 2028 Olympics.

text:
The plaintiffs challenging the Trump administration’s efforts to build a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas urged the Supreme Court on Thursday to leave in place an order by a federal trial judge in El Paso temporarily halting the construction. Eric Glitzenstein, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs, told the justices in a 40-page filing that granting the federal government’s request to lift that order would allow the Trump administration to “immediately resume blasting, bulldozing, road construction, and other border barrier-related construction across one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally significant landscapes in the United States.”

The dispute centers on three waivers of various environmental and conservation laws that then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued earlier this year to authorize construction of the border wall in the Big Bend region, including areas in Big Bend National Park. Noem and Mullin relied on a provision of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 that gives the Secretary of Homeland Security the power to “waive all legal requirements” necessary “to ensure expeditious construction” of border walls and roads. With the waivers, Noem and Mullin determined that additional border barriers are required in the Big Bend area because it “is an area of high illegal entry.”

The plaintiffs in this case – an environmental group, a local landowner, and a group formed to preserve a church – went to federal court to challenge the waivers’ legality. On Oct. 2, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone temporarily barred the Department of Homeland Security from continuing construction on the border wall in the Big Bend region “until and unless” the government complies with environmental and other applicable laws.

In a written opinion issued on Oct. 14 to explain her reasoning, Cardone concluded that the challengers were likely to prevail on their claim that under the major questions doctrine – the idea that if Congress intends to give a federal agency the power to make decisions of vast economic or political significance, it must say so explicitly – the DHS secretary did not have the authority to issue the waivers.

As an initial matter, Cardone rejected the government’s contention that she did not have the power to consider the challengers’ claims because they arose from a statute, while IIRIRA only allows federal courts to hear challenges to waiver decisions if they involve the Constitution. The major questions doctrine, she said, is a “constitutional … rule” based on the idea that “courts should expect Congress to speak clearly when it delegates major lawmaking authority to the executive.”

Turning to the question of whether the major questions doctrine barred the waivers, she observed that both the government and the challengers “appear to agree that the waiver of all legal requirements to construct a border wall in the Big Bend Sector is of ‘major economic and political significance.’” The key issue, she continued, is thus whether Congress clearly gave the DHS secretary the power to issue the Big Bend waivers. It did not, she wrote. She emphasized that another provision of IIRIRA authorizes the DHS secretary to “take such actions as may be necessary to install additional physical barriers and roads … in the vicinity of the United States border to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.” When that provision is read together with the waiver provision, she said, it means that the DHS secretary can only waive legal requirements for “construction ‘to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry.’”

But the Big Bend region is not, she contended, such an area: although it “comprises over 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border,” it accounts for only a tiny percentage (“between 0.3% and 2.2%”) of all of the people apprehended crossing the border. This means, she said, that “if the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector, and the waiver authority would apply to the entire U.S.-Mexico border. If that were the case, Congress could have simply authorized construction ‘to deter illegal crossings.’” The major questions doctrine instructs courts to avoid “interpretations that would render limiting language meaningless,” Cardone concluded.

The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court on Oct. 21, asking the justices to pause Cardone’s order and to grant review and summarily reverse it. First, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued, the district court did not have the power to consider the challengers’ claim based on the major questions doctrine because their complaint specifically alleged that the DHS secretary “lacked ‘clear congressional authorization’ … to issue the waivers” under the IIRIRA – a statutory claim that “Congress denied district courts” the authority “to entertain.” But in any event, Sauer continued, “[e]ven assuming that the Secretary’s waiver authority implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the Secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction.”

In their brief on Thursday, the challengers insisted that the major questions doctrine applied to their claim, stressing that “the decision to waive myriad federal, state, local, and tribal laws across vast geography for the purpose of building border infrastructure, even through national and state parks where border crossings are miniscule, is a truly ‘extraordinary’ assertion of power.” “Whatever authority Congress delegated, it did not clearly authorize the sweeping exercise of power asserted here, and” the government’s “actions therefore amount to a constitutional violation of the major questions doctrine.”

The challengers also argued that DHS will not suffer any permanent harm if the construction is temporarily blocked – one of the factors that courts consider in deciding whether to award temporary relief. To the contrary, they noted, before Cardone issued her order halting construction, “in response to intense local opposition,” DHS “voluntarily paused construction for weeks in vast portions of the project area.”

text:
State and federal officials subjected immigrants at Miami Correctional Facility to inhumane conditions that involved an "indiscriminate" use of solitary confinement, prolonged lockdowns, threatening racial slurs, "rampant" use of excessive force, and "dangerously inadequate" medical care that, in some cases, led to deaths and near-death experiences, according to a lawsuit on behalf on several detainees at the maximum-security prison.

The 72-page complaint filed Oct. 29 in federal district court in Northern Indiana describes one example after another of alleged abuses inside the facility, which began housing immigrant detainees a year ago as part of an agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The partnership, which has yielded millions of federal dollars for the state, has attracted public scrutiny, especially after the deaths of two ICE detainees earlier this year.

One of the named plaintiffs spent nine weeks in solitary confinement, during which he passed hours staring at the walls and talking aloud to himself to stay sane, according to the complaint. Another described spending three days in his sewage-flooded cell during a lockdown that lasted a week and a half, when detainees weren't allowed to leave their cells except to shower. Another plaintiff is a transgender woman who alleged that she was sexually assaulted by another detainee but didn't receive any medical care.

The plaintiffs are represented by a coalition of state and national organizations, including the American Civil Liberties Union of Illinois and Indiana, the MacArthur Justice Center and the National Immigrant Justice Center. The lawsuit was filed against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, ICE and several federal and state officials, including DHS Secretary MarkWayne Mullin, Acting ICE Director David Venturella and Indiana Department of Correction Commissioner Lloyd Arnold. The lawsuit, which will seek class-action status, raises due process violations.

Government agencies typically don't comment on pending litigation. IndyStar reached out to DHS, ICE and IDOC, but did not immediately receive a response.

In previous statements, ICE has maintained that it provides detainees with "safe, secure and humane environments," as well as "comprehensive medical care."

"Any claim that there are subprime conditions at the Miami Correctional Facility in Bunker Hill, Indiana, is false," an ICE spokesperson said in a statement in April, after Rep. Andre Carson, D-Indianapolis, visited the facility and raised concerns about conditions inside.

While immigrant detention facilities house some people who were convicted of crimes, including violent offenses, a majority of those detained nationwide have little to no criminal history. The named plaintiffs do not have criminal convictions and are held at the prison while immigration courts decide if they should be deported, according to the complaint. The legal process is civil, not criminal.

Yet, detainees were subjected to "punitive" and "dangerous" conditions that "needlessly" put their lives at risk, said Katie Hickey, a staff attorney with the ACLU of Illinois.

"The State of Indiana and Federal government are working together to create a human rights disaster in one of Indiana's most dangerous prisons," said Alexa Van Brunt, director of the MacArthur Justice Center's Illinois office. "The conditions are cruel and have resulted in the deaths of innocent people."

The prison, which also houses some of Indiana's most dangerous criminals and is one of the most violent correctional facilities in the state, was the subject of a recent IndyStar investigation that uncovered severe understaffing and failures to provide medical care to ICE detainees.

'Indiscriminate and indefinite' solitary confinement, prolonged lockdowns

One of the named plaintiffs, Sergei Vasenin, a Ukrainian-born immigrant from Russia, came to the United States in October 2022. He sought asylum and was granted humanitarian parole, a reprieve that allows foreign nationals to stay in the country temporarily.

Yet, according to the complaint, ICE agents arrested him in October 2025 and brought him to Miami Correctional, where he remains detained a year later.

Vasenin spent nine weeks in solitary confinement even after officials determined he did not do anything that warranted such punishment, the complaint alleges. While in segregation, Vasenin did not have timely access to his anti-depression medication and experienced suicidal thoughts.

Officials at the prison "regularly" placed detainees in segregation for "arbitrary and minor" offenses, according to the complaint, often based on "the unpredictable discretion" of correctional officers. Plaintiffs alleged that detainees were placed in solitary confinement that lasted weeks or months over "minor disagreements" with officers, when they'd been abused or assaulted, or for no reason at all.

"Defendants have sent so many detained immigrants to solitary confinement that some detainees … are required to double up, sharing a tiny isolation cell with another person," according to the complaint, which described the punishment a "torturous practice unfit for anyone."

The complaint described one detainee who was in segregation for a month for moving too slowly. Another, the complaint alleged, was placed in solitary confinement for more than two weeks after an officer pepper sprayed and assaulted him while he was restrained.

Detainees also often were placed in prolonged lockdowns, a form of "mass punishment" of an entire housing unit when one or two people misbehave or when there aren't enough correctional staff, according to the complaint.

One of the named plaintiffs, Kemoye Muslar, alleged that the toilet in his two-man cell clogged during a 10-day lockdown. He spent three of those days trying not to step on human waste in the sewage-flooded cell.

Muslar, an immigrant from Jamaica, was admitted into the U.S. in September 2024 and lived in upstate New York with his wife. Muslar had no criminal convictions or pending charges and had applied to become a legal permanent resident. In November 2025, he showed up for a scheduled meeting with an immigration officer as part of his residency application, according to the complaint. ICE agents arrested him that day and he has been detained since.

'Rampant' physical and verbal abuse

Abuses by officers, including use of force and racial slurs, were "rampant," the plaintiffs alleged.

Tasers and pepper spray were frequently used, according to the complaint. One former detainee, who has filed a separate lawsuit, alleged officers used pepper spray on him shortly after he returned from the hospital because of a severe epileptic seizure.

Detainees were also frequently subjected to racist and xenophobic language. Some prison staffers referred to detainees as "a plague" who should go back to their countries, according to the complaint. Staffers professed hating "Latinos and Mexicans," telling them "we don't want you here" and ordering those who ask for medical help to do so in English, the complaint alleges.

One officer, according to the complaint, threatened a detainee, telling him his "corpse will be sent back to [his] country."

Delays in medical care led to near-death experiences, suit says

The conditions were exacerbated by substandard and delayed medical care at the facility, the complaint claims.

Cynthia Acevedo, a transgender woman detained at the prison, requested a physical examination and a rape kit after she was sexually assaulted by another detainee, according to the complaint. Neither was done. Acevedo also sought HIV testing. Medical staff later took her blood sample, but Acevedo, does not know whether it's been tested for HIV or what the results are, the complaint says.

Acevedo, an immigrant from Guatemala, has lived in the U.S. for 26 years and was living in Florida, where she operated a house-cleaning business. She has no criminal convictions or pending charges. She was detained in July and has been at Miami Correctional since.

Acevedo, who was diagnosed with epilepsy 30 years ago, also alleged that medical staff gave her a different medication from what she was originally taking. The new medication, the complaint says, did not control her seizures and was frequently out of stock.

"As a result, Ms. Acevedo sometimes goes days without any medication," according to the complaint. "Her seizures have grown more frequent and more severe, causing her to fall off her bed, hit her head, break her teeth, and become incontinent."

Detainees also describe waiting for days for emergency care.

One detainee experienced intense pain on his leg where he was bitten by a spider years earlier. He submitted multiple requests for medical services over a span of several days and received no response, according to the complaint. After an officer finally showed a nurse a picture of oozing wounds and sores on the detainee's leg, he finally received treatment.

Other instances described in the complaint involved near-death experiences.

One detainee waited for nearly an hour for an ambulance after he was stabbed. Another waited for two days to be taken to the hospital after his lung collapsed. According to the complaint, he was rushed to emergency surgery and doctors told him he was lucky to be alive.

An IndyStar investigation found that Miami Correctional and Centurion Health, its for-profit medical care provider, were woefully unprepared for the influx of ICE detainees, who began arriving at the facility in October 2025 as part of a deal that Gov. Mike Braun had reached with the Trump administration. Severe staffing shortages led to massive medical care backlogs, far above the limits set in the company's $1 billion contract with the state.

Two detainees have died at the facility.

Lorth Sim, a Cambodian national, died on Feb. 16, six weeks after he was transferred to the prison. Sim, a 59-year-old Type 2 diabetic, was prescribed metformin to control his blood sugar levels. But Sim never received the medication, a former Centurion nurse told IndyStar. An independent autopsy sought by his family found significant levels of glucose in his blood.

Tuan Van Bui, a Vietnamese national, died six weeks later, on April 1. Unlike Sim, Bui, 55, was receiving medication for his health problems, including hypertension, according to an ICE detainee death report. But two detainees who saw him collapse said help arrived too late.

text:
Washington employers have spent the last several years adjusting to the state’s pay transparency requirements under the Equal Pay and Opportunities Act (EPOA) and responding to a growing number of lawsuits alleging noncompliant job postings.

The Washington Legislature significantly changed the landscape in July 2025 by revising the remedies available for pay-transparency violations. Among other changes, the Legislature replaced the prior fixed $5,000 statutory-damages framework with one authorizing courts to award between $100 and $5,000 per violation and created a temporary cure process for certain posting deficiencies.

Two questions will shape the next phase of EPOA litigation: which remedies apply to claims based on older job postings, and how broadly an EPOA class may be defined.

The Remedies Question in Milito

The first question is already before the Washington Court of Appeals in Milito v. TikTok Inc.[1] What remedies are available for alleged pay-transparency violations that occurred before the Legislature amended the EPOA in July 2025?

The Washington Court of Appeals recently granted discretionary review of that issue, recognizing that it presents a controlling question of law that could materially affect numerous pending EPOA cases. In the meantime, courts are staying parallel cases while awaiting appellate guidance.

The significance of Milito extends beyond the remedies potentially available to individual plaintiffs. The decision could affect how pending cases are litigated more broadly, including what evidence matters, the appropriate scope of discovery, and how parties approach dispositive motions, class certification, and settlement.

Why Courts Are Staying Parallel Cases

The reason is practical: many EPOA complaints involve the same plaintiff, similar allegations, and the same theory of liability based on allegedly deficient job postings. One federal court noted that a single plaintiff had reportedly filed more than 50 similar EPOA actions in King County Superior Court.

Proceeding through discovery, dispositive motions, or class certification while the Milito appeal remains pending could therefore impose substantial costs under a remedies framework that the Court of Appeals may ultimately determine does not apply.

A stay is procedural, not substantive. It does not mean that the underlying claims lack merit; it simply pauses the litigation until the appellate court provides guidance on an issue that may materially affect how those claims proceed.

The Class-Scope Question in Petzing

A second issue may soon reach the Court of Appeals: how broadly may an EPOA class be defined?

In Petzing v. Discount Tire, the trial court limited a proposed class to applicants who applied to the identical job posting as the named plaintiff, rather than extending the class to applicants who responded to other allegedly noncompliant postings.[2] The plaintiff has sought discretionary review of that ruling with the Washington Court of Appeals, Division One.

If review is granted, Petzing could provide important guidance on the permissible scope of EPOA class actions. A decision on that issue could have significant implications for the size of putative classes and, in turn, the potential exposure associated with pending and future EPOA litigation.

As of this writing, the Court of Appeals has not yet decided whether to accept review. On October 7, 2026, the court set the motion for consideration without oral argument on its February 26, 2027 calendar, and confirmed that the trial court retains full authority to proceed with the underlying case in the meantime.[3]

What the Decisions Could Mean for Pending Litigation

Taken together, Milito and Petzing could clarify two issues central to the future of EPOA litigation: the remedies available for alleged violations and the potential reach of class claims.

Milito will address which remedies framework applies to claims arising from older job postings, a question that could substantially affect the value and trajectory of pending cases. Parties involved in EPOA litigation should therefore reassess their strategies after the Court of Appeals issues its decision, including their approach to motions practice, class certification, settlement, and early resolution.

If the Court of Appeals accepts review in Petzing,that case could provide complementary guidance on how broadly an EPOA class may be defined.

Together, the two cases could shape both the potential value and potential scope of Washington pay-transparency litigation going forward.

[1] The appeal currently pending before the Washington Court of Appeals, Division One, stems from two related cases, Milito v. ByteDance Inc. and Milito v. TikTok Inc.., which the court consolidated for review under Milito v. TikTok Inc., COA No. 89079-4.

[2] No. 24-2-25791-8 SEA (Wash. Super. Ct. King County May 11, 2026).

text:
Following a sizable leak of personnel data about employees who work for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, social network Bluesky is now blocking its users from accessing a nonprofit’s website that hosts the leaked dataset.

Users reported that the links to nonprofit transparency collective DDoSecrets were marked as “malicious” soon after TechCrunch and other media outlets broke the news that Homeland Security had been hacked.

TechCrunch reported on Wednesday that a hacker obtained over 40,000 user account records from Homeland Security’s login system, including the names and contact information, such as work-issued phone numbers and email addresses, of employees and agents working for its various agencies like Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The data included information that was similar to that on an employee’s business card. DDoSecrets, which publishes leaked datasets in the public interest, also made the hacked data publicly available. Researchers who are investigating abuses by the Trump administration say that the data will be invaluable for seeking records from the government under public records laws.

A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch on Wednesday that it was “aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.”

In a statement, Bluesky chief operating officer Rose Wang told TechCrunch: “Our Community Guidelines protect people’s safety and privacy by prohibiting the unauthorized sharing of personal information and other content that could pose safety risks. Because the files include the email addresses and phone numbers of individuals, shared without their authorization, we are blocking links to the dataset.”

“When deciding between blocking a link and removing individual posts, we chose to block the links to avoid limiting public discussion or restricting broader access to reporting and commentary,” said Wang.

In a post on Bluesky, Wang said that the company plans to change the wording on the block message. “We should have changed the wording last night. Changes incoming shortly,” said Wang.

DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best told TechCrunch that while Bluesky’s terms of service prohibit sharing home addresses and personal contact information, Best said that neither of these is in the leaked dataset.

“The data contains professional contact information for government employees at a time when the public interest in that exact information has never been higher. By requiring the public to provide it for [Freedom of Information Act] requests, the government has made that exact information a crucial piece of the transparency channels they want the public to engage in,” said Best.

Homeland Security sends takedown notices

Best told TechCrunch that a website hosting a searchable copy of the stolen data was taken down by its domain registrar, effectively knocking the website offline for now.

A search site, dubbed Icepick, made by journalist maia arson crimew no longer loads as of Thursday morning. An internet record associated with the domain says it has been placed on “serverHold,” which generally means that the domain registrar locked or closed the domain for some reason.

Homeland Security filed a takedown notice via a security vendor called ZeroFox, which has authority to act on the department’s behalf until 2028 to seek the removal of data from the internet. TechCrunch has seen a copy of the takedown notice for the search site, which asks that the domain registrar “stop serving the personal contact and location data of individuals who did not consent to its publication.”

CentralNic, which hosts the domain name, did not respond to a request for comment from TechCrunch about the takedown or whether it was instructed to do so by a government demand. ZeroFox also did not respond to a request for comment.

The Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond to a follow-up regarding the takedown notice affecting Icepick’s website.

Crimew also made a locally hosted version of the data, allowing anyone to access it on their own computer.

text:
Good morning, I guess: Sometimes, when it’s my turn to write Slog AM, I wake up around 6 a.m., open a browser and whisper to myself “please no bad news, please no bad news, please no bad news” while the headlines load. Without fail, though, someone great has died, an old war has taken a new, nasty turn, and the Trump administration has meddled in the upcoming election. This morning is no different. There continues to be bad news. So while you read this morning’s dread report, I recommend having the Smithsonian’s live cheetah cam open in another window. These babies are just three weeks old! Eeeeeee!!!!

GROSS. The US Immigration and Customs Enforcement just awarded a $1.5 billion 10-year contract to private prison company GEO Group to keep running Northwest Detention Center (NWDC) in Tacoma, the Seattle Times reports. GEO Group has consistently blocked efforts from the state Department of Health to investigate the NWDC’s conditions. This is the same detention center where more than 140 detainees went on a hunger strike to protest inedible food. I highly recommend following and supporting La Resistencia’s efforts. They’ve been trying to get this shit shut down for years.

A woman is dead after ChatGPT told her to go off her epilepsy medication. The New York Times reports that Bowen Wan, a Chinese immigrant who was living in Seattle when she died, began messaging ChatGPT when her epilepsy medication wasn’t working, and she had to take disability leave from her software engineering job at Amazon. After using the chatbot to help make sense of her health insurance and disability benefits, she started asking about her medication. The bot told her to taper her dosage. Even when she told it she was feeling worse, it responded, “Maintain 0 mg tomorrow… you must persevere.” It’s a horrifying and heartbreaking story about our country’s fucked up healthcare and insurance nightmare, our fucked up immigration system, and our fucked up lack of mental health resources. Read it, but have a pillow nearby to scream into afterward.

A Washington court ruled Monday “that a lawsuit taking aim at city rental regulations could move forward,” reports the Seattle Times. The suit from a local real estate investment firm alleges city tenant protection laws like limiting winter evictions and requirements that landlords not discriminate based on criminal records “destroyed” a building’s value. This puts Seattle’s tenant protection laws in jeopardy. The Seattle City Attorney’s office could appeal the decision, but chief of staff Dan Nolte told the Times, “We’re reviewing the decision and are meeting internally to discuss next steps. We haven’t made a decision on an appeal yet.”

Accused rapist wants anti-rape lawyer off his rape case. One of the men accused of participating in the alleged gang rape at Cornell University wants Attorney General Letitia James removed as special prosecutor on the case because she expressed support for Jane Doe on X and Facebook before being appointed to the case. This comes weeks after Trump said she should be off the case because she’s a “dirty and disgusting cop.” Calling it now: At least one of the seven accused rapists will end up with a job on Fox News, and another will be offered some token position in the Trump Administration.

RIP Dolores Huerta: Civil rights leader Dolores Huerta died at age 96. Huerta co-founded the United Farm Workers (UFW) union in the midst of the historic five-year (!!!) Delano Grape Strike. Can you imagine striking for FIVE YEARS? After several more decades of fighting for workers’—and women’s and LGBTQ and immigrants’—rights, former President Barack Obama awarded Huerta the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012. This March, she revealed that UFW’s co-founder, César Chavez, who died in 1993, sexually abused her for years. She never told anyone because she didn’t want it to tarnish their work. But let’s not talk anymore about him in remembering her. Her life’s work was also celebrated in 2019 here in Washington, when then-Governor Jay Inslee officially declared April 10 as Dolores Huerta Day.

Let’s break for something fun: Audrey, Julianne, and Dave got to go to the unofficial Gremlins museum (AND THEY DIDN’T INVITE ME!!!!!)

One more Stranger thing to throw on the pile: Please read this piece by Hunter Pauli about tax reform and how “the 99 percent and the 0.1 percent join hands to fuck the petit bourgeoise” if only for the very good accompanying artwork.

Nearly 70 people are dead after two high-speed trains crashed in Spain, causing some train cars to tumble down an embankment. The cause is still being investigated.

There’s still no clear winner in Israel’s election. According to NPR, 90 percent of the votes are counted, and “Israel’s election has reached a deadlock.” It’s the first election since the October 7 Hamas attacks. It’s between Benjamin Netanyahu, who has been Prime Minister for 13 years, and Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israeli military, whose son was killed while fighting in Gaza. It could take weeks before a winner is chosen.

Trump’s election meddling has only just begun. As many predicted, Trump and his crooked bootlickers are attempting to discredit the midterm elections every chance they get. A federal judge in California just shot down Trump’s attempt to “segregate” about 20,000 ballots that Trump claims are “likely” not US citizens. The judge said this would “wreak havoc on the midterm elections.” The Justice Department also recently tried this shit here in Washington.

What are you doing tonight? How about a Halloween pre-funk with a night of death and hip-hop? The Stranger’s own Charles Mudede will join Dr. Daudi Abe and Vitamin D to celebrate some of hip-hop’s greatest songs about death and grief. “Hip-hop’s birth occurred in and around urban communities shaped by socially imposed poverty, violence, and gun culture, and this dire situation, which is still with us today, resulted in a relationship between music and death that’s unique,” writes Mudede. If you saw these three do the same for love and hip-hop songs at the Clock-Out Lounge earlier this year, you know you’re in for a treat. Tickets are just $10 here. See you at the crossroads.

text:
INDIANA — Three immigrants detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at the Miami Correctional Facility in Bunker Hill, Indiana are challenging the inhumane and horrific conditions at the facility on behalf of a class of other detained immigrants. The Department of Homeland Security glibly named Miami Correctional the “Speedway Slammer” when ICE began contracting with the State of Indiana and detaining immigrants there in 2025. It is now one of the largest and deadliest immigration detention centers in the Midwest. In the last year, at least two immigrants died while detained there, and another person recently attempted suicide.

An Indiana Department of Corrections official acknowledged the dangerous conditions at Miami Correctional when testifying before the Indiana State Budget Agency, noting that “we’ve struggled with . . . the ability to keep those incarcerated [at Miami Correctional] safe.” Yet state and federal officials still detain immigrants in unconstitutional conditions.

The three named individuals, who are from Jamaica, Russia, and Guatemala, are being denied adequate medical care, live under constant threat of prolonged solitary confinement without justification, subjected to racist and xenophobic abuse, and forced to endure filthy conditions, inadequate access to food, water, clothing, essential medications, and hygiene items. They are housed in two-person cells measuring just five by eleven feet, each containing a metal sink and toilet.

“Immigration detention is not supposed to be punitive – being held in Miami Correctional is not just punitive; it is dangerous,” said Katie Hickey, Staff Attorney with the ACLU of Illinois. “The federal and Indiana governments have needlessly chosen to put people’s lives at risk.”

“The State of Indiana and Federal government are working together to create a human rights disaster in one of Indiana’s most dangerous prisons,” said Alexa Van Brunt, director of the MacArthur Justice Center’s Illinois Office. “The conditions are cruel and have resulted in the deaths of innocent people. Both the state and federal government must be held accountable for their heinous treatment of people locked inside Miami.”

The conditions being experienced by immigrants civilly detained at Miami facility include:

Inadequate health care – including dangerous understaffing, inadequate health screenings, delays and denials of urgently needed medications and treatment, and ineffective emergency response. One of the lead plaintiffs has been treated for epilepsy for years but is being denied proper medication, and another lead plaintiff was denied mental health care for weeks. These accounts echo other stories involving medical neglect at Miami Correctional and a report exposing widespread failures in medical care at the facility.

The use of abusive punishment – including forcing people into solitary confinement for 23 and 24 hours each day, with little or no justification, use of force by staff without accountability and consequences, and untrained staff who degrade immigrants being held at the facility with racial and xenophobic slurs, including calling them a “plague.”

Inhumane conditions – including inadequate and unhealthy food, lack of access to water, inadequate clothing and shoes (especially during winter), inability to access hygiene items and little or no access to recreation. The conditions are described as “filthy” in most parts of the facility. These disturbing conditions represent a pattern at Miami Correctional, where previous lawsuits recently resulted in $1.2 million in settlements for inmates forced to endure months in total darkness, sewage-flooded cells, and exposed live electrical wires.

“ICE turned to Miami Correctional Facility to detain people at the height of its violent arrest operations in Chicago and Minnesota, and since then has disappeared hundreds of people into this isolated prison where they are forced to either endure deadly conditions, or abandon their immigration cases and their loved ones in the United States and ‘voluntarily’ depart the country,” said Mark Feldman, senior litigation attorney at the National Immigrant Justice Center. “No one should have to choose between their safety and their right to seek immigration relief in this country. ICE’s use of Miami Correctional as a tool of coercion and abuse must end.”

“Every person in government custody is owed adequate medical care, basic safety, and humane treatment under our Constitution,” said William Isaacson, Founding Partner of Dunn Isaacson and Rhee. “There is no excuse for immigrants in an ICE detention facility being treated as less than human beings. We are proud to stand up for basic human decency and the rights of these individuals.”

Today’s lawsuit asks the court to order the federal and state government officials to stop their mistreatment, provide of the immigrants detained with constitutionally adequate care and to take immediate steps to protect the people detained by ICE at Miami Correctional.

title: Appeals court looks set to deny DHS bid to continue harassing voters over citizenship
description:
A federal appeals panel sounded skeptical Thursday of the Trump administration’s bid to continue conducting aggressive field investigations into noncitizen voting.
A district court ordered a block on the probes, which is being appealed to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals by the Department of Justice (DOJ).

The federal agents have notoriously brought film crews with them as they confront people they suspect are noncitizens and then use the footage to create video content used for social media.

text:
A federal appeals panel sounded skeptical Thursday of the Trump administration’s bid to continue conducting aggressive field investigations into noncitizen voting.

Pro-voting groups, along with the city of San Francisco and Santa Clara County, Calif., charged that the investigations are voter intimidation in a lawsuit they filed in September.

A district court ordered a block on the probes, which is being appealed to the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals by the Department of Justice (DOJ).

In Thursday’s hearing of a panel of 9th Circuit judges, the Trump administration struggled with answering the judges’ questions about why the investigations needed to happen so close to Election Day, and why the administration was using social media to publicize operations featuring armed agents using militarized tactics.

The field investigations, which have involved armed federal agents badgering people about their citizenship and voting statuses, are a key component of the Trump administration’s wider campaign to drum up fears about noncitizen voting.

“We have to establish that there is an objectively reasonable fear arising from the defendant’s conduct and threats,” said the pro-voting groups’ attorney Hayden Johnson. “And that voters … are taking steps to mitigate their risks. That’s what plaintiffs have done here, and that’s sufficient.”

Two of the appeals court judges repeatedly asked during Thursday’s hearing why the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) needed to do these stinging probes while people are actively voting.

“So, why is the rush?” Judge Sidney Thomas, an appointee of President Bill Clinton, asked. “What’s the irreparable harm for four days to, as the district court said, let the elections occur, and then … if you want to prosecute later, fine.”

DOJ lawyer Gabriel Schonfeld said the “injunction would be improper on any time frame.”

But Judge Thomas continued to prod him with questions about what the investigations could accomplish before Election Day.

“What do you need in the next four days?” Judge Thomas asked. “What are you prevented from doing in the next four days? You can’t prosecute anybody in four days. You can’t convict them in four days. Why do you need this?”

“I can’t speak to the specifics of what might happen in any given investigation, your honor,” Schonfeld answered. “The government is facing a far broader chill than just the relatively narrow set of investigations that are into naturalized citizens predicated on pre-naturalization conduct.”

However, Judge Kim Wardlaw, a Clinton appointee, appeared more concerned about the chilling effect of public videos depicting the militarized tactics that ICE agents have used in their field operations.

The federal agents have notoriously brought film crews with them as they confront people they suspect are noncitizens and then use the footage to create video content used for social media. The clips show armed agents pulling people out of their homes and cars, and then forcefully shackling and arresting them.

“I’m wondering where the PR aspect of this fits in,” Judge Wardlaw said, “because it seems what you’re publicizing — militarized people with masks on pulling people out of the house, and the people wearing their pajamas — I mean, isn’t part of this that the program, or whatever it’s called, ‘initiative,’ has an aspect of it that seemingly actually wants to intentionally make an effort to instill fear?”

The pro-voting groups’ attorney, Johnson, said “the fear is the harm” committed against voters who, upon seeing these videos and being aware that ICE’s initiative is impacting naturalized citizens, are being intimidated from participating in the midterms.

ICE’s violent social media videos are “a key part of the program,” Johnson said. He pointed to a DHS memo entered as evidence explaining how DHS has set up an online portal so that federal agents can immediately upload photos and clips of their often-violent encounters with suspects.

“That is something that DHS has never done before,” Johnson said. “That’s a totally new system set up just for this purpose. The goal is to send a signal during the voting period. This isn’t DHS doing … banal investigations of the vanishingly rare incidents of non-U.S. citizens wrongly participating in elections. This is as loud as possible, and that has a serious chilling effect and intimidating effect on voters.”

The third judge on the appeals court panel was Anthony Johnstone, who was appointed by President Joe Biden.

Members of the California Nurses Association and Voto Latino Foundation, two of the groups who brought the lawsuit, say the targeted stings are preventing their members from carrying out voter mobilization duties, such as promoting early voting and registering new voters.

They fear that even their eligible voter members will be swept up by the federal government’s hostile dragnet operations.

A lower district court ruled on October 21 that the DHS investigations promote “ongoing intimidation.” It barred the DHS and ICE from continuing the operations in nine states, and from using “target lists,” assembled from flawed databases, to identify noncitizens.

The injunction blocking the government’s investigations expires after Election Day.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — U.S. Representatives Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Immigration, Integrity, Security, and Enforcement, and Jamie Raskin (MD-08), Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee, are demanding answers on a slew of shootings by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agents. “This pattern of deeply disturbing conduct from DHS officers and agents prior to or immediately following the shootings they committed is of great concern,” wrote the Members. “DHS received more than $210 billion from taxpayers for immigration enforcement. It owes the taxpayers and this Congress transparency and accountability for what it is doing with our money. DHS has claimed its officers are striving to protect public safety, yet instead they are unleashing deadly force on our streets. We deserve to know exactly who DHS is arming up and sending out into American communities, especially once they have shot, injured, and even killed American citizens and their loved ones.”

Since President Trump took office in January 2025, DHS agents have shot at least 25 people and killed six of them, including three U.S. citizens.

In the case of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in Minnesota, Christian Castro, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer who shot Mr. Sosa-Celis, was federally indicted for making false statements, and arrested on state charges of assault and false reporting of a crime after he claimed Mr. Sosa-Celis attacked him.

Federal prosecutors were forced to drop charges against Marimar Martinez, a woman who was shot five times by ICE. Charles Exum, the Border Patrol agent who shot her, falsely claimed she had attacked him. Following the shooting, Exum bragged about shooting Ms. Martinez in the back.

Johan Sebastián Guerrero was shot in Maine by David Brouillette, an ICE officer with a history of violence and disturbing domestic abuse allegations. And Oscar Bengal was shot while his five-year-old son was in the car by ICE officer Brendan Cuni, who is involved in multiple use-of-force lawsuits, including one alleging he tased someone six times while they were handcuffed and on the ground.

The Members are requesting detailed information on any DHS agents involved in shootings, including their roles, length of service, and any disciplinary actions against them by DHS during their tenure.

title: Trump's Mandatory Immigration Detention Policy Fails the Textualist Test - Yahoo
description:
Should federal immigration law treat that person the same way it treats someone who was just apprehended at the border?
The legal dispute turns on two phrases in one section of this federal immigration law.
But if nearly everyone who ever illegally entered the country is already subject to mandatory detention, as the administration asserts, then all of those carefully drawn separate categories for mandatory detention suddenly become superfluous and pointless for noncitizens who illegally entered the country, an objection that Douglas raised in dissent⁠.
The administration may believe mandatory detention makes immigration enforcement faster or more effective.
Whether mandatory detention would accelerate Trump's deportation program is a question of policy.
text:
Assume the following: A person unlawfully entered the United States 20 years ago and has since started a business and raised U.S.-citizen children, has no criminal record, and has never been found to be dangerous. Should federal immigration law treat that person the same way it treats someone who was just apprehended at the border? Should the law treat that person as if Congress had specifically made them subject to mandatory detention for criminal or terrorism-related conduct?

Under the Trump administration, the answer is yes. President Donald Trump's current policy treats noncitizens who entered without lawful admission as subject to mandatory detention without bond throughout removal proceedings, even if they have lived in the United States for decades and have no criminal record⁠. The executive branch adopted that position in new Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) guidance issued in July 2025⁠, reversing its prior interpretation of the same detention law.

The U.S. Supreme Court will now decide whether Congress actually required the result Trump is seeking. On October 1, the justices agreed to hear the case of Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha⁠. Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a Brazilian national, entered the United States without inspection around 2005. He later applied for asylum, received work authorization, and eventually bought a home. He operates a small construction business and lives with his wife and two U.S.-citizen children. He has no criminal record. But immigration officers still arrested him while he was driving to work in Massachusetts in September 2025.

After Cunha challenged his detention, a federal court ordered a bond hearing and an immigration judge found that he posed neither a danger nor a flight risk and therefore released him on bond while his case proceeded. The Trump administration then appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit and lost. Now the Supreme Court will have the final word⁠.

The Supreme Court is not deciding whether Cunha may ultimately remain in the country. Instead, it is deciding the narrower question of whether the Immigration and Nationality Act mandates detention pending removal proceedings for someone like Cunha who is present in the United States without having been lawfully admitted⁠.

The legal dispute turns on two phrases in one section of this federal immigration law. According to Section 1225, a noncitizen present in the United States who has not been legally admitted is considered an "applicant for admission." But when Congress imposed mandatory detention later in that same section, it used additional language, applying it to an applicant for admission who is "seeking admission."

That distinction may sound technical and trivial, but its consequences are enormous. If every statutory "applicant for admission" is automatically still "seeking admission," then the government can treat someone who crossed the border 20 years ago the same as someone arriving today and keep them in jail without the possibility of bond. If the two phrases mean two different things, however, then Cunha and others like him are generally eligible for a bond hearing under Section 1226, which permits both detention and release on bond or conditional parole⁠.

The Trump administration argues that if Congress has deemed someone an applicant for admission, that person must necessarily still be seeking the admission for which they are considered an applicant. But the administration's argument asks the Court to stretch federal law beyond its reasonable limits. Congress expressly deemed certain people "applicants for admission." It did not separately deem them to be "seeking admission."

This case, in short, is about textualism. And as the late Justice Antonin Scalia and his co-author Bryan Garner argue in their book, Reading Law: The Interpretation of Legal Texts, one of the key principles of textualism is that "a material variation in terms suggests a variation in meaning." When Congress uses different words in closely related provisions, in other words, courts should hesitate before assuming that the different words mean the exact same thing.

In ordinary English, it is certainly difficult to describe a man driving from home to work after living in the United States for over two decades as presently "seeking admission." He is not seeking to enter the U.S.; he already entered decades earlier. The 2nd Circuit's unanimous opinion—written by Judge Joseph Bianco, a Trump appointee—reached this conclusion, holding that "seeking admission" describes ongoing activity rather than merely a retained statutory status⁠.

Meanwhile, when the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit upheld the administration's position in a similar case, Judge Dana Douglas, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, invoked the same Scalia-Garner textualist principles in dissent.

The legal dispute, therefore, does not follow neat partisan lines. Judges from different ideological backgrounds have both concluded that the administration's reading goes beyond the words that Congress wrote.

The broader statutory structure also supports that conclusion. Congress has long required mandatory detention in Section 1226 for specified criminal and terrorism-related grounds⁠. And the Laken Riley Act of 2025 expanded those mandatory-detention categories⁠. But if nearly everyone who ever illegally entered the country is already subject to mandatory detention, as the administration asserts, then all of those carefully drawn separate categories for mandatory detention suddenly become superfluous and pointless for noncitizens who illegally entered the country, an objection that Douglas raised in dissent⁠.

History also clarifies the point. For nearly 30 years, across five presidential administrations (including Trump's first), the government generally treated people like Cunha as potentially eligible for bond. Trump only reversed course in July 2025. The 2nd Circuit thus accurately described the earlier interpretation as a well-established executive branch practice⁠.

Of course, past executive practice cannot override clear statutory language. But if Congress really did mandate a sweeping detention regime in 1996⁠, it is striking that every presidential administration since then has operated under a totally different understanding⁠.

None of this gives Cunha lawful immigration status. Nor does it guarantee his release or prevent the government from deporting him. Rather, it allows an immigration judge to ask a basic question: Is keeping this particular person in jail actually necessary while his case proceeds?

The administration may believe mandatory detention makes immigration enforcement faster or more effective. And Congress is free to adopt that policy if it chooses to do so. But Congress does have to choose it first.

Protecting the constitutional separation of powers is one of textualism's most important functions. Textualism is often described as a conservative method of statutory interpretation. But its deeper value is constitutional. It forces both courts and presidents to follow the law Congress actually passed. Sometimes that produces harsher results. Sometimes it produces more humane ones. But either way, it restrains the executive and judicial branches from exceeding their proper spheres.

Whether mandatory detention would accelerate Trump's deportation program is a question of policy. Whether it is just is a question of ethics. Whether Congress authorized it is a question of law.

In Cunha, the best textualist reading is that Congress preserved the possibility of bond and left room for an immigration judge to determine whether detention is necessary. That textualism, liberty, and compassion point to the same result is not the reason to reach it. In this case, however, it is a welcome coincidence.

text:
Five Cuban nationals and one U.S. citizen were sentenced today for their roles in a vast conspiracy involving alien smuggling, asylum fraud, and money laundering.
