Operation Take Back America is empowering the Justice Department to put more criminals like these behind bars and enforce the rule of law.”

“The conspirators in this case used sophisticated methods to violate our nation’s immigration laws while personally seeking to enrich themselves,” said U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe for the Middle District of Florida. “We will continue to work with our task force partners to thwart these illegal activities and ensure that our borders are protected.”

“This investigation exposed a transnational criminal organization that treated our immigration system as a profit center, exploiting vulnerable people, manufacturing fraudulent immigration claims, and laundering millions of dollars in ill-gotten gains,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Nicholas Ingegno of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Tampa. “These criminals undermined the integrity of lawful immigration processes and created significant public-safety and national-security concerns. HSI and our law-enforcement partners will continue to identify, investigate, and dismantle transnational criminal networks that exploit our borders and our communities for financial gain.”

“Today’s sentencing is a clear warning to anyone seeking to profit by exploiting, abusing, or undermining America’s legal immigration system,” said Director Joseph B. Edlow of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). “USCIS will bring to bear all law enforcement resources at its disposal to dismantle criminal operations threatening the American people.”

According to court documents, Liannys Yaiselys Vega-Perez, 27, Miguel Martinez Vasconcelos, 31, Layra Libertad Treto Santos, 30, Luis Emmanuel Escalona-Marrero, 32, Walbis Pozo-Dutel, 32, and Emanuel Martinez Gonzalez, 29, conspired with others to operate an alien smuggling organization (ASO), which encouraged or induced thousands of Cuban aliens to enter the U.S. The ASO smuggled the Cuban aliens illegally across the southern border and used fraudulent Electronic System for Travel Authorization (ESTA) visa waivers to help people enter through ports of entry. The defendants advertised their smuggling services and bogus immigration services across multiple social media platforms targeted toward Cuban nationals living in Cuba. The ASO advertised services included assisting Cubans with European citizenship to enter the U.S. on a European tourist visa waiver or ESTA and filed hundreds of fraudulent ESTA applications with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), using fake addresses and false information. Cuban residents are not eligible for the ESTA program, and to obtain ESTAs, the ASO made false representations that the applicants had not been present in Cuba since 2011. The defendants knew that Cubans are not eligible for the ESTA program, and that the applicants were residing in Cuba at the time the ESTA applications were submitted. The defendants also operated a fraudulent immigration benefits business. Once in the U.S., the ASO assisted many aliens with filing fraudulent asylum paperwork to remain in the country.

Passports and boarding passes obtained as part of the scheme Social media account advertising ASO services Social media account using photo from human smuggling event to advertise ASO services

Liannys Yaiselys Vega-Perez furthered the conspiracy by assisting in the logistics of moving aliens from their country of origin, including Cuba, into the United States, such as purchasing international and domestic flights for aliens to transport them towards, into, and throughout the United States. Vega-Perez was also the primary manager of the immigration benefits business and personally filed hundreds of fraudulent asylum applications. In addition, she and other defendants prepared, drafted, and submitted fraudulent asylum applications, immigrant visa applications, lawful permanent residence applications, and other applications for immigration benefits, in exchange for a fee.

Miguel Martinez Vasconcelos furthered the conspiracy by purchasing airline tickets to move individuals being smuggled from their country of origin towards the United States. He also provided funding to purchase charter flights to transport aliens to unlawfully enter the U.S., with the purpose of growing and advancing the ASO’s operations. Vasconcelos personally transmitted at least $150,000 to companies operating outside the U.S. in furtherance of these unlawful activities.

Layra Libertad Treto Santos furthered the conspiracy by personally filing fraudulent asylum claims on behalf of the immigration fraud benefits business while she was an employee and manager. Treto Santos used the ASO’s smuggling services for herself and her family members and referred multiple Cuban nationals to the ASO for smuggling services.

Luis Emmanuel Escalona-Marrero furthered the conspiracy by working with a co-conspirator in Mexico to ship Cuban passports to the United States. The purpose was to avoid the passports being confiscated by U.S. Border Patrol so that aliens could use the passports to apply for asylum once they entered the United States. He also formed a shell company that, along with other companies, was used to move illegal proceeds of smuggling through to conceal the funds’ source and nature before distributing the funds back to himself and his co-conspirators.

Walbis Pozo-Dutel furthered the conspiracy by assisting with the logistics of transporting foreign nationals from their countries of origin, including Cuba, into the United States. For example, Pozo-Dutel provided foreign hotel and flight information to facilitate the aliens’ travel along the route into the United States. Pozo-Dutel also instructed the individuals on what to say if questioned by CBP officers.

Emmanuel Martinez Gonzalez furthered the conspiracy by helping coordinate the logistics of transporting aliens. Martinez-Gonzalez worked with his paramour and codefendant, Marianny Lucia Lopez-Torres, to arrange the travel of aliens upon their arrival in the United States and accepted payments from those aliens as a part of the smuggling operation.

Vega-Perez, Martinez Vasconcelos, and others, conspired to regularly move funds to companies operating outside of the United States and to other places outside the United States, such as by purchasing international flights for aliens to travel into the U.S. Between July 2022 and November 2024, the ASO spent more than $600,000 with a single airline for commercial flights.

Vega-Perez, Escalona-Marrero, and Treto Santos and others conspired to conduct financial transactions that were designed in whole or in part to conceal and disguise the nature, location, source, ownership, and control of proceeds of alien smuggling. The defendants set up multiple shell companies, through which illegal proceeds were moved before distributing the proceeds to the defendants. Between 2021 and 2025, more than $22 million was laundered by the defendants.

Liannys Yaiselys Vega-Perez was sentenced to four years in prison. Vega-Perez previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain, conspiracy to commit asylum fraud, conspiracy to commit international money laundering, and conspiracy to commit concealment money laundering. Miguel Martinez Vasconcelos was sentenced to two years in prison. Martinez Vasconcelos previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain and conspiracy to commit international money laundering. Layra Libertad Treto Santos was sentenced to 30 months in prison. Treto Santos previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain, conspiracy to commit asylum fraud, and conspiracy to commit concealment money laundering. Luis Emmanuel Escalona-Marrero was sentenced to two years in prison. Escalona-Marrero previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain and conspiracy to commit concealment money laundering. Walbis Pozo-Dutel was sentenced to two years in prison. Pozo-Dutel previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain. Emanuel Martinez Gonzalez was sentenced to two years in prison. Martinez Gonzalez previously pleaded guilty to conspiracy to smuggle aliens for financial gain. Escalona-Marrero was ordered to forfeit $2.9M, Vasconcelos was ordered to forfeit $150,000, and Treto Santos was ordered to forfeit $95,000.

Twelve individuals were charged in a superseding indictment for their roles in the conspiracy. Yuniel Lima-Santos, 32, and Gisleivy Peralta Consuegra, 41, pleaded guilty and are awaiting sentencing. Erik Ventura-Castro, 25, was sentenced on July 29 to 30 months in prison. Lazaro Alain Cabrera-Rodriguez, 29, was found guilty after trial in September and is awaiting sentencing. Marianny Lucia Lopez-Torres and Frandy Aragon-Diaz are at large.

This case was supported and prosecuted by Joint Task Force Alpha (JTFA), the U.S. Department of Justice’s lead effort in combating human smuggling and trafficking committed by cartels and Transnational Criminal Organizations throughout the Americas. In partnership with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS), JTFA investigates and prosecutes the most prolific and dangerous human smuggling and trafficking networks that impact public safety and border security. Led by the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section and supported by other Criminal Division components, JTFA has dedicated prosecutors from U.S. Attorneys’ Offices along the Southwest border, Southern Florida, Northern New York, and Vermont. JTFA partners with U.S. Attorneys’ Offices throughout the country and supports high-priority cases in any district. All JTFA cases rely on substantial law enforcement resources from DHS components, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security Investigations, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, U.S. Border Patrol, and the Office of Field Operations. JTFA also partners with FBI and other law enforcement agencies. To date, JTFA’s work has resulted in more than 486 domestic and international arrests of leaders, organizers, and significant facilitators of alien smuggling and trafficking; more than 447 U.S. convictions; and more than 377 significant jail sentences imposed and forfeitures of substantial assets.

HSI Tampa, U.S. Border Patrol Miami Sector, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ Fraud Detection and National Security led U.S. investigative efforts, with substantial assistance from HSI’s Human Smuggling Unit in Washington, D.C. and CBP’s National Targeting Center International Interdiction Task Force. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs and authorities in the Cayman Islands provided valuable assistance.

Trial Attorney Amanda Brown of the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Courtney Derry for the Middle District of Florida are prosecuting the case.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and other transnational criminal organizations, and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime. Operation Take Back America streamlines efforts and resources from the Department’s Project Safe Neighborhoods.

text:
Search More Than 500 Cases of U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents

Experts have long warned that immigration dragnets will inevitably result not only in the erosion of rights for immigrants but also for citizens. Since the start of this Trump administration, we've watched those warnings come true.

So we have once again done what the government won’t: We have tallied and cataloged every case we can find of an immigration agent reportedly detaining a citizen during the current administration — more than 500 cases from Inauguration Day through Oct. 21, 2026.

Read our earlier reporting on U.S. citizens being detained.

We compiled our list by scouring social media, court records and local media, and we included an incident only if we could find at least two sources for it. We asked the Department of Homeland Security about each incident, and we searched for any federal criminal charges that were brought in relation to each incident. (DHS has repeatedly said it is not arresting U.S. citizens.)

Since the government itself does not track these cases, our list is almost certainly an undercount. Below, we're showing you every case we found — the reality that the administration denies — along with the receipts. Read more about how we reported this project.

A citizen riding a bike was tasered, injured and handcuffed after colliding with an ICE vehicle in Long Beach, California. Video footage shows the ICE vehicle driving the wrong way down a one-way street then swerving toward the cyclist. DHS denied hitting the citizen and accused him of smashing the vehicle’s mirror, which is not captured on available video.

One citizen was detained in Santa Maria, California.

One citizen was detained in Naples Manor, Florida.

One citizen was injured and detained by ICE agents who were looking for someone who matched his description in Evanston, Illinois. A responding Evanston police officer said one agent had blood on his hands and the citizen was taken to the hospital. DHS claimed the man didn’t cooperate with “lawful commands” and agents detained him until he identified himself.

Two citizens were detained in San Diego, California.

Two citizens who are enrolled members of the Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe were detained in Bemidji, Minnesota, during a worksite raid.

A citizen leaving a coffee shop in Annapolis, Maryland, was handcuffed, denied a phone call and held for almost two hours. DHS said it took the citizen to another location to interview him because “agitators” had gathered.

One citizen was detained in Newark, New Jersey.

A citizen documenting ICE activity in Ventura, California, was tackled and tasered while he was already pinned to the ground.

A citizen mother of four was detained in Lafayette, Louisiana, at a local law enforcement checkpoint outside her apartment, then transferred to ICE custody and booked into a detention facility before her attorney won her release. ICE and the local law enforcement agency that detained her still dispute her citizenship.

Jeury Concepcion, a 19-year-old citizen, was walking in front of a barbershop in the Bronx when three masked agents tackled him, mistaking him for someone else. The teen said that they released him far from home with his head bloodied, and that an agent apologized to him. A DHS statement said agents temporarily detained the teen to safely finish their questioning. A video associated with this incident appears in our main story.

An immigration lawyer who is a citizen was detained and shackled in New Orleans, Louisiana, while trying to film her clients’ detention.

A citizen was accused of assaulting an officer during the arrest of her husband in Asbury Park, New Jersey. She was detained for eight hours in Delaney Hall, an ICE detention facility, before being released without any known charges. Videos showed her 9-year-old daughter and toddler left crying alone in her vehicle, with ICE agents standing guard until family arrived to pick them up.

One citizen was detained in McAllen, Texas.

A 25-year-old citizen from Denver, Colorado, was detained and deported after a traffic stop in Fredericksburg, Texas, when he was unable to provide identification or proof of citizenship. He was held without access to his phone or a lawyer for several days before he agreed to leave the country. He was allowed to cross back into the U.S. using his Colorado birth certificate in August.

authors: Mark Betancourt | The Texas Newsroom and The California Newsroom, www.tpr.org

text:
The Trump administration is still detaining pregnant migrant youth in a region of Texas where a lack of specialized obstetric care can be life threatening for them, an investigation by The Texas Newsroom and The California Newsroom has found. The practice continues despite vocal concern from its own current and former officials, and from members of Congress.

Government records also show that at least four pregnant girls in detention have had to be transferred out of state since last July to receive specialized medical care, including at least one abortion, that is unavailable in Texas.

"The first time that happened should have been a wake-up call for the administration, and they should have stopped placing kids in any remote area where they can't get care," said Jen Smyers, who during the Biden administration helped oversee the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), which is responsible for migrant youth who are apprehended without a parent or guardian.

She called the policy to send pregnant children to South Texas "enraging."

This spring, The Texas Newsroom and The California Newsroom published a joint investigation revealing the administration's policy of detaining pregnant unaccompanied minors as young as 13 at a single shelter in the Rio Grande Valley. The investigation detailed serious concerns that health experts inside and outside the government had raised about the policy, given that adolescent pregnancies are inherently high risk and there is a lack of specialized obstetric care in the region.

Since then, the administration has denied the policy exists and said it is ensuring that the girls have access to the care they need.

In an unsigned email in September, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees ORR, wrote that "ORR's policies for placing children in its custody into care provider facilities are based on child welfare best practices in order to provide a safe environment and place the child in the least restrictive setting appropriate for the child's needs. This is especially true for expectant minors in ORR care."

Yet the administration's own records, as well as interviews with multiple government officials, suggest otherwise.

The documents, which were obtained through a public records request, show that ORR explicitly directed its staff in July 2025 to send all pregnant youth to the shelter in San Benito, just outside Brownsville.

Several months later, internal agency data showed that pregnant girls started being funneled to a different shelter nearby instead, according to three ORR officials who asked not to be named because they feared retaliation.

Forty-eight Democratic members of Congress expressed concerns about the policy in a pointed letter to the Department of Health and Human Services back in April.

They received a response in September from an assistant secretary at HHS, Alex J. Adams, who wrote that ORR "does not make placement decisions for pregnant youth based on a blanket rule or one-size-fits-all approach" and that it "takes seriously its responsibility to protect the health, safety, dignity, and well-being of every unaccompanied alien child in its custody."

HHS did not respond to requests for comment about the discrepancy between the statements in Adams' letter and the government's own records.

"Obviously, they're not being honest about their policy," said U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro, a Democrat from San Antonio, whose office authored the letter to HHS.

"It's irresponsible that they would wait several months to respond to basic questions about the care of some of the most vulnerable people within the system," Castro said, adding that the administration failed to explain "what seems to be an informal but strict policy of sending these girls to deep South Texas, which lacks the medical care that the girls need."

U.S. Rep. Dan Crenshaw, a Republican from Texas who has been vocal about the welfare of unaccompanied children and serves on a congressional committee that oversees HHS, did not respond to requests for comment.

Unaccompanied migrant children have historically been placed in shelters across the United States, but this summer, the Trump administration began detaining far more of them in Texas.

According to internal reports provided independently by two officials at ORR, both of whom asked not to be named due to fear of reprisal by their supervisors, 95% of the roughly 300 children apprehended by immigration officials in September were placed in detention in Texas, up from 45% in June.

Advocates for unaccompanied migrant children, former government officials, and some members of Congress have criticized the move, arguing that the state is not prepared to handle an influx of vulnerable children who need special care.

The fact that ORR has had to transfer several pregnant unaccompanied minors out of Texas to receive medical care, they say, is proving their point.

"If the government had to fly or transport these pregnant children across the country to get them the medical care they need, why on earth did it deliberately send them to Texas in the first place?" said U.S. Rep. Judy Chu, a Democrat from Southern California, who was unaware of the transfers until a journalist described the newsrooms' findings.

Chu pointed to the fact that many of the pregnant children who enter federal immigration custody are the victims of sexual assault.

"If there is a 13-year-old girl who has survived rape," she said, "she should be met with compassion, safety and appropriate medical care. Instead, this administration is placing children like her in a state where they will be deprived of access to basic healthcare. It's dangerous, and it's cruel, and there's no excuse for treating children this way."

Government records contradict Trump administration's claims

Unlike Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which detains migrant adults and families in large, prison-like facilities, ORR detains unaccompanied children in group or foster homes overseen by private contractors. Laws, agency regulations and court orders require that the children receive comprehensive healthcare and appropriate education while they're detained.

In an unsigned email last month, a spokesperson for HHS said that placing children in Texas is "operationally efficient" and that ORR's facilities in the state "provide all requirements and more." But records obtained through a public information request cast doubt on that assertion.

The records show between July of 2025, when ORR began placing pregnant girls in South Texas, and May of 2026, four of them had to be transferred to other states to receive medical treatment.

That's roughly one in five of the more than 20 pregnant girls the agency placed in the region in that time frame, according to one ORR official.

In detailed notes for one of those cases, ORR staff wrote that a pregnant 12-year-old girl was transferred from the Rio Grande Valley to a shelter in New York on the recommendation of ORR's division of health. The records note that the child needed access to specialists whose availability in South Texas is "extremely limited."

In a note for another case, staff wrote that a pregnant girl was transferred to California due to an unspecified "high risk medical need." In at least one case, a girl was transferred out of Texas because she had requested an abortion, the records show.

Marsha Griffin, a retired professor of pediatrics at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley School of Medicine, said such outcomes were inevitable. Griffin said the shelters have very few medical staff on hand and the region does not have enough specialized obstetricians.

"Young girls who are pregnant, especially those from 10 to 14 years of age, are automatically a high-risk population," said Griffin, who oversaw medical students volunteering in ORR facilities in South Texas.

Internal communications, also obtained through a public records request, show that officials in ORR's own division of health warned the agency's leadership about the lack of pregnancy-related healthcare in the Rio Grande Valley.

"Texas has one of the worst rates of maternal mortality in the U.S.," wrote Joanna Gaines, who at the time was ORR's acting health director, in a July 18, 2025, email to Melissa Johnston, the agency's head of operations. She added that the state "lack[s] access to quality perinatal healthcare" and that "Cameron County has one of the higher rates of infant mortality in Texas."

Four days later, ORR issued a directive to begin placing "any pregnant children" at a shelter in Cameron County called Urban Strategies San Benito.

Tracey Wilkinson, a pediatrician in Indiana who specializes in reproductive healthcare access for minors, said that even if the government is transferring children to get medical care, waiting until they need it puts them in danger.

"When you're talking about labor or pregnancy complications, every minute counts," Wilkinson said. "If it was a medical emergency that required this young person to be transported out of the state, the risk to her survival would be lower for no reason other than she was placed in the middle of nowhere, far away from medical care."

'They are trying to deliberately mislead Congress members'

Shortly after The Texas Newsroom and The California Newsroom revealed the Trump administration's policy of detaining pregnant migrant youth in Texas, Castro launched an inquiry into the practice. He soon arranged a visit to the San Benito shelter.

But by the time of his visit on April 7, internal agency data showed that ORR had stopped placing newly detained children with known pregnancies at the facility, three officials said. Instead, the agency was sending them to a different shelter, in Los Fresnos, just 20 minutes away.

Castro said he was not told of the change at the time of his visit, nor was it mentioned in ORR's formal response to the congressional inquiry last month.

In a recent interview, he described his visit to the San Benito shelter as "a very secretive process" and said he was not allowed to see or speak with any of the children there.

An HHS spokesperson did not respond to questions about the location change, writing only that "there have been no operational changes regarding the placement of pregnant unaccompanied children."

Chu, the Congresswoman from California, said she believed the Trump administration made the change in order to "deliberately mislead Congress members as well as the public from really knowing where these pregnant children have been."

Compass Connections, the San Antonio-based nonprofit that operates the shelter in Los Fresnos where pregnant girls are now being held, is one of the largest ORR contractors; it has been awarded over $1.9 billion in federal grants to house and care for unaccompanied minors over the past four years, according to USAspending.gov. Asked for comment, the company referred the newsrooms to HHS.

In his letter to Castro, Assistant Secretary Adams wrote that "placement and transfer decisions are individualized and consider the child's safety, medical and behavioral health needs, pregnancy-related needs, available services, legal access, family unity, least restrictive placement requirements, and the best interest of the child."

'In California, they would have more access to all reproductive healthcare'

Congress members and advocates in California said the state offers much more support for pregnant girls in federal custody than they can receive in Texas.

As the Trump administration has withdrawn federal support for legal representation of unaccompanied children — and at the same time streamlined the process of deporting them — the state of California, as well as several of its cities and counties, have ramped up funding for their own legal services programs for undocumented kids.

"Pregnant unaccompanied children have rights to medical care, safety, family unity and due process, but those rights mean little without a lawyer to defend them," said Marion "Mickey" Donovan-Kaloust, director of legal services at Immigrant Defenders in Los Angeles. "California's support systems can provide pregnant unaccompanied children with the stability, dignity and specialized care they need to be safe and thrive."

In addition to concerns about their access to healthcare and legal services, advocates worry that the Trump administration is knowingly putting pregnant children at risk to advance an ideological goal: denying them access to abortions by placing them in Texas, where abortion is virtually banned.

Current federal regulations require the government to move detained minors who request abortions to states where it's legal. In January, the Trump administration announced it plans to rescind that rule, though it hasn't yet done so.

An HHS spokesperson said in February that claims the department is attempting to restrict unaccompanied children's access to abortion are "completely inaccurate."

Congressman Gil Cisneros, a Democrat from Southern California, said, "In California, they would have more access to all reproductive healthcare, and then they could make decisions based on discussions with their healthcare professional and what's best for them."

Chu noted that the midterm elections will determine whether Democrats regain control of the U.S. House of Representatives. If they do, she said, they will redouble their efforts to ensure pregnant children in federal immigration custody are given proper care.

"There will be greater oversight," she said, "and we will hold the decision-makers responsible."

In a recent Fox News poll, most Americans believe the Trump administration has "gone too far" in enforcing immigration laws, including 60% of independents.
According to The Economist/YouGov polling cited earlier, 1% of Democrats named immigration as their top issue in September 2026.
Remarkably, without Democrats' endorsement of a single new immigration policy idea, independents now express greater trust in Democrats than Republicans on immigration, 41% to 27%, according to a September 2026 Marist survey.
After the global pandemic halted most human mobility in 2020, the Biden administration sought to avoid the immigration issue altogether.
No mandate for inaction Should Democrats win majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives in 2026, the issue of immigration is highly unlikely to be resolved.
text:
In a 2025 investigation, The New York Times reported that officials in President Joe Biden's administration, in the wake of Biden's 2020 election win, had viewed rising immigration as "a distraction" best ignored so that the administration could concentrate political resources on more important economic matters.

Scott Shuchart, a Biden appointee who joined the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency in 2022, told the newspaper that the White House was "wishing the problem would go away so that they could focus on the things they cared about."

But two years after Donald Trump leveraged voter dissatisfaction with the Biden administration's management of the U.S. southern border to win the 2024 election and enforce his immigration crackdown, the issue has suddenly become a secondary matter.

Amid the rising U.S. cost of living, a destabilizing war in Iran and a disrupted system of global commerce, the now-quiet border has relieved Democrats of their thorniest issue just in time for midterm elections.

From liability to advantage

For the past three decades, the Democratic Party and its candidates have struggled to develop and pass new immigration policies and communicate related political messages.

Bipartisan attempts at comprehensive immigration reform died on Capitol Hill in 2006, 2007 and 2013. Since then, a majority of Americans has trusted Republicans more with governing the issue. That has given the GOP an advantage when the salience of immigration policy has risen due to border crises and related high-profile events, even if that edge has recently narrowed.

In a February 2024 poll, 28% of U.S. respondents told Gallup that immigration was the country's most important problem – matching the largest share since tracking began in 1981. By May 2026, that figure was 8%, a staggering drop in such a short period.

In a different poll by The Economist/YouGov, the share of U.S. registered voters who identified immigration as the country's most important issue fell from 14% in October 2024 to 5% in September 2026.

Erik Iverson, a Republican Senate campaign pollster, recently told Axios that declining border crossings have reduced the urgency of immigration, depriving Republicans of an issue that previously energized voters and offered conservatives an advantage.

"You become a victim of your own success," he said.

But this success is dubious. President Trump's approval ratings on immigration are underwater.

In the RealClear Polling average from September to October 2026, his net approval was at negative 10.8%. In a recent Fox News poll, most Americans believe the Trump administration has "gone too far" in enforcing immigration laws, including 60% of independents.

Despite Republicans' insistence that the mass removal of undocumented immigrants and a halt to new migrants would raise wages and make housing more accessible, Americans are experiencing high inflation rates, slow gross domestic product growth and sour consumer sentiment.

Ominously for the White House, Trump's negative 10.8% net approval score on immigration is actually among his best. On inflation, the economy and foreign policy, his net approval rating is at negative 42.8%, negative 31.7% and negative 27.8%, respectively.

These dynamics bode well for Democrats' midterm election prospects.

Republicans are now less concerned about immigration – what has been their greatest source of political energy and the left's greatest political liability – as both parties' voters are focused on other matters.

Despite the White House's aggressive and frequently violent pursuit of undocumented immigrants, its proposal to end birthright citizenship, and its near closure of U.S. borders, even Democrats are no more likely to identify immigration as the country's top issue today than they were previously.

According to The Economist/YouGov polling cited earlier, 1% of Democrats named immigration as their top issue in September 2026. In October 2024, 3% said the same.

Remarkably, without Democrats' endorsement of a single new immigration policy idea, independents now express greater trust in Democrats than Republicans on immigration, 41% to 27%, according to a September 2026 Marist survey.

Democrats' trial and error

Democrats' sudden edge arises after a decade of trialing different approaches to counter the nativism and popular discomfort that Trump has harnessed.

Before Trump's 2016 election victory and immediately thereafter, Democratic leaders sought to ameliorate the image of foreigners in the U.S., by highlighting that immigrants start more businesses, file more patents and commit fewer crimes than native-born U.S. citizens on average.

During this period, Democrats commonly cited immigrants' acute vulnerability and their willingness and ability to fill critical low-skilled and high-skilled labor gaps. But the praise and pity produced resentment among many Americans who did not want an admissions system that elevated foreigners to a higher pedestal.

Toward the end of the first Trump administration, Democratsbegan citing the immense macroeconomic and fiscal benefits driven by immigrants' long-term settlement in the U.S.

Economists attribute to immigrants the bulk of U.S. population growth from 1990 to 2015. And economists have shown that continued immigration mitigates inflation and extends the solvency of Social Security and Medicare funds. Immigration also provides workers for industries like construction, agriculture, food production and healthcare.

However, the benefits of these relationships for average voters tend to be diffuse and realized in the medium-to-long run. That makes them hard to recognize.

After the global pandemic halted most human mobility in 2020, the Biden administration sought to avoid the immigration issue altogether. It's a strategy that Democrats have now carried over while the dynamics of being out of power still permit doing so.

No mandate for inaction

Should Democrats win majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives in 2026, the issue of immigration is highly unlikely to be resolved. As a matter of constitutional oversight, Democrats plan to commence investigations into the Trump administration's abusive immigration enforcement tactics, questionable case adjudication and alleged corruption.

It will be almost impossible to pass meaningful immigration legislation in such an environment.

The Biden-era approach was a pivotal electoral liability in 2024. And the Obama administration's series of immigration executive actions instigated a tennis match of such orders between subsequent administrations ever since.

Democrats will soon feel some pressure to develop bipartisan approaches to immigration governance that ensure order at U.S. borders and a strategy for immigrant selection and integration that is designed with the national interest in mind.

Anything less, and the dysfunctional system – with its massive political risks – will return.

text:
Talent argued to the panel that the Immigration and Nationality Act requires local law enforcement authorities to share information about illegal immigrants detained by state and local police, along with allowing federal officers to take possession of those criminal illegal immigrants once their state or local detention has concluded. He added that Illinois, Cook County, and Chicago have made it more difficult for federal authorities to arrest criminal illegal immigrants through policies that bar information sharing and require immigration officers to try to arrest illegal immigrants on the streets after they are released from state or local custody.

“If Congress authorized federal officials to assume custody before the end of the scheduled period of state incarceration, states could not plausibly claim a 10th Amendment right to refuse to relinquish custody and release the alien onto the street,” Talent said. “Congress’s decision to instead allow states to complete the scheduled prison sentence for these criminal aliens does not perversely have the effect of authorizing the states to interfere with the orderly enforcement of federal law.”

The appeals court panel appeared skeptical of the Trump administration’s arguments, questioning how much the policies impede federal immigration operations, whether Illinois’s policies violate federal law, and whether there is discretion in the INA for local governments’ cooperation with federal immigration officials.

“Whatever discretion the states have in the INA, they can’t actively thwart the implementation of federal officials. They can’t actively thwart federal officials who are trying to implement Congress’s purposes to take these individuals in custody and expeditiously remove them,” Talent said.

Alex Hemmer, Illinois deputy solicitor general arguing on behalf of the state, emphasized to the panel that under federal law, state and local law enforcement do not have to use their resources to help with federal immigration enforcement, pointing to the federal district court’s decision to dismiss the case.

“The state of Illinois, like its municipal counterparts, has chosen not to require state police officers to assist the federal government in enforcing civil immigration law on the state’s time and dime,” Hemmer said. “As the district court held, the INA does not preempt that choice, and that’s true.”

The panel questioned Hemmer over whether the state was “overexaggerating” the “effort and how much funds needed” to tell federal officials when criminal illegal immigrants would be released from state custody. Hemmer responded by arguing that the amount of effort or funding does not change their stance that the INA does not require the level of cooperation the DOJ is demanding.

The three-judge panel included U.S. Circuit Judges Kenneth Ripple, an appointee of former President Ronald Reagan; Michael Scudder, an appointee of President Donald Trump; and Rebecca Taibleson, also a Trump appointee. The panel did not indicate how it would rule, but it did offer sharp questions to lawyers on both sides of the case.

USCIS, under President Trump, takes nearly seven times more immigration enforcement actions than during Biden’s final two years combined

WASHINGTON — Under the leadership of President Donald J. Trump and Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) is delivering on the Administration’s agenda and putting the American people first. The agency has restored integrity and order to the nation’s immigration system, reversing the downstream effects of the Biden border crisis. Since January 20, 2025, USCIS has carried out immigration enforcement actions to revoke or terminate the status of approximately 2.2 million illegal aliens. These actions are in addition to the millions of visa revocations and denials issued by the U.S. Department of State and removals carried out by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

USCIS’s enforcement actions include:

Ending the misuse of Temporary Protected Status so that TPS is once again truly temporary;

Denying applications to extend or change nonimmigrant status when no legal basis exists;

Issuing Notices to Appear (NTAs) to place removable aliens into removal proceedings before an immigration judge;

Ending the automatic extension of employment authorization documents, ensuring every alien is properly screened and vetted before any work authorization is renewed; and

Terminating categorical parole programs and returning parole to strict case-by-case review as Congress intended.

These actions have real consequences. Every fraudulent application identified, every ineligible benefit denied, and every national security threat flagged represents an immigration system working to uphold the law and protect the American people. By strengthening screening and vetting, preventing the exploitation of immigration benefits, and initiating removal proceedings against those who violate our laws, USCIS is closing the gaps that undermine public safety and national security.

USCIS is exercising its full legal authorities to deny meritless applications, terminate unlawfully granted immigration benefits, initiate removal proceedings, and revoke improper approvals—all while promoting accountability and preventing the misuse of public benefits.

“President Trump promised the American people that our immigration laws would be enforced, and these numbers reflect the scale of that commitment,” said Secretary Mullin. “Those who abuse or flagrantly disregard our immigration system are now on notice that these violations of law will not be tolerated or overlooked. Securing our border was only the beginning. We are restoring integrity to the entire immigration system and putting the safety of our American citizens first.”

The Trump Administration’s approach is producing fundamental change in how immigration laws are enforced. At their core, these enforcement actions help protect American communities. Returning to the failed policies of the past would undo that progress and put countless American lives at risk.

WASHINGTON (OSV News) — Pope Leo XIV sent a special message of support to an interfaith immigration policy summit hosted by the Catholic Legal Immigration Network, also known as CLINIC, Oct. 29.

The Oct. 29-30 virtual summit, which brings together faith leaders, legal practitioners, advocates, and scholars from Catholic, Protestant, and Jewish faith traditions, sought to find areas of commonality in their work serving immigrant communities.

Pope Leo thanked CLINIC for its work, “together with that of the many people, families, civic bodies and church communities who strive to uphold the dignity of migrants and refugees.”

“Too often, these most vulnerable members of society are caught in situations which strip them of their human rights — an injustice that cries out to heaven,” he said. “It is my hope, therefore, that this summit will encourage the participants to stir the hearts and minds of their fellow citizens to overcome that indifference and detachment which reduces the human person to a statistic.”

Pope Leo said he would pray the meeting “will help find new ways to awaken consciences to our shared moral duty for these brothers and sisters of ours, who, as Sacred Scripture and the saints untiringly remind us, are Christ visiting us in disguise.”

Anna Gallagher, executive director of CLINC, said in remarks at the summit that Pope Leo’s message was “a meaningful charge for the beginning of an interfaith gathering.”

“We are here to learn from one another, to strengthen our work, and to consider how we can help our communities see more clearly and respond more faithfully,” she said.

The summit came shortly after a divided panel of the U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia allowed a lawsuit against the federal government from a coalition of more than two dozen religious organizations to proceed. The group is challenging a Trump administration policy that rescinded long-standing restrictions on arrests at sensitive locations, also including schools and hospitals, with exceptions for public safety or national security threats.

Catholic population hard hit by mass deportation push

The gathering also took place shortly after the Archdiocese of St. Louis filed a lawsuit against the federal government over a policy it said prohibits priests from distributing holy Communion to and hearing confessions of Catholics detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

A joint report from the National Association of Evangelicals, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops’ Migration and Refugee Services, the Center for the Study of Global Christianity at Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary, and World Relief estimated that more than 10 million Christians living in the U.S. would be vulnerable to deportation under Trump administration policies implemented in 2025, and 61% were Catholic.

It also found more than 1 in 6 Catholics are either vulnerable to deportation themselves or could see a family member deported, barring law or policy changes.

“The Holy Father’s message asks us to resist the indifference that reduces a person to a statistic,” Gallagher said.

“Those of us who work in communications, law, ministry, or advocacy know how easily that reduction happens,” she added.

text:
A Los Angeles federal judge has granted a preliminary injunction blocking the Trump administration from conducting suspicion-free and racially discriminatory immigration stops across Southern California, the latest turn in a lawsuit that arose from a 2025 Pasadena incident.

U.S. District Judge Maame Frimpong also partly certified a class of individuals who have been affected by the practice.

Following evidence presented in the case, the court order prohibits defendants from enforcing the policy and practice of conducting detention stops in the Central District of California based on racial stereotyping except when such a stop is conducted at a port of entry, checkpoint or other functional equivalent of the border.

The ruling applies to the Central District of California, which includes the seven counties of Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside, San Bernardino, San Luis Obispo, Santa Barbara and Ventura.

The order was issued Friday, but largely sealed from public view until the following Thursday.

The order specifies that in developing reasonable suspicion, “an immigration agent or officer must consider the totality of circumstances and may not rely solely on apparent status as low-income or working-class and Latino, even when an identified target is allegedly low-income or working-class and Latino.”

Evidence showed federal agents were carrying out an ongoing campaign of warrantless and discriminatory immigration enforcement stops in the region since the summer of 2025.

The request for a preliminary injunction stemmed from a case in which residents, Latino workers and immigration advocacy groups sued the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, alleging unconstitutional detention practices.

According to the ACLU of Southern California, which is representing plaintiffs in the case, the Trump administration is targeting “people who appear Latino and low-income or working-class.”

In a video discussed in the plaintiffs’ motion for a block on the alleged stops, a DHS agent is captured saying to another: “Yeah, just plug us in wherever you see some tonks,” while other agents guessed whether people were “wet” simply based on appearance.

The complaint says “tonks” is a derogatory and violent term understood to refer to the sound of a flashlight striking a migrant’s head. “Wet” is short for “wetback” and is a racist slur historically directed at Mexican and other Latino immigrants crossing the Rio Grande.

In response to the suit, the DHS has frequently insisted federal agents in the field are operating within the law to protect American citizens.

“Our agents are focused on protecting the American people — not entertaining performative outrage,” according to a statement from DHS. “Where is the media’s outrage for Angel families who lost a loved one to illegal alien crime?”

“Angel families” refers to the relatives of those killed by undocumented individuals present in the United States.

This ruling emerges from a Pasadena incident. The federal case of Vasquez Perdomo vs. Mullin was filed in July 2025 by the ACLU of Southern California, NDLON, and other community groups challenging the aggressive immigration enforcement raids and detention practices across the Los Angeles area as a violation of the Fourth Amendment.

On June 18, 2025, three men — Pedro Vasquez Perdomo, Isaac Villegas Molina and Carlos Osorto — were waiting for the bus across from a Winchell’s Donuts store on Orange Grove Boulevard when they were surrounded by federal immigration agents in unmarked cars and detained. It was about 6 a.m. and they were on their way to Altadena to help rebuilding efforts there.

The ACLU, the Los Angeles Worker Center Network, United Farm Workers (UFW), and Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA) filed the lawsuit on behalf of the three Pasadena men, as well as two others: Jorge Hernandez Viramontes of Baldwin Park, who was questioned and detained from his job at an Orange County car wash, and Jason Brian Gavidia of East L.A., who was stopped and questioned from a tow yard in L.A. County.

A federal district court initially issued a temporary restraining order limiting certain enforcement actions. At issue was whether the government’s roving immigration patrols involved racial profiling and were based on perceived ethnicity and without probable cause.

In August 2025, the Supreme Court granted the government’s request to stay that order while litigation proceeds, allowing the challenged practices to continue, but Wilfong said it did not offer any explanation with the action.

Earlier this month, Frimpong partially granted a restriction on alleged race-based suspicion-free stops of suspected illegal immigrants by federal agents across the district in the first step toward Thursday’s ruling.

Frimpong heard arguments in September in Los Angeles federal court.

“(Thursday’s) order recognizes that the armed goons who targeted and abducted Latino community members in Southern California were in fact simply racially profiling as many people as they could get handcuffs on, a practice that violates multiple provisions of the U.S. Constitution,” Mohammad Tajsar, director of immigrants’ rights at the ACLU Foundation of Southern California, said in a statement.

“Having spent more than a year amassing reams of evidence of widespread illegal behavior, we will now closely monitor compliance with this court order to make sure we end this project of racist immigration enforcement once and for all.”

The July motion for restrictions on immigration stops includes body camera footage and depositions of federal agents as part of evidence ordered by Frimpong after the U.S. Supreme Court stayed an earlier temporary restraining order last year which allowed the challenged practices to continue unabated.

Plaintiffs argue the Constitution prohibits law enforcement from using race as a substitute for individualized suspicion. The motion alleges the stops violate both the Fourth Amendment and the Fifth Amendment’s guarantee of equal protection.

“For over a year, agents have been showing up at car washes and taking people without a warrant, never asking whether they have a family and a home to return to,” said Flor Melendrez, executive director of CLEAN Carwash Worker Center, a member of the Los Angeles Worker Center Network, a plaintiff in the case.

“The law requires more than a biased guess about someone’s status, and today the court made the government follow it. Our community fought for this protection, and we will hold the government to it on every street and at every car wash.”

City News Service and Staff Writer Anissa Rivera contributed to this report

text:
She called the policy to send pregnant children to South Texas “enraging.”

This spring, The California Newsroom and The Texas Newsroom published a joint investigation revealing the administration’s policy of detaining pregnant unaccompanied minors as young as 13 at a single shelter near the border with Mexico. The investigation detailed serious concerns that health experts inside and outside the government had raised about the policy, given that adolescent pregnancies are inherently high risk and there is a lack of specialized obstetric care in the region.

Since then, the administration has denied the policy exists and said it is ensuring that the girls have access to the care they need.

In an unsigned email in September, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees ORR, wrote that "ORR's policies for placing children in its custody into care provider facilities are based on child welfare best practices in order to provide a safe environment and place the child in the least restrictive setting appropriate for the child’s needs. This is especially true for expectant minors in ORR care.”

Yet the administration’s own records, as well as interviews with multiple government officials, suggest otherwise.

The documents, which were obtained through a public records request, show that ORR explicitly directed its staff in July 2025 to send all pregnant youth to the shelter in San Benito, Tex., just outside Brownsville.

Several months later, internal agency data showed that pregnant girls started being funneled to a different shelter nearby instead, according to three ORR officials who asked not to be named because they feared retaliation.

Forty-eight Democratic members of Congress had also expressed concerns about the policy in a pointed letter to the Department of Health and Human Services back in April. They received a response in September from an assistant secretary at HHS, Alex J. Adams, who wrote that ORR “does not make placement decisions for pregnant youth based on a blanket rule or one-size-fits-all approach” and that it “takes seriously its responsibility to protect the health, safety, dignity, and well-being of every unaccompanied alien child in its custody.”

HHS did not respond to requests for comment about why, contrary to Adams' statement that there was no "one-size-fits-all approach," the government's own records indicate that all unaccompanied youth with known pregnancies have been sent to specific Texas shelters.

“They're definitely playing games,” said U.S. Rep. Gil Cisneros, (D-Calif.). “They're not looking out for the welfare of these young women.”

U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-TX, whose office authored the letter to HHS, called it “irresponsible that they would wait several months to respond to basic questions about the care of some of the most vulnerable people within the system,” adding that the administration failed to explain “what seems to be an informal but strict policy of sending these girls to deep South Texas, which lacks the medical care that the girls need.”

Unaccompanied migrant children have historically been placed in shelters across the United States, but this summer, the Trump administration began detaining far more of them — even those who are not pregnant — in Texas. According to internal reports provided independently by two officials at ORR, both of whom asked not to be named due to fear of reprisal by their supervisors, 95% of the roughly 300 children apprehended by immigration officials in September were placed in detention in Texas, up from 45% in June.

Advocates for unaccompanied migrant children, former government officials, and some Democratic members of Congress have criticized the move, arguing that the state is not prepared to handle an influx of vulnerable children who need special care.

The fact that ORR has had to transfer several pregnant unaccompanied minors from Texas to California, New York and Arizona to receive medical care, they say, proves their point.

“If the government had to fly or transport these pregnant children across the country to get them the medical care they need, why on earth did it deliberately send them to Texas in the first place?” said U.S. Rep. Judy Chu, D-Calif., who was unaware of the transfers until a journalist described the newsrooms’ findings. Chu’s district, California’s 28th, is home to several communities with high numbers of immigrants, such as Rosemead and Monterey Park.

Chu expressed concern that many of the pregnant children who enter federal immigration custody are victims of sexual assault.

“If there is a 13-year-old girl who has survived rape,” she said, “she should be met with compassion, safety and appropriate medical care. Instead, this administration is placing children like her in a state where they will be deprived of access to basic healthcare. It's dangerous, and it's cruel, and there's no excuse for treating children this way.”

Government records contradict Trump administration’s claims

Unlike Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), which detains migrant adults and families in large, prison-like facilities, ORR detains unaccompanied children in group or foster homes overseen by private contractors. Laws, agency regulations and court orders require that the children receive comprehensive healthcare and appropriate education while they’re detained.

In an unsigned email last month, a spokesperson for HHS said that placing children in Texas is “operationally efficient” and that ORR’s facilities in the state “provide all requirements and more.”

Records obtained through a public information request cast doubt on that assertion. The records show that between July of 2025, when ORR began placing pregnant girls in South Texas, and May of 2026, four of them had to be transferred to other states to receive medical care.

That’s roughly one in five of the more than 20 pregnant girls the agency placed in the region in that time frame, according to one ORR official.

In detailed notes for one of those cases, ORR staff wrote that a pregnant 12-year-old girl was transferred from South Texas to a shelter in New York on the recommendation of ORR’s division of health. The records note that the child needed access to specialists whose availability in South Texas is “extremely limited.”

In a note for another case, staff wrote that a pregnant girl was transferred to California due to an unspecified “high risk medical need.” In at least one case, a girl was transferred out of Texas because she had requested an abortion, the records show.

Marsha Griffin, a retired professor of pediatrics at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley School of Medicine, said such outcomes were inevitable. Griffin said the shelters have very few medical staff on hand and the region does not have enough specialized obstetricians.

“Young girls who are pregnant, especially those from 10 to 14 years of age, are automatically a high-risk population,” said Griffin, who oversaw medical students volunteering in ORR facilities in South Texas.

Internal communications, also obtained through a public records request, show that officials in ORR’s own division of health warned the agency’s leadership about the lack of pregnancy-related healthcare in the region of South Texas where the girls are held.

“Texas has one of the worst rates of maternal mortality in the U.S.,” wrote Joanna Gaines, who at the time was ORR’s acting health director, in a July 18, 2025, email to Melissa Johnston, the agency’s head of operations. Gaines added that the state “lack[s] access to quality perinatal healthcare” and that “Cameron County has one of the higher rates of infant mortality in Texas.”

Four days later, ORR issued a directive to begin placing “any pregnant children” at a shelter in Cameron County called Urban Strategies San Benito.

Tracey Wilkinson, a pediatrician in Indiana who specializes in reproductive healthcare access for minors, said that even if the government is transferring children to get medical care, waiting until they need it puts them in danger.

“When you're talking about labor or pregnancy complications, every minute counts,” Wilkinson said. “If it was a medical emergency that required this young person to be transported out of the state, the risk to her survival would be lower for no reason other than she was placed in the middle of nowhere, far away from medical care.”

‘They are trying to deliberately mislead Congress members’

Shortly after The California Newsroom and The Texas Newsroom revealed the Trump administration’s policy of detaining pregnant migrant youth in Texas, Castro launched an inquiry into the practice. He soon arranged a visit to the San Benito shelter.

By the time of his visit on April 7, internal agency data showed that ORR had stopped placing newly detained children with known pregnancies at the facility, three ORR officials said. Instead, the agency was sending them to a different shelter, in Los Fresnos, just 20 minutes away.

Castro said he was not told of the change at the time of his visit, nor was it mentioned in ORR’s formal response to the congressional inquiry last month.

In a recent interview, he described his visit to the San Benito shelter as “a very secretive process” and said he was not allowed to see or speak with any of the children there.

An HHS spokesperson did not respond to questions about the location change, writing only that “there have been no operational changes regarding the placement of pregnant unaccompanied children.”

Chu said she believed the Trump administration made the change in order to “deliberately mislead Congress members as well as the public from really knowing where these pregnant children have been.”

Compass Connections, the San Antonio-based nonprofit that operates the shelter in Los Fresnos where pregnant girls are now being held, is one of the largest ORR contractors; it has been awarded more than $1.9 billion in federal grants to house and care for unaccompanied minors over the past four years, according to USAspending.gov.

Asked for comment, the company referred the newsrooms to HHS.

In his letter to Castro, Assistant Secretary Adams wrote that “placement and transfer decisions are individualized and consider the child’s safety, medical and behavioral health needs, pregnancy-related needs, available services, legal access, family unity, least restrictive placement requirements, and the best interest of the child.”

‘In California, they would have more access to all reproductive healthcare’

Congress members and advocates in California said their state offers much more support for pregnant girls in federal custody than they can receive in Texas.

“One thing is very clear,” Chu said: “There are many of us that care about what's happening to our immigrants.”

As the Trump administration has withdrawn federal support for legal representation of unaccompanied children — and at the same time streamlined the process of deporting them — the state of California, as well as several of its cities and counties, have ramped up funding for their own legal services programs for undocumented kids.

“Pregnant unaccompanied children have rights to medical care, safety, family unity and due process, but those rights mean little without a lawyer to defend them,” said Marion "Mickey" Donovan-Kaloust, director of legal services at Immigrant Defenders in Los Angeles. “California's support systems can provide pregnant unaccompanied children with the stability, dignity and specialized care they need to be safe and thrive.”

In addition to concerns about their access to healthcare and legal services, advocates worry that the Trump administration is knowingly putting pregnant children at risk to advance an ideological goal: denying them access to abortions by placing them in Texas, where abortion is virtually banned.

Current federal regulations require the government to move detained minors who request abortions to states where it’s legal. In January, the Trump administration announced it plans to rescind that rule, though it hasn’t yet done so.

An HHS spokesperson said in February that claims the department is attempting to restrict unaccompanied children’s access to abortion are “completely inaccurate.”

Cisneros said that “In California, they would have more access to all reproductive healthcare, and then they could make decisions based on discussions with their healthcare professional and what's best for them.”

Chu noted that next month’s election will determine whether Democrats regain control of the House. If they do, she said, they will redouble their efforts to ensure pregnant children in federal immigration custody are given proper care.

“There will be greater oversight,” she said, “and we will hold the decision-makers responsible.”

Mark Betancourt is a freelance journalist based in Washington, D.C.

text:
Transcript

A MARTÍNEZ, HOST:

The number of children in U.S. public schools is falling. By the end of the decade, enrollment will be down by millions. Education experts say lower birth rates over the last two decades are the big factor. President Trump's immigration crackdown is also taking a toll. NPR's Brian Mann is covering this. Brian, so how many millions are we talking about?

BRIAN MANN, BYLINE: Well, it's a lot. Public schools now have been losing kids for years. Forty states have seen declines. And the U.S. Education Department projects that by 2030 - that's just a few years from now - the drop could reach 4 million children. And while this is happening in most of the U.S., some districts are being hit much harder. The Los Angeles Unified School District, A, has lost half its kids over the last 20 years. And superintendent Andres Chait announced this fall that he's launching a citywide program aimed at closing schools.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

ANDRES CHAIT: It is a simple if painful reality that we used to have 700,000 students, and now we have fewer than 400,000.

MANN: And public school enrollment nationwide is expected to keep falling. Officials in California say their state alone will lose another 700,000 public school students over the next decade.

MARTÍNEZ: Wow. Now, we mentioned some of the factors that go into this. Break that all down for us.

MANN: Yeah, so what most researchers say is that it's a one-two punch here caused first by low birth rates, and then now by Trump's immigration crackdown. There are roughly 700,000 fewer babies born every year in the U.S. That's compared with 20 years ago. So that's a lot fewer kids turning up for kindergarten. Until last year, in much of the country, that trend was offset at least partially by immigrants coming into the U.S. A lot of them put their kids in public schools. Now, at least in the short term, a lot of those students are suddenly vanishing.

MARTÍNEZ: Vanishing. What does that mean, vanishing?

MANN: Well, let's take LA again. After Trump's immigration crackdown began there last year, LA Unified School District officials say their enrollment decline got a lot worse. They lost twice as many kids as they expected. Texas also lost roughly 76,000 public school kids statewide in 2025. It's only the second drop in the state's modern school history. A study by state officials there found most of those losses came among Hispanic families and among the children of immigrants.

More big enrollment drops this year in some of Florida's school districts. The Trump administration there, of course, stripped a lot of Haitian immigrants of their temporary protected status. I spoke about all this with Thomas Dee. He's an economist who studies population and education trends at Stanford University. He thinks what Trump is doing will take a bigger and bigger toll on school districts.

THOMAS DEE: So it's really the effects of both an exodus of existing families and also stopping the inflow that would've normally occurred.

MANN: And here's an important thing. Because public school funding is typically tied to enrollment, these losses could cripple some public schools. Two education think tanks, Bellwether and WestEd, released a study this summer showing the budget impacts of all this could top $11 billion a year.

MARTÍNEZ: What has the Trump administration said about the impact of its immigration policy on schools?

MANN: Yeah, we asked the White House repeatedly for an interview. They haven't responded. In public statements, the Trump administration, A, has celebrated the fact that there are millions fewer foreign residents. That means legal and undocumented immigrants living in the U.S. Trump has described curbing immigration as one of the big policy wins of his second term. But with U.S. birth rates also falling - they hit a new record low last year - that means school districts around the country have to plan for a future with fewer children.

MARTÍNEZ: All right. That's NPR's Brian Mann. Brian, thanks.

MANN: Thank you.
