title: Lawsuit seeks to block ICE from hiding locations of detainees with final removal orders
description:
WASHINGTON — Groups that provide legal services to immigrants filed a lawsuit Wednesday seeking to stop the Trump administration's new policy of hiding the locations of tens of thousands of detainees with final deportation orders.
As of last month, the move affected more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 detainees who were in ICE custody.
ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, have not publicly confirmed the change but have said they are prioritizing people with final removal orders for deportation.
The agencies have denied that they are disappearing detainees, saying they remain free to make phone calls.
“Illegal aliens in detention have several ways to communicate with their family members and lawyers,” DHS said in a statement responding to the lawsuit.
text:
WASHINGTON — Groups that provide legal services to immigrants filed a lawsuit Wednesday seeking to stop the Trump administration's new policy of hiding the locations of tens of thousands of detainees with final deportation orders.

The policy, adopted suddenly last month to expedite deportations, interferes with immigration lawyers’ rights by making it difficult, and sometimes impossible, to locate their clients, according to the lawsuit filed in federal court in Boston. It asks a judge to issue an order blocking the “unlawful and inhumane” change.

“No one should be denied a meaningful opportunity to defend their rights because the government has made it impossible for their lawyer to find them,” said Jacquelynne Bowman, executive director of Greater Boston Legal Services, one of the four groups listed as plaintiffs. “This arbitrary new administrative change leaves hundreds of thousands of people at risk of potentially life-altering consequences without essential legal help."

The lawsuit challenges U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's decision, first reported by The Associated Press, to remove the locations of people facing final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System and to instruct staff not to reveal their whereabouts. As of last month, the move affected more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 detainees who were in ICE custody.

ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, have not publicly confirmed the change but have said they are prioritizing people with final removal orders for deportation. They have also said they are facing a “historic number of injunctions” from courts blocking their efforts. The agencies have denied that they are disappearing detainees, saying they remain free to make phone calls.

“Illegal aliens in detention have several ways to communicate with their family members and lawyers,” DHS said in a statement responding to the lawsuit. “The appropriate process due to an illegal alien with final deportation orders is removal, plain and simple.”

Since 2010, lawyers and family members have used ICE's online system to track detainees as they get moved from facility to facility through ICE's sprawling detention network.

Approximately 1.4 million people living in the U.S. are subject to final orders of removal, which means an immigration judge has ruled they should be deported and the decision has been upheld on appeal or not appealed.

Those individuals still have several options to challenge the conditions of their detention and looming deportations, including asking to reopen proceedings, seeking relief from removal to third countries and challenging violations of their rights. Federal judges have ruled thousands of times that detainees should be released or granted bond hearings.

Since the change went into effect, lawyers have been unable to find clients and potential clients and have spent “significantly more time” tracking down others, the lawsuit says. Calls to ICE, including to its Detention and Removal Information Line, “lead to long wait times on hold, sudden hang-ups, a general lack of information or no answer at all,” it says.

As a workaround, some lawyers have tried to find their clients through an ICE program that schedules legal calls, but only a small percentage of detention centers use it, the lawsuit says. The result has been delayed or missed legal filings and fewer cases taken, according to the organizations.

The lawsuit argues the change violates the Administrative Procedure Act because it was adopted without explanation and the First Amendment, which protects lawyers' ability to advise people of their legal rights and seek prospective clients.

title: Woman seen in KMBC video attempting to set fire to proposed ICE facility sentenced to prison
description:
— The woman seen on KMBC video trying to set fire to a south Kansas City warehouse has been sentenced to prison.
Dara S. O'Connor, 30, was sentenced to 24 months in prison in federal court Wednesday followed by two years of supervised release.
In addition, O'Connor has been ordered to pay $43,612 for damages as a result of using "unregistered destructive devices."
See video of woman attempting to set proposed ICE detention facility on fire: O'Connor previously pleaded guilty to one count of knowingly possessing two destructive devices that were not registered in the National Firearms Registration and Transfer Record related to this incident back in May.
Our crews rolled video as she doused a small section on the building's south side in fluid.
text:
GRANDVIEW, Mo. —

The woman seen on KMBC video trying to set fire to a south Kansas City warehouse has been sentenced to prison.

Dara S. O'Connor, 30, was sentenced to 24 months in prison in federal court Wednesday followed by two years of supervised release. O'Connor was seen on KMBC's video using lighter fluid and other items as a "molotov cocktail" to set fire to the warehouse, which had been proposed as a possible immigration detention center, at 49 Crossing in south Kansas City.

In addition, O'Connor has been ordered to pay $43,612 for damages as a result of using "unregistered destructive devices."

See video of woman attempting to set proposed ICE detention facility on fire:

O'Connor previously pleaded guilty to one count of knowingly possessing two destructive devices that were not registered in the National Firearms Registration and Transfer Record related to this incident back in May.

KMBC 9 News was on the scene reporting that the proposed sale of the warehouse to the U.S. Government had been canceled when reporter Andy Alcock saw a woman drive up, park in a spot near our marked news vehicle, and walk over to the warehouse.

Our crews rolled video as she doused a small section on the building's south side in fluid.

From there, video shows she went to work attempting to use matches to light the fluid on the building's windows and on rocks on the ground outside. She then used a strip of fabric of some type to spread the fire to two additional windows, continuing to spread some type of accelerant to keep the blaze going.

Alcock dialed 911 as our photographer continued to record. At one point, the woman could be seen throwing the plastic bottle of accelerant, later identified as lighter fluid, at the fire, collecting a bag of items she left in the middle of the parking lot, and sitting on the curb outside of the building, all while KMBC's camera rolled.

The woman waited for a period of time before she walked back across the parking lot near where our crews were working, got into a gray four-door passenger vehicle, and drove away.

In a news release Wednesday, authorities noted O'Connor has already paid restitution in this case.

title: New Polling from American University and YouGov Shows Where U.S. Voters Stand on ...
description:
But how important is immigration to voters, really?
Do voters trust ICE to responsibly and humanely manage immigration enforcement?
My colleague at American University, immigration sociologist Ernesto Castañeda and founder of the Immigration Lab, joined me to talk about a new poll that does what few other polls do: dig into the nitty-gritty details of voters’ views on immigration.
Ernesto and I talked at length about the poll’s findings that voters hold more nuanced views of immigration than we often give them credit for.
There remains deep anxiety over repeating the Biden administration’s immigration policies based on a view that Democrats lost the 2024 election because of immigration, but Ernesto isn’t so sure that the data bear this out.
text:
With the election just days away and voters souring on President Trump’s deportation hysteria, this midterm is set to be a referendum on the Republican Party’s failed policies. But how important is immigration to voters, really? What do voters want to see in immigration policy? Do voters trust ICE to responsibly and humanely manage immigration enforcement?

My colleague at American University, immigration sociologist Ernesto Castañeda and founder of the Immigration Lab, joined me to talk about a new poll that does what few other polls do: dig into the nitty-gritty details of voters’ views on immigration. Ernesto is one of the most curious and prolific academics I know, squarely rooting his work in public impact. He frequently coauthors books with collaborators, including Global Pathways to Becoming New Americans, Migration and Migration Status, and Reunited: Family Separation and Central American Youth Migration. This poll reflects that same commitment to putting careful research in front of the public when it can make a difference.

It will not surprise you to know that the poll found large disapproval rates for the president’s handling of the immigration issue, but a sizable contingent of Americans still believes in these policies — a reminder that if everyone inside of your digital and social bubble doesn’t like what’s happening, it might not reflect the full spectrum of views.

Ernesto and I talked at length about the poll’s findings that voters hold more nuanced views of immigration than we often give them credit for. Voters do not view immigrants as a uniform bloc; their level of support for deportation varies based on sympathetic factors such as whether they are working to regularize their status or pursuing humanitarian protection. This doesn’t necessarily mean that voters have an accurate or consistent view of what these things mean, or the fact that, for many immigrants, there simply is no pathway available for bureaucratic reasons beyond their control. Nevertheless, there is at least some growing awareness of the various forms of protection like asylum and TPS that few voters were even aware of about a decade ago.

Ernesto emphasized that this poll shows that politicians, especially Democrats who may have a shot at some reforms in the coming years, should not be afraid of the immigration issue. Immigration is not a losing issue. There remains deep anxiety over repeating the Biden administration’s immigration policies based on a view that Democrats lost the 2024 election because of immigration, but Ernesto isn’t so sure that the data bear this out. Rather, politicians have the opportunity to champion real change boldly with the knowledge that voters are not going to punish them for taking a stand.

Relatedly, much has been written about the impact of immigration enforcement and mass deportation on the economy. That’s an important argument, to be sure. But (and this isn’t the first time I’ve seen this) the data don’t quite bear out the idea that voters are solely self-interested economic actors. The biggest concern people have right now with how our immigration laws are being enforced comes down to moral and ethical concerns over family separation, harm to immigrants themselves, and the lack of humane options for leaving the country.

I’m not really a polling data kind of person, so I found this conversation educational and enlightening — and I think you will, too. Huge thanks to Ernesto for joining me and to the audience who tossed us great questions and comments throughout.

English- and Spanish-language reporters are encouraged to reach out to Ernesto to talk about the findings in this poll. Contact Ernesto here.

title: US: New Hurdles to Having Votes Counted | Human Rights Watch
description:
“The use of the SAVE tool is causing new hurdles for some voters,” said Katherine La Puente, US democracy researcher at Human Rights Watch.
In South Dakota, nearly 6,000 voters have been categorized as federal-only voters as well as 47,000 in Arizona.
Earlier in 2026, Utah audited its voter rolls, finding that it could not verify the citizenship status of over 5,000 registered voters.
Nationwide, CBS News reported, 156 people had been charged with offenses related to voter fraud since January 2025, out of approximately 227 million registered voters.
“Election officials should take steps to eliminate hurdles to vote and ensure that voters feel confident to go to the polls,” La Puente said.
text:
(Washington, DC) – US states’ use of a tool to verify citizenship that is marred by inaccurate and incomplete data is creating new hurdles for the right to vote with the midterm elections only days away, Human Rights Watch said today. The Supreme Court ruled in late September 2026 that states could use the tool, Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE), to screen lists of registered voters for citizenship status, at least for the time being.

“The use of the SAVE tool is causing new hurdles for some voters,” said Katherine La Puente, US democracy researcher at Human Rights Watch. “Sending vaguely worded letters as early voting began or offering federal-only ballots to some registered voters risks a discriminatory impact on people’s right to vote.”

The Trump administration expanded use of the problematic SAVE online system, which previously had been used only for public benefits and was not designed for verifying voter eligibility, in 2025 to now use it for these purposes. Some states have adopted their use of SAVE to verify voter eligibility, and the recent Supreme Court ruling has allowed its use for individualized inquiries. Federal law does not require proof of citizenship when registering to vote, but states have passed these laws requiring proof for state and local races, resulting in bifurcated voter systems.

In Utah, thousands of voters flagged by the SAVE database were sent notification letters over the summer, and in October over 4,000 who didn’t respond were mailed ballots with only federal races.

In South Dakota, nearly 6,000 voters have been categorized as federal-only voters as well as 47,000 in Arizona. In Utah and Arizona, they can provide proof of citizenship and vote in person on Election Day but can’t vote by mail, a method relied on by most voters.

In North Carolina, vaguely worded letters sent to 1,400 registered voters flagged through SAVE asking for proof of citizenship may deter people from going to the polls.

Earlier in 2026, Utah audited its voter rolls, finding that it could not verify the citizenship status of over 5,000 registered voters. It sent them letters indicating that they needed to provide documentary proof of citizenship. Many were older voters who did not need documentation when they registered to vote. Fewer than 2,000 have responded. The others will receive ballots only for federal offices.

In South Dakota, new state laws requiring documentary proof of citizenship and residential addresses quadrupled the voters in the “federal-only” category because they did not submit proof of citizenship or list a mail forwarding service or P.O. Box as their address when they registered. County clerks sent notification letters to these voters that misstated the reasons for their change in status.

After advocates filed a federal lawsuit against the state, officials issued corrected notices in September. South Dakota’s online Voter Information Portal does not tell voters if they are registered as federal-only and changes were only allowed until the state’s October 19 registration deadline.

The North Carolina State Board of Elections sent letters to nearly 1,400 registered voters flagged through SAVE just two days before early voting began on October 15. The board of elections has since confirmed that all citizens are still entitled to vote even as it resolves these queries, and voting rights groups are emphasizing that all those flagged should still be able to vote. But people who got the letters may think they cannot vote or may run into issues at the polls.

In July, with less than a month to the August primary, the director of Alaska’s Division of Elections admitted in a legislative hearing that her office had mailed letters to more than 3,000 voters asking to confirm their citizenship and marked them inactive. Though hundreds have had their registration restored, others will only be able to vote with a questioned ballot, which is only counted once the voter’s eligibility is verified.

Earlier in 2026, a new law took effect in Ohio that requires the Office of the Secretary of State to review its voter registration database at least monthly and direct elections officials to promptly cancel a flagged person’s registration. Citizen groups have raised concerns that this could lead to mistaken removals close to elections, with 75 people removed in September and 90 in October.

In Arizona, the Maricopa County recorder flagged 207 voters identified through SAVE as “not eligible” to vote, which means the voters would stay on the rolls, but would not receive mail-in ballots and would need to use a provisional ballot. Of an initial investigation of 60 of these voters, the Maricopa County attorney determined at least 52 were citizens. But the county did not restore some people’s eligibility until the state attorney general filed suit and a resolution was negotiated. Arizona has required proof of citizenship to register to vote in state and local elections since 2004. Clean Elections Arizona estimates that 47,000 voters are now in this federal-only category.

Naturalized citizens, people who automatically became citizens during childhood when their parents naturalized, US citizens born abroad, and those without easy access to documentation are particularly at risk as a result of these moves. Often, individuals who secured their citizenship through a parent’s naturalization or at birth abroad may not have access to the original documents confirming their status, which they obtained as children.

The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which the United States has ratified, requires governments to ensure the right to vote without unreasonable restrictions or discrimination. The International Convention on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination requires the United States to eliminate racial discrimination and to guarantee the right to vote “without distinction as to race, colour, or national or ethnic origin.”

In its concluding observations for its review of the United States in 2022, the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination expressed concern about practices that “constrain the exercise of the right to vote with a disproportionate impact on people of African descent, indigenous peoples, persons of Hispanic/Latino origin and other ethnic minorities,” and said that the United States should “facilitate access to voting and eliminate unreasonable restrictions to the exercise of the right to vote.”

A survey by the Brennan Center found that more than 9 percent of those polled did not have proof of citizenship readily available, which would mean 21.3 million people nationally if the results are accurate. A study by the Center for American Progress found that fewer than half of US citizens held a valid US passport in 2024. Communities of color, immigrants, low-income, and older people are less likely to have identity documents such as passports or birth certificates.

There is no evidence of widespread, unlawful voting by noncitizens in US elections, and such claims have been disproven in other states like Nevada and Missouri. Nationwide, CBS News reported, 156 people had been charged with offenses related to voter fraud since January 2025, out of approximately 227 million registered voters.

Other statements and actions made by the Trump administration leading up to the elections could deter people from voting. In several states, Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agents have questioned people in their homes about their immigration status and voting history, though a judge recently restricted these operations in nine states. Neither President Donald Trump nor the heads of the DHS and the Federal Bureau of Investigation have been willing to rule out the possibility that federal agents, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, may be at polling places.

“Election officials should take steps to eliminate hurdles to vote and ensure that voters feel confident to go to the polls,” La Puente said.

text:
New Trump administration policy subjects thousands to intentional disappearance, keeping attorneys and families in the dark

October 28, 2026 1:00 pm

Media Contact

125 Broad Street

18th Floor

New York, NY 10004

United States

BOSTON — A group of legal services organizations today filed a lawsuit challenging the federal government’s new policy of hiding the locations of thousands of people detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The policy unlawfully interferes with communication between detainees, their families, and their lawyers.

The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts on behalf of Greater Boston Legal Services, Rian Immigrant Center, Florence Immigrant and Refugee Rights Project, and Amica Center for Immigrant Rights. The groups argue the new policy unlawfully blocks them from locating, communicating with, and providing legal services to their clients and potential clients.

For over 16 years, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security has made the location of detained noncitizens available via its Online Detainee Locator System. In September, DHS abruptly changed course and stopped sharing the location of detained people with final orders of removal, either via the locator service or in direct response to queries from family members or attorneys. This policy of mass disappearance has thrown thousands into an administrative black box without any justification.

The new policy facilitates the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign by making it more difficult to provide detainees with access to attorneys and the judicial system — and thus more difficult to challenge unlawful detention and pursue lawful pathways to remain in the United States. Noncitizens with final orders of removal may still pursue a number of legal remedies to challenge their detention and deportation — but if they cannot access legal counsel or the courts, they may never have a chance to seek these remedies before they are deported.

The lawsuit alleges that ICE’s implementation of this new policy is arbitrary and capricious, and thus a violation of the Administrative Procedure Act. The complaint also alleges that ICE’s policy violates the plaintiffs’ First Amendment rights. Finally, the complaint alleges violations of the Freedom of Information Act because the government failed to publish details of their new policy. The plaintiffs are asking the court to vacate the new policy, and will shortly file a motion to stay the new policy while their case proceeds.

The plaintiffs are represented by the National Immigration Law Center, National Immigration Project, the American Civil Liberties Union, the ACLU of Massachusetts, and Annelise Araujo Law.

The following are statements from the plaintiffs and their legal counsel:

Attorneys representing the plaintiffs: “The Trump administration’s new policy of mass disappearance should send a chill through everybody’s spine. By choosing to hide even the most basic information about thousands of people in its custody, the government is unlawfully blocking their access to legal counsel and the courts, and keeping desperate loved ones in the dark. This shockingly malicious policy was implemented suddenly, without any legal basis or justification, and with immediate, devastating impacts for our clients and the people they serve. The government must reverse course immediately, restore the Online Detainee Locator System, and stop hiding people in its vast network of detention facilities.”

Jacquelynne J. Bowman, executive director of Greater Boston Legal Services: “No one should be denied a meaningful opportunity to defend their rights because the government has made it impossible for their lawyer to find them. Even with representation, navigating the legal system is complex for immigrants facing deportation. This arbitrary new administrative change leaves hundreds of thousands of people at risk of potentially life-altering consequences without essential legal help.”

Jackie Kelley, director of immigration legal services at the Rian Immigrant Center: “We cannot allow the United States government to indefinitely disappear human beings. If we cannot locate our clients, we cannot pursue the relief for which they are legally eligible. The law gives our clients the right to seek protection. This policy obstructs that right when our clients need it most.”

Laura St. John, legal director at the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project: “The Trump administration is disappearing people within the immigration detention system. This should terrify every single one of us. Thousands of people are no longer being shown on the online detainee locator system, making it impossible for attorneys to locate their clients or identify people who might need emergency legal assistance. How can people in detention possibly have access to due process and safety if there is no way for their families or advocates to know where they are being held?”

Aimee Mayer-Salins, deputy program director of legal coordination at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights: “When someone you love is in ICE custody, they shouldn’t simply disappear into a black hole. Families deserve to know where their loved ones are being held, and this lawsuit is about protecting that basic right.”

authors: TIM SULLIVAN Associated Press, NICHOLAS RICCARDI Associated Press, ABC News
description:
That turmoil faded as President Joe Biden tightened immigration enforcement after Trump clamped down even more.
Now any chaos is on American streets, where violent and even deadly clashes have defined a deportation campaign that's designed to fulfill hardliners' goals of uprooting anyone in the country illegally.

text:
MINNEAPOLIS -- When Donald Trump was running for president two years ago, Americans’ television screens were filled with images of migrant chaos. There were tent camps on both sides of the border, caravans of people trudging through Central America and concerns about newcomers overwhelming social services.

That turmoil faded as President Joe Biden tightened immigration enforcement after Trump clamped down even more. Now any chaos is on American streets, where violent and even deadly clashes have defined a deportation campaign that's designed to fulfill hardliners' goals of uprooting anyone in the country illegally.

The shift helps explain why Trump's effort to fulfill his promises has turned into a backlash, undermining one of the core issues that fueled his return to the White House. While Trump maintains some support for his handling of the border, polling shows voters disapprove of his approach to immigration, a striking turnaround that could undermine Republican attempts to maintain control of Congress in the midterms.

“The American people supported strong border security,” said Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat who has become a prominent critic of the administration’s policies. “What they got instead was shredding the Constitution, mass deportations and killing American citizens on the streets of Minneapolis.”

Trump's allies say the president is the victim of his own success.

“The disaster at the border and the impunity of people just walking over and being released into the country was hard to ignore,” said Mark Krikorian, executive director of the Center for Immigration Studies. Trump dramatically reduced illegal border crossings, Krikorian said, “and that’s often politically bad."

Krikorian praised Trump for adopting low profile but highly effective sweeps that have achieved month after month of record arrests. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrested almost 51,000 immigrants in the country illegally in August, according to the Department of Homeland Security, up from 49,000 in July and 43,000 in June. An estimated 660,000 people have been deported in the past fiscal year, according to the Migration Policy Institute, short of the administration’s goal of 1 million annually.

Biden's immigration policies remain a regular target for Republicans this year. Trump said at a recent Florida rally that Democrats let migrants “pour across our borders from all over the world.”

“If they win in the midterms, they'll do it again,” he warned.

In 2024, Trump warned repeatedly of an immigrant “invasion.” “They’re poisoning the blood of our country,” he said of people crossing the border illegally. He insisted, falsely, that immigrants were behind spikes in crime and eating household pets.

Even as Trump drew criticism for his rhetoric, his focus on the issue resonated with voters who had seen illegal immigration soar during the Biden administration, with border arrests from Mexico reaching a record 250,000 in December 2023.

Trump's victory seemed poised to reshape immigration politics. Forty-six Democrats in the House and a dozen in the Senate joined Republicans in voting for the Laken Riley Act, a bill named after a Georgia student killed by a man in the country illegally. The law requires detention without bond for noncitizens accused of murder and other violent crimes.

After Trump took office, he cranked deportations into higher gear. Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident, was one of the people caught up in that net. Despite a court order forbidding it, the administration sent him to his native El Salvador, where he was confined to that country's notorious central prison that was also used to house other Trump deportees.

The U.S. Supreme Court directed the administration to “facilitate” Abrego Garcia's return, and Van Hollen flew to El Salvador to meet with him. Some Democrats questioned the wisdom of confronting Trump on an issue where the president was so popular, the senator recalled. Now his party is more emboldened on the issue.

“We’ve gone from some of that sniping on the sidelines to a clear vote among Democrats to defund ICE,” Van Hollen said.

The early face of the Trump crackdown was top Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino, who swaggered through raids in tactical gear and deployed forces to Los Angeles and Chicago, where he led a helicopter raid on an apartment building.

But Minneapolis was the turning point. More than 2,000 federal officers were sent to the city, and scenes of masked agents spilling from convoys of unmarked vehicles became commonplace. Tens of thousands of protesters took to the streets.

Two U.S. citizens — Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both 37 — were killed during confrontations with agents. In the weeks that followed, the White House pushed aside Bovino and Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

Michael Pretti, Alex's father, said this week that the family is still troubled by the bystander videos of the shooting. He had a holstered gun that he was legally allowed to carry, and none of the footage shows him brandishing the weapon or attacking federal agents in the moments before he was killed.

“I think it haunts many Americans to see a U.S. citizen who was peaceful and in his community shot multiple times on the back, in the back, while on the ground,” he told reporters.

Arrests dropped after the killings, although they eventually returned to record numbers. But the politics became more complicated, and Republicans’ immigration message has fractured.

There are hardliners like U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee, who is vowing more deportations as she runs for governor. And there's Cuban-American Florida Rep. Maria-Elena Salazar, who criticized Trump’s migrant crackdown in a campaign advertisement filmed outside the White House.

Salazar has sponsored legislation that would allow immigrants who are in the country illegally to remain as long as they have otherwise followed the law. Among the sponsors is Republican Rep. Gabe Evans, the grandson of a Mexican immigrant, who is trying to distinguish himself from Trump while running in a Colorado swing district.

In New Hampshire, former Sen. John Sununu, running for an open Senate seat, has been critical of ICE tactics and the agency's use of masks to conceal agents' identities.

Republicans often try to connect immigration to voters' concerns about high prices. Ohio Sen. Jon Husted blasts Democratic opponent Sherrod Brown as someone who “voted to raise your taxes repeatedly and give those tax dollars to illegals.”

“Republicans are trying to turn voters against Democrats because of what Joe Biden did in failing to control the border effectively,” said Frank Sharry, a longtime immigrants' rights activist who consults with the centrist Democratic group Third Way. “So they’re trying to define Democrats as being for open borders and not serious about removing criminals.”

But that comes as many Democratic candidates are shifting away from Biden-era messaging about immigration.

In Texas, Senate candidate James Talarico calls himself a “border security Democrat” who wants to hire more Border Patrol officers and increase the use of surveillance technology.

Talarico criticizes many of Trump’s immigration policies as wasteful, but doesn’t hold back when it comes to criticizing the last Democratic president.

“Joe Biden and his administration failed us on our southern border,” he said in a July press conference in a Texas county on the Mexico border.

Even some of the most liberal Democratic candidates, like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, are careful to note that they want strong borders.

“I don’t know of a candidate who’s in a swing race who’s saying anything other than ‘We’ve got to secure the border’ and ‘We’ve got to remove criminals,’” Sharry said.

___

Riccardi reported from Denver. Associated Press writer Aaron Kessler in Washington contributed to this report.

text:
A recent Pew Research Center survey finds that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is by far the most unpopular federal agency, easily outstripping even the widely despised IRS. According to Pew, 56% of Americans disapprove of ICE, compared to only 35% who approve. That's substantially worse than the IRS (which is disapproved by only a 46-37 margin).

Other recent surveys show growing public support for abolishing ICE. For example, a July YouGov poll indicates that 48% support abolition, compared to 40% who oppose it. Another survey, conducted in March of this year, showed a similar 50-39 margin in favor of abolition.

The fact that ICE is unpopular doesn't by itself prove the agency should be abolished. Having written a book and many other publications on widespread public ignorance about government policy, I would be the last to argue that popularity is a good metric of a policy's - or an agency's - merit. But, in this case, public opinion is right. As I explained in an August 2025 article in The Hill, and a follow-up piece for the Boston Globe, (non-paywalled version here), ICE's many abuses do indeed justify abolishing it. And the case for doing so has been strengthened by more recent events, such as the brutal killing of two US citizens in Minnesota.

While ICE abuses have been exacerbated by the policies of the second Trump Administration, many predate it, and are inherent in the entire enterprise of mass deportation.

As explained in my article in The Hill, abolishing ICE would not completely end interior deportations. But it would make them heavily dependent on the cooperation of state and local governments, thereby strengthening constitutional federalism and reducing incentives for abuse, at least to a significant degree.

In that article, I also explain how support for abolition be further bolstered by combining it with shifting ICE funds to state and local law enforcement. This undermines the principal political obstacle to abolition: the fear that getting rid of ICE would increase crime. Transferring the funds to state and local police would help defuse such concerns, win the support of law enforcement agencies, and foster genuine reductions in violent and property crimes; social science evidence shows that putting more police on the streets has that effect, whereas deportations do not.

text:
Groups that provide legal services to immigrants filed a lawsuit Wednesday seeking to stop the Trump administration’s new policy of hiding the locations of tens of thousands of detainees with final deportation orders.

The policy, adopted suddenly last month to expedite deportations, interferes with immigration lawyers’ rights by making it difficult, and sometimes impossible, to locate their clients, according to the lawsuit filed in federal court in Boston. It asks a judge to issue an order blocking the “unlawful and inhumane” change.

“No one should be denied a meaningful opportunity to defend their rights because the government has made it impossible for their lawyer to find them,” said Jacquelynne Bowman, executive director of Greater Boston Legal Services, one of the four groups listed as plaintiffs. “This arbitrary new administrative change leaves hundreds of thousands of people at risk of potentially life-altering consequences without essential legal help.”

The lawsuit challenges U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s decision, first reported by The Associated Press, to remove the locations of people facing final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System and to instruct staff not to reveal their whereabouts. As of last month, the move affected more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 detainees who were in ICE custody.

ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, didn’t immediately respond to a message seeking comment on the lawsuit.

The agencies have not publicly confirmed the change, but have said they are prioritizing people with final removal orders for deportation. They have also said they are facing a “historic number of injunctions” from courts blocking their efforts. The agencies have denied that they are disappearing detainees, saying they remain free to make phone calls.

Since 2010, lawyers and family members have used the online system to track detainees as they get moved from facility to facility through ICE’s sprawling detention network.

Approximately 1.4 million people living in the U.S. are subject to final orders of removal, which means an immigration judge has ruled they should be deported and the decision has been upheld on appeal or not appealed.

Those individuals still have several options to challenge the conditions of their detention and looming deportations, including asking to reopen proceedings, seeking relief from removal to third countries and challenging violations of their rights. Federal judges have ruled thousands of times that detainees should be released or granted bond hearings.

Since the change went into effect, lawyers have been unable to find clients and potential clients and have spent “significantly more time” tracking down others, the lawsuit says. Calls to ICE, including to its Detention and Removal Information Line, “lead to long wait times on hold, sudden hang-ups, a general lack of information or no answer at all,” it says.

As a workaround, some lawyers have tried to find their clients through an ICE program that schedules legal calls, but only a small percentage of detention centers use it, the lawsuit says. The result has been delayed or missed legal filings and fewer cases taken, according to the organizations.

The lawsuit argues the change violates the Administrative Procedure Act because it was adopted without explanation and the First Amendment, which protects lawyers’ ability to advise people of their legal rights and seek prospective client

A federal judge has denied an unprecedented, emergency request by the Department of Justice to segregate thousands of California ballots in the midterm elections.

The Justice Department wants California election officials to stop processing ballots pertaining to 20,000 individuals that federal officials say are "likely" noncitizens.

State and local officials in California have countered that the DOJ's list of "likely" noncitizens is unreliable, with a preliminary analysis by Los Angeles County showing that many on the list do not have active voter registrations. The officials also claim that setting aside ballots just days before Election Day, when voting and processing mailed ballots are already underway, would be unlawful and infeasible and would disenfranchise eligible voters.

In his 26-page ruling issued Wednesday evening, U.S. District Judge David Carter, a Clinton appointee, denied the Justice Department's request for a temporary restraining order to stop processing the ballots in question.

"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," he wrote.

Carter also expressed concern about taking action that could disenfranchise eligible voters and create chaos.

"Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred," Carter wrote at the conclusion of his order. "If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process."

The judge said that the federal government can address the issue by continuing to indict people for the crime of illegally voting as noncitizens. DOJ officials say in the last two months they have charged dozens of people for registering or voting without being a U.S. citizen.

The DOJ's lawsuit in California, which was filed Oct. 15, is among a flurry of unprecedented actions the department has waged in states close to Election Day, raising alarms about federal interference in state election procedures.

Like in California, on Monday federal prosecutors asked Washington state election officials to review a list of 400 registered voters the DOJ believes are likely noncitizens. And last week, the DOJ filed an unusual lawsuit in Alaska that seeks to stop the state from certifying the results in its Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses due to votes for a longshot candidate with a similar name who is accused of being a spoiler candidate.

In California's most recent motion to the court, state Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, asked the judge to take into account the circumstances of DOJ's demand. "This litigation is a precursor to further interference here in California," Bonta wrote. "The Court must not be drawn into this chilling degradation of democratic values and constitutional principles."

The Department of Justice is expected to appeal Carter's denial, and the matter could ultimately wind up before the U.S. Supreme Court.

The DOJ has argued the issue is urgent since ballots are already being processed. Once signatures are verified on returned mail ballot envelopes, the ballots are separated from their envelopes to retain voter confidentiality and it then becomes impossible to retrieve an ineligible ballot.

Federal prosecutors have argued that votes by noncitizens dilute the votes of U.S. citizens. Voting by noncitizens has been shown by audits and investigations to be extremely rare.

The accuracy of the DOJ's list of "likely" noncitizens is still an ongoing matter of dispute.

A Los Angeles County analysis of a small sample of people on the DOJ's list found that a significant portion had said in records they were born in the U.S. But U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services senior official Nicolas Bartell contested that in recent court filings, writing that his office's review of those individuals found none were U.S.-born.

Bartell did acknowledge the review found four of those people "might have a claim to U.S. citizenship."

He also provided the court additional details about the federal government's methodology in creating the list in recent court filings.

But University of Delaware political scientist Kassra Oskooi, who has been tapped as an expert witness by voting rights groups who are intervening in the case, responded in his own declaration to the court that he believes USCIS's matching protocol "is likely to be unreliable."

California’s Public Utilities Commission will decide on Thursday whether to claw back or keep $37.5 million in grant funding meant to bring fast, reliable internet to Catalina Island.

The island is home to more than 4,000 residents, and it draws thousands of tourists each year. Its slow, unreliable internet connection affects everything from remote learning to emergency response.

Lance Ware is CEO of AVX Networks, the company awarded the grant from the CPUC in December 2025. He told LAist host Nereida Moreno that the island depends on a very limited wireless internet link.

“When the town is busy, for instance, a cruise ship comes … the internet just gets crippled along with all the telephone services,” Ware explained.

Months after AVX Networks was awarded the grant, CPUC staff accused the company in July 2026 of breaking federal spending rules, citing insufficient justification and documentation for invoices.

The proposed plan would build the fiber-optic network under the San Pedro Channel from two points on Catalina Island to landings near Huntington Beach. Those cables will then connect to the Middle Mile Broadband Network in Stanton.

Where do things stand today?

CPUC staff allege that AVX Networks violated several program requirements, according to records.

“Since the award, AVX Networks has not shown itself to have the requisite administrative, technical, and operational capacity to deliver on its project, and AVX Networks has failed to comply with the terms and conditions of its award,” the CPUC agenda item records state.

Ware said he “vehemently disagrees” with those statements.

“There are allegations on things in there that do not make sense to us in that we've had no due process or cure and correct period to address,” Ware said.

What’s next?

If the commission terminates the contract and pulls the funding, Ware said the project will be delayed, but not stopped.

“This is not curtains down for us,” Ware added. “It's gonna take longer, and we'll have to find some other way to finance it, but we certainly haven't given up.”

Southern Californians are feeling squeezed by the rising costs of, well, everything. And now their local governments are asking for more money, too.

By LAist’s count, more than 30 cities or districts in Los Angeles and Orange counties are asking residents to approve tax measures on Election Day, Nov. 3, citing stagnant revenues that haven’t kept pace with the rising costs of insurance, maintenance and infrastructure projects, and employee pensions. Big cities, suburbs and small towns are all facing multimillion-dollar budget deficits and asking residents to open their wallets — or potentially see deep cuts to basic city services.

The list of local measures on ballots from Culver City to San Clemente includes sales taxes, hotel taxes, business taxes, parcel taxes and utility taxes. Some ballot measures would extend or increase existing taxes while others are brand-new.

Much of the answer to why so many tax measures are on the ballot lies in Proposition 13, which capped property taxes in 1978.

Before Prop. 13, cities and counties relied on property taxes for nearly all of their revenue. In the decades since, they’ve increasingly turned to other types of taxes. Hotel and utility taxes, for example, were essentially nonexistent before the mid-1970s, and sales taxes represented a small sliver of revenue. Even as these taxes have grown, they’ve struggled to replace property tax revenue.

How Proposition 13 reshaped local taxes

Before 1978, California municipalities could raise taxes without voter approval. But in addition to capping property taxes, Proposition 13 also changed the rules for other taxes. Section 4 of Proposition 13 states that any special taxes (which are taxes designated for a specific use) must be approved by two-thirds of voters. A later proposition passed in 1986 requires that general taxes be approved by a simple majority of voters. General taxes are general purpose funds that cities can allocate as they please.

The rules could change again this year with Proposition 43, which would raise the share of votes needed to pass local special tax measures proposed by citizens to two-thirds. Currently, citizen-led special tax initiatives only need to win a simple majority.

Despite what the Nov. 3 ballot might suggest, sales tax measures are actually becoming less common, according to Michael Coleman, author of the California Local Government Finance Almanac. “More and more governments have started to exhaust the capacity for that. There’s a limit in how much you can do both legally and in terms of the tolerance of voters,” Coleman said.

State law caps the maximum combined local and county sales tax rate, and many Southern California cities are already at or near that cap, Coleman said. And sales tax isn’t as reliable as it used to be, amid the broader retail downturn and shift to a service-based economy (most services aren’t taxable in California).

All of that means cities are increasingly turning to “ticky-tacky, peculiar taxes” to come up with revenue, according to Kirk Stark, a professor of tax law and policy at UCLA.

The “conventional tax instruments” — property, income and sales taxes — are all limited by state law, Stark said. “Local governments that are hoping to satisfy demand for any kind of public expenditure have to turn to other, less conventional sources of revenue.”

This year, cities are asking Southern Californians to say yes to a wide range of taxes. Below, we look at three examples in South Gate, Orange and Diamond Bar.

South Gate: A utility users tax

South Gate is asking voters to approve something less common: a utility users tax, or UUT for short. If Measure SG is approved, the 8% tax would be added to bills for utilities such as electricity, water, natural gas, cable and phone service. The tax would bring in an estimated $10.4 million per year.

The city is facing a potential fiscal emergency and a $9.4 million budget deficit. Earlier this year, South Gate began cutting back services, including eliminating its crossing guard program and assigning fewer police officers per shift.

At a City Council meeting on the tax measure earlier this year, several residents spoke against the measure, with some calling the deficit a result of potential financial mismanagement that shouldn’t be pushed onto residents. Others said the monthly costs would simply add a new burden to already tight budgets.

“Being a homeowner here for the past 13 years, I have seen my utilities go up as well as the cost of living, my insurance for my house, and my car insurance go up. I believe there’s got to be a way to fix this problem without the UUT measure,” one resident told the City Council.

“I’m extremely frustrated that you now want to do electricity, water, sewer, cable, cell phone, gas. ... That hurts us. You’re passing that on to us, and that is absolutely not acceptable,” said another.

The only other utility users tax on the ballot in Los Angeles or Orange counties this year is in San Marino, where residents will decide whether to extend the city’s existing 5% utility users tax, which is set to expire on March 31, 2027, and increase it to 6%. Last year, the tax provided almost $2.2 million in revenue. As of 2021, a total of 162 out of 540 California cities and counties had a utility users tax, according to Coleman’s California Local Government Finance Almanac.

Orange: Hotel and sales taxes could go up

Most people don’t book a hotel in their own city. That’s made hotel taxes an easier pill to swallow for voters, since the tax is mostly levied on visitors.

The city of Orange is asking voters to approve Measure J, which wouldraise the hotel tax from 10% to 14%. Orange is one of 10 cities across Los Angeles and Orange counties where voters will decide in November whether to increase or establish a local hotel tax, also known as a “transient occupancy tax.”

Orange residents will also vote on a 1-cent sales tax measure, as the city projects a $27.6 million deficit that it calls “one of the largest financial challenges in the city’s history.” The sales tax is expected to bring in $37 million annually, and the hotel tax would add $3 million.

Diamond Bar: A new 1-cent sales tax

Diamond Bar voters will decide on Measure Q, a 1% local sales tax that would add a penny per dollar to purchases of taxable items. The city estimates the tax will bring in an additional $6 million annually, which could help plug a projected budget deficit of $5 million a year by 2030.

“The city’s challenge is simple: costs for city services are going up faster than revenues,” states Diamond Bar’s fact sheet on the measure, which cites rising public safety costs and $100 million in infrastructure and maintenance needs.

Several other cities have local sales tax measures on the ballot, including Santa Ana’s 1.5% sales tax extension and Los Angeles’ sales tax increase for the Los Angeles Fire Department, Measure FD.

“There’s a variety because circumstances among these local governments vary. The types of economies among governments vary, the local conditions, even the preferences for what type of revenue measure or tax measure might work varies,” Coleman said. “A local government that’s looking at one of these is going to look at a number of different options and consider what might be most palatable to the voters in their community.”

What’s on your ballot?

Our LAist Voter Game Plan is here to help guide you through the Nov. 3 election with guides to races across Los Angeles and Orange counties — and that long list of state propositions — to help you cast a ballot that’s in line with your own personal beliefs and values.

But the one thing we don’t do? We don’t tell you how to vote. That part is left up to you.

You can find it all at LAist.com/Vote.

At the height of the Los Angeles fires in 2025, millions of residents were exposed in a 24-hour period to toxic lead levels from smoke that were 80 times higher than the typical background level, according to a new study.

Researchers from the California Institute of Technology compared the chemical composition of smoke from the Eaton Fire with that of a wildfire and found that the urban plume had more lead, arsenic and halogens (which include chlorine and bromine) linked to burning vehicles, building materials and electronics.

“The main, key finding is really that wildfire smoke is very different fundamentally from the urban smoke,” said Nga Lee “Sally” Ng, an author of the study published Wednesday in the journal Science Advances. With the new technology they used to measure what was in the smoke, they were able to “actually see the very detailed component of these particles that we are breathing.”

Co-author Haroula Baliaka said understanding the different chemical compositions of smoke from an urban versus a wildland fire helps bridge a missing gap in research. Wildfires are growing larger, more intense, faster-moving and more frequent largely because of drier and warmer weather associated with human-caused climate change. As urban growth and climate change push more fires into cities, researchers said monitoring and emergency response will have to adapt.

Ed Avol, professor emeritus in the Keck School of Medicine at the University of Southern California who has researched the health effects of air pollution for decades, said significant exposure to heavy metals is consistent with what he’d expect, “but certainly surprising because we haven’t been able to document this sort of thing.”

“One of the real advantages of this study is that it had the opportunity to make measurements sort of hour-by-hour across the sampling network. And typically we make measurements of airborne particulates and so forth a couple of times a week, at best,” said Avol, who wasn’t involved in the study.

Thousands of structures burned, releasing toxic chemicals

The two wind-whipped infernos in Altadena and the Pacific Palisades that ignited on Jan. 7, 2025, killed at least 31 people and destroyed more than 16,000 structures, mostly homes, and everything in them — cars, paint, furniture, chemicals under sinks and more. Millions of people were exposed to smoke, which across the entire United States has been linked to tens of thousands of deaths annually. A recent study found that metal mixtures in the leftover smoke, ash and debris from the deadly 2023 Maui wildfires were harmful to the lung health of people living nearby long after the burning ended.

During the fires, researchers measured trace elements of fine particulate matter, or PM2.5, every hour reported by instruments in the Atmospheric Science and Chemistry mEasurement NeTwork ( ASCENT ), a relatively new network of air quality monitors across the U.S. that measures the size and chemical composition of these particulates in real time. Ng said ASCENT is the U.S.'s first measurement network able to measure the chemical composition of airborne particles in real time.

Researchers were able to see what chemicals were in the smoke, track how its composition changed over the fire’s course, and distinguish emissions coming from burning structures. From there, they estimated how many people across Los Angeles were exposed to the heavy metals, particularly lead, during the fire’s first days.

They compared the typical value of lead before the fires and the chemical makeup of smoke from a 2024 fire in Riverside County that burned mostly vegetation with data from the Eaton Fire plume. Contrasted with the wildfire smoke, the plume from the LA fire contained 50 times more lead, three times more arsenic, and seven times more halogens. At the peak of burning, about 7 million people were exposed for 24 hours to lead levels more than 80 times what’s typical.

Lead is a neurotoxin that can stunt children’s development, lower IQ scores and increase blood pressure in adults. Scientists still don’t know how short-term, high exposure to lead impacts human health. Arsenic exposure is associated with various cancers.

Yaguang Wei, assistant professor in the department of environmental medicine at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai who researches the health impacts of air pollution, wildfire smoke and severe weather, said their findings reinforced some conclusions of a recent study he co-authored that found, in part, that PM2.5 from wildfire smoke was more toxic than particulates from other sources.

“I think their findings are not surprising,” said Wei, who was not involved in the study. When fires burn properties, they’re also burning “a lot of lead on your wall paint and the plastics and electronics and those are very toxic” when they burn, he said.

Monitoring, policies and emergency response need to adapt, experts say

Wei said the study has “important policy implications.” He thinks governments should take stronger actions to protect public health during these fires by investing in more wildfire monitoring and public alerts, and having more prescribed fires.

For Avol, the study is a reminder of our “strange and increasingly dangerous new world” where urban and wildland intersect — and increasingly catch fire.

“It reminds us to be cautious and be concerned and, you know, think about what we can do to minimize this. We’re not going to stop using all these materials containing metals and halogens and so forth in our homes,” he said. “How do we protect people from being exposed to that?”

text:
Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.

The leak includes names, work addresses and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work they do for each agency.

Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted by leaks or hacks.

A DHS spokesperson said the agency is "aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively."

"We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected," the spokesperson added.

"We will update the public when more information is available."

The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was made public online. A group called the Department of Peace accessed the information from DHS, while journalist and cybersecurity researcher maia crimew alongside the website Distributed Denial of Secrets put it online.

The information was put in a database named Icepick.

Most of the agents included, more than 21,000 of them, work for CBP, according to the data. Nearly 6,600 work for ICE.

Other records show agents with Homeland Security Investigations, the Federal Protective Service and even people working for the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

The leaked information also included dozens of previously unknown operation names, the agents that led and worked on those operations, and some of the technology they used in their work, including tech provided by Cellbrite and Palantir.

The groups wrote in an online statement that the the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets.

"The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in it's simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.

BlueLeaks refers to a massive leak of US police data in 2020, data from which DDoSecrets also hosted.

A spokesperson for the Department of Peace pointed directly at actions by ICE agents for the groups work to hack DHS records.

"On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was 'turning up the heat'. This is what happens to ICE when you do that," the spokesperson wrote on Wednesday.

Mullin in March became Secretary of Homeland Security.

The Department of Peace said it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.

Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.

A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."

Last month, the FBI was hacked by a group called ShinyHunters, which took personal information about thousands of agents.

In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt.

Public backlash to US immigration enforcement has been building as the Trump Administration has pushed a huge increase in arrests and deportations of people suspected of being in the country illegally.

Immigration operations this year have repeatedly turned violent, with ICE agents shooting at more than two dozen people and killing at least nine people.

text:
As the Trump administration pursues mass deportations, a former inspector general for the Homeland Security Department argued that the current oversight structure for Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities is obfuscating unsafe conditions.

“This is essentially a Potemkin village of reports that are put up for largely disinformation value to try to explain to the public that there is no problem when in fact there's significant problems in all these facilities that need to get fixed,” said John Roth during a webinar Tuesday put on by the Project on Government Oversight.

The webinar focused on an August report by the nonprofit’s news reporting division that found the percentage of detention facilities receiving the highest inspection rating by ICE’s Office of Detention Oversight “nearly tripled since fiscal 2024 as of July 23, after declining by 61% between fiscal 2022 and 2024.” René Kladzyk, one of the researchers behind the analysis, provided an update during the event that, by the end of fiscal 2026, about 71.5% of inspected facilities scored a “superior” rating.

At the same time, the average daily population of noncitizens detained by ICE increased by 71% between January 2025 and July 2026, and 33 people in ICE custody died in 2025, which was a more-than-two-decade high.

“You don't have to be a former IG or an investigative reporter to understand that it's facially incredible that the number of perfect reports are going up at the same time that we are facing unprecedented detentions in these facilities,” Roth said.

Roth criticized DHS for weakening internal watchdogs, such as DHS’ Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties and Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman, through staff cuts and shutting down their operations.

The former IG recommended that Congress could strengthen oversight of ICE detention facilities by:

Enacting a uniform inspection standards for such facilities, as ICE currently develops its own criteria.

Shielding internal oversight bodies from influence by the administration.

Encouraging external oversight, including from IGs and third-party organizations.

“You need a combination of both internal oversight, which has meaningful reporting to people who are decision makers and meaningful power, as well as independent oversight, because without that, then you're not going to have the kind of oversight that you need for a high-risk system like this,” Roth said.

He noted that the DHS IG currently performs unannounced inspections of ICE detention facilities, but the former watchdog argued that that isn’t comprehensive enough.

“There has to be a deeper dive into the root causes as to why it is that we're where we are,” Roth said. “Is this because we are not holding the contractors responsible? Is this a funding issue? Is this a technical issue? Is this a legal issue? What is the fundamental root problem of why we can't detain people humanely and in accordance with specific standards?”

ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

On Monday, the DHS IG reported, based on an unannounced inspection of a since-closed ICE facility in El Paso, Texas, that the agency held detainees in a short-term environment for an average of 36 hours longer than standards provided. The watchdog also found that the facility did not comply with other standards regarding “use of force, personal property, hygiene and food and beverage.”

The DHS IG also reported in September that an ICE facility in Florida, which was nicknamed “Alligator Alcatraz” and has shut down, “did not provide detainees with sufficient living space, creating cramped conditions for detainees who spent most of their time in their housing units, which may harm detainees’ physical and mental health.”

And the Government Accountability Office found in June that an immigration detention facility in Texas experienced “gaps in medical services, the loss of a loaded firearm and unsanitary conditions, among other issues” that “posed serious risks to the safety and security of both detained noncitizens and staff in the facility.”

Kladzyk, the POGO investigator, emphasized that ICE detention oversight has “life-and-death implications.”

“I think it's important to think about ICE oversight in those terms,” she said. “If some of these problems had been addressed earlier, maybe we would not be seeing the current numbers we're seeing in terms of deaths in custody.”

text:
The Trump administration has offered few specifics on how it created the list of alleged noncitizens on California’s voter rolls, which is at the center of its lawsuit against the state.

But the list appears to have been created using a deeply flawed process recently disclosed by a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) whistleblower, court filings in the lawsuit suggest.

That matters because the DHS process described by the whistleblower scrutinized voters nationwide, not just Californians. As a result, it would strongly indicate that the Trump administration has lists — with all the flaws the whistleblower described — on several states, and potentially all states.

The whistleblower said the investigation — called the “Unlawful Voter Initiative” — posed a particular risk for Californians: They could face disenfranchisement and even criminal investigations because their state has uniquely rigorous data privacy protections, meaning DHS would be working with less detailed information about voters.

Now, that concern appears to have come true.

This month, the Department of Justice (DOJ) sent California elections officials a DHS-produced list allegedly containing the names, birthdates and addresses of around 20,000 likely noncitizens registered to vote in the state. It then filed an extraordinary lawsuit to block California officials from counting the affected voters’ ballots and pressed charges against 28 people on the list.

And growing evidence suggests the DOJ suit against California is just the start.

Making the list

At the center of both the initiative and DHS’s California list is the Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate (FDNS), a specialized unit in DHS’s U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).

This unit normally investigates suspected immigration fraud and national security threats. But beginning in August, the Trump administration reassigned much of the directorate to hunt for evidence for President Donald Trump’s baseless claims that illegal voting by noncitizens is rampant in U.S. elections.

To that end, the whistleblower said Homeland Security leaders tasked FDNS immigration officers with finding potential matches between hundreds of thousands of voters on state registration lists and people in federal immigration records.

If someone’s registration or voting data could be linked to an immigration record, officers were ordered to create a law enforcement report, called a TECS record, against that person. The record was then passed on to Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. TECS records could initiate additional scrutiny against flagged individuals, including possible criminal proceedings.

DHS’s California list appears to have been created the same way.

In court declarations, FDNS Associate Director Nicolas Bartell said “immigration officials who are trained to determine citizenship status” manually reviewed California’s public registration roll to match voters with immigration records.

After the review, Bartell said, “FDNS compiled a refined list of individuals who the agency believes are highly likely to be noncitizen aliens registered to vote in the 2026 federal election in California and then FDNS provided HSI with the refined list of individuals.”

Bartell said FDNS first “enhanced” California’s “raw voting record data” with personal information that the agency obtained from LexisNexis’ Accurint, a large-scale analytics platform that aggregates billions of public records to create highly personal data profiles on people.

Bartell’s Accurint disclosure directly aligns with the whistleblower’s report. Because public voting records generally do not include unique personal identifiers — like Social Security and driver’s license numbers — and may not include people’s registration date and voting history, the anonymous official said DHS could not match voting data alone to immigration records or determine whether someone illegally registered or voted.

To fill this gap, the whistleblower said DHS used Accurint and Thomson Reuters’ CLEAR, a similar analytics platform, to get people’s personal information and voting records and combined that data with state registration records.

Limited data, unlawful actions

But the DOJ’s disclosures omit the numerous ways the administration’s processes for identifying noncitizens on state voter rolls could wrongly flag someone as a noncitizen — shortcomings the whistleblower detailed.

The official said FDNS officers were assigned a strict quota of 40 reviews a day, giving them only a few minutes to resolve complex questions of identity and citizenship to determine whether someone should be flagged as an unlawful voter. And agents were required to produce TECS records against people even when they strongly doubted the accuracy of the data they were cross-referencing.

California posed an additional challenge, the whistleblower said. Because of the state’s privacy rules, DHS obtained the state’s voter data from unclear sources.

As a result, agents were reluctant to file TECS records against Californians because they had limited means to corroborate the data. Still, FDNS agents were required to assume the voter records were factual — even if they conflicted with other data available to them.

“The result is that a significant number of TECS records, potentially thousands or tens of thousands, will be created against California residents based on data that an officer may have good reason to believe is unreliable or inaccurate without corroboration,” the whistleblower warned.

With other states, FDNS agents used voting data from Accurint to corroborate DHS-provided data. But the database was less useful in California: FDNS agents could not obtain Californians’ specific voting data — like their registration date or voting history — from the tool, because the state’s election code explicitly bars companies from collecting and selling its election-related data.

The only way agents could verify DHS-provided registration records, the whistleblower said, was by using people’s personal information, including their Social Security numbers, to access individual voting records through California’s registration portal. However, doing so meant FDNS agents were essentially impersonating people and potentially violating the state’s privacy laws.

When agents raised concerns about the legality of searches, USCIS leaders said individual officers “would not be personally liable for conducting the searches when they are done as part of their official duties and properly documented,” the official said.

Calling citizens noncitizens

While the whistleblower was particularly concerned that the initiative would erroneously flag naturalized citizens as noncitizens, Los Angeles County’s analysis of a 7,035-person sample of DHS’s list found that roughly 1 in 4 people appeared to be natural-born citizens who marked the U.S. as their birthplace.

It’s unclear why birthright citizens would appear on the DOJ’s list. Because natural-born citizens acquire citizenship at birth, it’s highly unlikely they would interact with DHS in a way that would generate a factual record associated with them that could be matched with California’s voter data.

DHS officials have pushed back on Los Angeles’ analysis. But according to the whistleblower, FDNS agents were required to watch a training video that acknowledged Social Security numbers associated with voters “may not be accurate” and told agents not to rely solely on the numbers.

The video also reportedly said that U.S. citizens sponsoring their foreign-born spouses’ immigration cases could lead to further mix-ups with Social Security numbers.

“In other words, the current process is knowingly sweeping known US citizens in as potentially “unlawful voters,” the whistleblower said.

Just the beginning?

There are also signs the process described by the whistleblower is being used against other states.

On Oct. 26, Charles Neil Floyd, the acting U.S. attorney in Seattle, sent Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs a letter demanding that his office set aside potential ballots from 405 people whom DHS has flagged as noncitizens.

At a press conference that day, Floyd broadly described how DHS identified the alleged noncitizens — an account that overlapped with both the DOJ’s explanation of the California list and the whistleblower’s account.

“Let me explain our methodology. DHS has obtained publicly available lists of registered voters in Washington. Those lists are compared with DHS information to identify registered voters who are not citizens,” Floyd said. “We then further investigate to see if that person actually cast ballots in Washington.”

That strongly suggests this process can be applied to any other state the Trump administration decides to target.
