text:
Last month, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced it was establishing an office to provide public defender–style legal representation to unaccompanied immigrant minors. For teens and younger children who crossed the U.S. southern border without an adult relative and later appeared in immigration court, HHS would try to provide a lawyer to speak for them.

Many immigration advocates aren’t impressed.

While HHS said it was creating a new division within its Office of Refugee Resettlement to provide representation to minors, that’s the same office responsible for overseeing the care and custody of unaccompanied minors. And those minors are children the Trump administration is seeking court permission to deport. Critics say the setup creates an inherent conflict of interest.

“This is the agency that’s detaining them as part of an administration whose job it is to try to remove these children,” said Jennifer Podkul, chief of global policy and advocacy for KIND—Kids in Need of Defense.

The maneuver is just the latest in a series of steps the Trump administration has taken that many immigration advocates say make it harder for unaccompanied immigrant children to obtain representation—and therefore appropriate protections against wrongful deportation—in immigration court. But the Trump administration argued that it’s actually trying to assist children who cross the border without adult relatives. Meanwhile, some experts blame Congress for failing to better protect unaccompanied minors in federal immigration law.

Respondents in immigration courts, unlike defendants in traditional federal courts, don’t have a right to an attorney. But they can receive attorney representation either through a pro bono program or for a fee.

Having representation increases an immigrant’s chances of staying in the United States by up to 366%, according to a Vera Institute of Justice report focused on Chicago-area immigrants. The Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC) reported in 2015 that representation in immigration court cases for women with children led to a 14-fold increase in their chances of being able to stay in the United States.

“There are a large number of pro bono providers and what we call ‘low bono’ providers—they will offer legal services, in particular to unaccompanied alien children, for a low or reduced cost,” said Andrew Arthur, a former immigration judge and a current senior fellow at the Center for Immigration Studies. “And, in addition, a lot of major law firms will have their junior associates, mid-level associates, provide pro bono legal services.”

But sometimes, respondents navigating immigration courts don’t have a lawyer representing them as the government tries to deport them. And sometimes, those respondents are children.

The federal government defines unaccompanied alien children as individuals who are under the age of 18 without a parent or legal guardian in the United States. The Pew Research Center estimated in 2014 that most unaccompanied alien children who were arriving in the United States were between the ages of 13 and 17, though around 16% were age 12 and under. Since fiscal year 2019, more than 60% of the unaccompanied alien children in the Office of Refugee Resettlement’s care each fiscal year have been 15 or older, according to data from ORR.

Days after President Donald Trump took office in 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice rescinded Biden-era administration guidance ordering immigration judges to conduct court cases with minors in a “child-friendly” manner. That move reinstituted previous guidance that simply told immigration judges to be aware that minors could require special considerations.

From 2005 to 2017, roughly 36% of the nearly 300,000 children who appeared in immigration court didn’t have an attorney, TRAC reported. Roughly 7 out of every 10 children who didn’t have an attorney during that time were ultimately deported.

But the federal government isn’t technically responsible for making sure young immigrants have legal representation, Arthur explained. “To the degree that this is happening, it’s because the NGOs and the organizations that used to provide those services aren’t doing it anymore,” he said.

Arthur argued that unaccompanied alien children generally don’t arrive in the United States accidentally, but family members often pay smugglers fees of around $7,000 to bring them in. Still, since 2008, the federal government has provided funding each year to provide attorneys for unaccompanied immigrant children.

Jennifer Podkul from KIND pointed to hundreds of millions of dollars that Congress has annually allocated to the HHS Office of Refugee Resettlement, which then contracted with private groups that provided legal services.

ORR primarily worked with the Acacia Center for Justice, Podkul explained. The Acacia Center then subcontracted with roughly 100 organizations such as KIND through its Unaccompanied Children Program, working with about 26,000 unaccompanied minors.

But even with the federal money, many unaccompanied minors navigating the immigration court system throughout the years never received legal assistance, Podkul said. “Even in the best of times, it was still like less than half the kids had lawyers,” she said.

And in March 2025, the federal support disappeared when the Trump administration terminated much of the Unaccompanied Children Program. Advocates sued the administration over the decision, alleging it violated federal law. The next month, a judge ordered the federal government to continue funding the program, and the Trump administration reinstated the contract accordingly.

An ORR spokesperson explained to WORLD that the office realized last year that, depending on the week, between 40% and 70% of the unaccompanied alien children in its care didn’t have a lawyer. ORR said it asked the Acacia Center to provide nonprivileged information about which children its subcontractors were representing and how it was billing the federal government for each client. According to the agency, the Acacia Center refused to provide that information.

The Acacia Center for Justice disputed that characterization. It told WORLD the annual federal funding isn’t anywhere close to enough to provide every unaccompanied immigrant child with legal representation.

“Instead of trying to close this gap, the administration repeatedly tried to eliminate legal representation for these children,” said Bilal Askaryar, director of communications at the Acacia Center. Providing the documents the federal government requested would have revealed case strategy and violated attorney-client privilege, he added.

Fast-forward to July 2026, when HHS ended its partnership with the Unaccompanied Children Program at the Acacia Center for Justice. The move threatened the legal representation of more than 20,000 children, according to the center.

The Trump administration offered the center a new contract that would have required it to provide clarity on which children in ORR custody its subcontractors were representing, and what services it was billing the government for related to those clients’ cases. The Acacia Center turned down the contract, ORR told WORLD.

“ORR’s proposal for the new contract was filled with poison pills that would have required us to hand over privileged information,” Askaryar said. “During every stage of the negotiation, we told them we would not violate our [clients’] privileged information, and no other ethical provider would either.”

Just weeks later, the administration awarded a federal funding contract to the organization Our Rescue for providing legal representation to minors in immigration court. But the federal government is unable to provide any money to Our Rescue through that contract, ORR told WORLD. That’s because the Acacia Center for Justice filed a protest against the contract in August. ORR can’t provide funding to Our Rescue through the contract until the dispute about the contract is resolved.

While that contract dispute plays out, ORR has enlisted the assistance of the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants to provide legal services to the minors in its custody, the office said. According to the Acacia Center, however, Our Rescue and the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants did not have experience representing minors in immigration court.

The number of unaccompanied immigrant children facing deportation without a lawyer has increased significantly since Trump took office, according to the Vera Institute. More than half of the roughly 700,000 unaccompanied children facing deportation in August 2026 never had an attorney representing them. Overall, the number of unaccompanied minors whose immigration court cases closed without them ever receiving assistance from an attorney was up 45% compared with before Trump took office, the Vera Institute said.

As it shifts funding away from previous projects that provided unaccompanied children with legal representation, the Trump administration has also reportedly taken steps to speed up the resolution of unaccompanied immigrant children’s cases. Outlets like ABC News and Bloomberg Law have also reported that the Trump administration has offered payments to children to self-deport.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security told WORLD that it has only offered payments to children in its custody who are older than 14, aren’t citizens of Mexico, and have no gang affiliation.

“This administration was trying to convince kids just to drop their claims and to say, ‘OK, never mind, we’ll go back,’ by offering them money,” Jennifer Podkul from KIND said. “We’re very worried. Who is checking to make sure that when that kid goes back, there aren’t dangerous people waiting for the kid?”

Podkul added: “They almost made it more dangerous for kids to go back because now these kids are going to be carrying around a couple thousand dollars of cash, right? And these are places where kids have already left because they didn’t feel safe there.”

Government attorneys and lawyers acquired through new contracts could provide at least some children with legal representation. But the attorneys who’ve represented children in immigration court through previous federal funding have developed a speciality in the area, said Jennifer Anzardo Valdes, director of Children’s Legal Services at the International Rescue Committee.

“IRC, as well as the other legal service providers that were on this contract, have spent years building a specialty really around working with children and understand the responsibility of helping children understand the process and protect their rights and present that information in a child-friendly way,” Anzardo Valdes said. “We use puppets, fidget toys, art. We even have a model courtroom that’s made out of bricks in which to teach children what their rights are, what it would be like when they go to court and talk to a judge.”

But Andrew Arthur from the Center for Immigration Studies says federal government attorneys already represent individuals during courtroom proceedings in other contexts.

“We have public defenders. They’re government employees. … Why would this be any different?” Arthur said. “And the sort of people that would take a job like that probably would not be the sort of attorneys who would be 100% MAGA-focused on removing everybody who is unlawfully present.”

But whether they have a lawyer or not, children shouldn’t have their cases heard in the adversarial setting of an immigration court, said Arthur, who pins the blame for that reality on Congress.

“There’s no real reason why [unaccompanied alien children] should be in immigration court at all,” Arthur said. “And if this is an issue, Congress probably wants to reconsider whether there is some better way to screen these children to determine whether they need immigration protection or are eligible for any immigration benefits, and to handle that administratively in a nonconfrontational proceeding.”

Podkul explained that in her work—whether in the courtroom or outside—her biggest priority is getting the right answer for the children.

“I think as a lawyer. I’m drawn to fairness, right?” Podkul said. “Making sure kids—this population—has the opportunity to tell their story, and we get to the right answer for a kid. You know, the right answer could be they stay in the United States because they need protection. The right answer could be, ‘It’s OK, they can go back to their country of origin, and we can support them, and they can flourish and make their countries better.’ But it’s about getting to the right answer for these kids.”

text:
Unless the court intervenes, the civil rights groups will have to shut their doors in Florida on November 5

TALLAHASSEE — The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida heard arguments today in a lawsuit challenging Florida officials’ baseless and unconstitutional designation of the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) and its Florida chapter as “domestic terrorist organizations.” Unless the court intervenes to prevent it, the largest Muslim civil rights organization in the country will have to shut their doors in Florida on Nov. 5.

“CAIR and CAIR-Florida are critical resources that people and institutions across Florida rely on to protect civil rights and liberties, and all we want to do is get back to that important work,” said Hiba Rahim, executive director of CAIR-FL. “Florida’s new law silences free speech, criminalizes association, and eradicates due process, and we are hopeful that the court will act to safeguard our constitutional rights. History reminds us that our country has endured dark chapters, but also that people who refused to accept injustice moved us closer to our founding ideals.”

At today’s hearing, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) urged the court to grant emergency relief for the organizations, explaining the instant and debilitating harm CAIR and CAIR-FL will face if the court does not rescind the designation and stop it from going into effect. In the alternative, they are asking the court to prevent Florida state prosecutors from enforcing the law’s harsh criminal penalties against the nonprofits and third parties who associate with and support them.

As the ACLU argued in court, CAIR and CAIR-Florida have done nothing to deserve this devastating designation. The state has never indicted, much less convicted, either CAIR or CAIR-Florida under any criminal law — and certainly not a criminal law involving the serious charge of terrorism. If the state tried to do so, it would fail. The reason is simple: Neither CAIR nor CAIR-Florida is engaged in terrorist activity, and the state would be unable to prove its case to a jury in a court of law.

“Florida’s new law is an unprecedented abuse of state authority,” said Ashley Gorski, senior counsel with the ACLU’s National Security Project. “It gives state officials sweeping power to punish American organizations they brand as ‘terrorists,’ without due process and in violation of the First Amendment. We’re asking the court to block this unconstitutional law and ensure that our clients’ crucially important civil rights work serving Floridians is not silenced.”

Once a designation becomes effective, an organization’s lawful, constitutionally protected speech and association are immediately rendered illegal and impossible. Under HB 1471, five Florida executive officials have the power to designate and debilitate U.S. groups — including nonprofits engaged in First Amendment-protected advocacy — without filing charges, initiating judicial proceedings, proving their case beyond a reasonable doubt, submitting the case to a jury, or complying with any of the other required constitutional protections of the criminal legal system. An elaborate set of prohibitions makes it a serious crime for the targeted American organization to do virtually anything in the state, and for others to work for or otherwise actively associate with or support the designated group. The consequences of violating these prohibitions are severe, including up to life imprisonment.

“Florida’s designation of CAIR and CAIR-Florida flies in the face of fundamental rights guaranteed to all Americans by the Constitution,” said Scott McCoy, deputy legal director at SPLC. “All Floridians should be concerned that this law allows Florida officials to do an end run around the Constitution, shut down disfavored speech and advocacy, and impose draconian criminal penalties. If they are permitted to do it to these civil rights nonprofits, what’s to stop them from doing it to any Floridian with whom they disagree?”

The impact on the Floridian communities CAIR and CAIR-Florida serve would also be immense. CAIR-Florida provides a range of pro bono legal services to Florida residents, including those who suﬀer government and workplace discrimination in violation of their civil rights, as well as those navigating the immigration system.

“The state does not get to decide whose speech is constitutionally protected or whose due process rights deserve respect. The Constitution decided that long ago,” said Daniel Tilley, legal director of the ACLU of Florida. “And Florida must not strip CAIR and CAIR-FL of their ability to advocate and organize for the civil rights of Floridian Muslims. This dangerous designation regime, crafted by the DeSantis administration, seeks to criminalize protected speech, plain and simple — and with no regard for the harm it causes to the thousands of people our clients support and serve. We are proud to stand with our clients against this abuse of state power.”

CAIR and CAIR-Florida are represented by the ACLU, ACLU of Florida, the Southern Poverty Law Center, and Bondurant Mixson & Elmore LLP.

Detroit activists dedicated to monitoring ICE activity sounded an alarm on Wednesday, Oct. 28, about what they described as a "surge" of activity from the federal agency in Southwest Detroit, a neighborhood notable for Mexican immigrants.

The People's Assembly, along with other activists the Free Press spoke to, described ICE agents stopping even U.S. citizens along Vernor Highway — one of the neighborhood's main drags — as well as Clark Park, Western International High School, and Maybury and Earhart elementary schools.

An early voting station is currently stationed inside Clark Park, which the People's Assembly noted on social media.

ICE did not immediately return Free Press requests for comment.

Jessica Avila, a community leader in Southwest Detroit, told the Free Press she was on Wednesday morning documenting stops and arrests by ICE as she was on the way to Ecorse, where she received another tip on ICE activity.

The community is on edge, she said, especially given the fact that ICE was reported near schools. Parents are asking for volunteers for people to go to Maybury and Earhart to help protect children in case anyone is taken, she said.

The reported surge in Detroit is part of President Donald Trump's unprecedented nationwide campaign of immigration enforcement.

Some local advocates also said they see the uptick in ICE activity ahead of next week's midterm elections in Southwest as voter intimidation, meant to inhibit the area’s majority Latino population from showing up at the polls.

“We’re less than a week away from elections, Michigan is a swing state, ICE has been known to be an arm of this administration, so that’s where we’re operating from,” said Andrew Reinel, deputy director of adult and neighborhood organizing at 482 Forward, a Detroit-based educational access nonprofit.

text:
As the Trump administration pursues mass deportations, a former inspector general for the Homeland Security Department argued that the current oversight structure for Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities is obfuscating unsafe conditions.

“This is essentially a Potemkin village of reports that are put up for largely disinformation value to try to explain to the public that there is no problem when in fact there's significant problems in all these facilities that need to get fixed,” said John Roth during a webinar Tuesday put on by the Project on Government Oversight.

The webinar focused on an August report by the nonprofit’s news reporting division that found the percentage of detention facilities receiving the highest inspection rating by ICE’s Office of Detention Oversight “nearly tripled since fiscal 2024 as of July 23, after declining by 61% between fiscal 2022 and 2024.” René Kladzyk, one of the researchers behind the analysis, provided an update during the event that, by the end of fiscal 2026, about 71.5% of inspected facilities scored a “superior” rating.

At the same time, the average daily population of noncitizens detained by ICE increased by 71% between January 2025 and July 2026, and 33 people in ICE custody died in 2025, which was a more-than-two-decade high.

“You don't have to be a former IG or an investigative reporter to understand that it's facially incredible that the number of perfect reports are going up at the same time that we are facing unprecedented detentions in these facilities,” Roth said.

Roth criticized DHS for weakening internal watchdogs, such as DHS’ Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties and Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman, through staff cuts and shutting down their operations.

The former IG recommended that Congress could strengthen oversight of ICE detention facilities by:

Enacting a uniform inspection standards for such facilities, as ICE currently develops its own criteria.

Shielding internal oversight bodies from influence by the administration.

Encouraging external oversight, including from IGs and third-party organizations.

“You need a combination of both internal oversight, which has meaningful reporting to people who are decision makers and meaningful power, as well as independent oversight, because without that, then you're not going to have the kind of oversight that you need for a high-risk system like this,” Roth said.

He noted that the DHS IG currently performs unannounced inspections of ICE detention facilities, but the former watchdog argued that that isn’t comprehensive enough.

“There has to be a deeper dive into the root causes as to why it is that we're where we are,” Roth said. “Is this because we are not holding the contractors responsible? Is this a funding issue? Is this a technical issue? Is this a legal issue? What is the fundamental root problem of why we can't detain people humanely and in accordance with specific standards?”

ICE did not respond to a request for comment.

On Monday, the DHS IG reported, based on an unannounced inspection of a since-closed ICE facility in El Paso, Texas, that the agency held detainees in a short-term environment for an average of 36 hours longer than standards provided. The watchdog also found that the facility did not comply with other standards regarding “use of force, personal property, hygiene and food and beverage.”

The DHS IG also reported in September that an ICE facility in Florida, which was nicknamed “Alligator Alcatraz” and has shut down, “did not provide detainees with sufficient living space, creating cramped conditions for detainees who spent most of their time in their housing units, which may harm detainees’ physical and mental health.”

And the Government Accountability Office found in June that an immigration detention facility in Texas experienced “gaps in medical services, the loss of a loaded firearm and unsanitary conditions, among other issues” that “posed serious risks to the safety and security of both detained noncitizens and staff in the facility.”

Kladzyk, the POGO investigator, emphasized that ICE detention oversight has “life-and-death implications.”

“I think it's important to think about ICE oversight in those terms,” she said. “If some of these problems had been addressed earlier, maybe we would not be seeing the current numbers we're seeing in terms of deaths in custody.”

text:
A woman whose father was detained in Burien described her family's anguish, joining community members sharing the toll of rising immigration enforcement in the South End.

Jacquelyn Jimenez Romero

At an Oct. 27 news conference at Casa Latina, advocates and community members urged elected officials to stop Washington's Department of Licensing from sharing drivers' information with federal immigration authorities, citing a surge in enforcement across the Seattle area.

"The surge is here," said Roxana Norouzi, executive director of OneAmerica. "It is happening right now, right here, in our home in Washington State."

Advocates also urged immigrant community members to stay informed, attend legal clinics, contact an attorney, prepare an emergency plan with family members, and store documents in a safe place.

The impacts of immigration detention echoed for community members like Alondra Miranda Garcia, whose father was detained on Oct. 17 and is currently at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma. She said he has no criminal record and has been living in the United States for more than 20 years.

Miranda Garcia broke down and cried as she recounted her father's detention. He was on his way to do a plumbing job in Burien when he was stopped by two unmarked vehicles and detained by immigration authorities.

"In an instant, our family's world was shattered," Miranda Garcia said. "Now we are left wondering when we will see him again, and we worry about his well-being. We miss his presence in our home."

The room was filled with grief and sorrow as other community members shared stories of the impacts of the recent surge. Those recently detained included a refugee from Laos, a 19-year-old student about to start her freshman year at the University of Washington, and caregivers who provide around-the-clock care to seniors and people with disabilities.

At the center of the room — adorned with candles, skulls, food, and papel picado, colorful sheets of paper decorated with patterns — stood an altar honoring people who had been detained or lost their lives in ICE custody.

"When an aggressive hunt sweeps through our neighborhood, no one is left untouched," said Savong Lam. "It traumatizes children who come home to not seeing their parents, destabilizes local workplaces, fractures our schools, and shatters the trust that keeps every community safe."

In the past several weeks, ICE leadership told agents to ramp up daily immigration arrests to detain 1,000 more people a day. Community members across South Seattle and South King County have shared on social media footage of these arrests, including in Burien and White Center, where an agent appeared to be carrying a rifle.

More than 50 people have died in ICE custody during President Donald Trump's second term. Their names were written on a scroll where community members placed marigolds.

Marigolds are typically used during Dia de los Muertos, known as Day of the Dead, which is a tradition celebrated in Mexico and parts of Latin America that honors and welcomes back the spirits of deceased loved ones. It is believed that the flower's scent helps lead the souls from their burial place to their family homes.

In 2025, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE and other immigration enforcement branches, received $170.7 billion in funding from H.R. 1. Norouzi said that funding has played a large role in how communities have been impacted.

"[ICE] is way more organized, and they're way more cruel," she said. "The cruelty, the violence, the lengths that they're willing to go to, and the scale feels very different this time around."

A January report from the University of Washington Center for Human Rights also found that federal immigration authorities continued to access the state's Department of Licensing data through a national data-sharing system. Researchers documented queries of that data in connection with immigration enforcement actions.

"The ICE raids have been horrible," Norouzi said. "Over the last few months, the devastating growth of ICE raids, deportation, and detention has spiked to unprecedented levels."

Immigration advocates urged elected officials to continue funding and providing support to immigrant communities who fear deportation, stop the state from sharing data with immigration authorities, and cease the use of surveillance technology.

"We're here to demand change, and there is real change needed," Norouzi said. "We can't guarantee anyone's safety anymore. … We have to fight back and fight for the future we want, and that's what we're doing every day."

Miranda Garcia said her father is surviving "as much as he can" while in detention.

"It's been a struggle. We try not to miss work because we still have to be able to sustain ourselves," she said in an interview after the news conference.

So far, the family has raised more than $10,000 through a GoFundMe fundraiser to support their needs and is planning on doing bake sales to raise additional funds.

"We've had to make so many sacrifices already, so that just makes everything much harder," said Miranda Garcia. "We feel really lucky as a family to have each other, but we definitely have that missing piece in our heart."

title: A cattle rancher voted for Trump. But now he's 'had enough of this crap' - USA Today
description:

He even broke with Trump recently, opposing the president's foreign beef import efforts.
Farmers facing 'ridiculous' prices A convergence of issues is uniquely testing the loyalty of farmers and ranchers to Republicans this election cycle.
As the overall U.S. beef and dairy cattle herd hit a 75-year low, prices went up, making groceries more broadly expensive for Americans.
Walter Schweitzer, president of the Montana Farmers Union, likened some of those measures, however, to "pissing on a forest fire."
text:
MISSOULA, MT – Wally Congdon is done with Donald Trump.

The 69-year-old cattle rancher, a member of the Montana Cowboy Hall of Fame, voted for him in 2024 amid frustrations with the Biden administration’s immigration agenda. He also supported Rep. Ryan Zinke, a Republican retiring from Congress this year.

Two years later, turmoil in the Middle East has sent diesel prices soaring to record highs. Fertilizer costs have skyrocketed, too. The president's trade wars, including with neighboring Canada, are raging. And Trump has repeatedly moved against the wishes of many of his GOP allies to import more foreign beef, undercutting domestic producers like Congdon, who raises highland cows about 30 miles east of his home in Missoula.

"We've had enough of this crap," Congdon said. This fall, he wants to send a Democrat to represent him in Washington instead.

Independent-minded voters like Congdon are part of what has made the race for Montana's western congressional district unexpectedly competitive – and it's not alone. Similar dynamics are playing out in other contests across the country, putting into play red-state seats that Republicans earlier this year considered for months to be comparatively safe bets.

While farmers and ranchers have for decades been a relatively reliably conservative voting bloc in many cases – and there's no indication that's fundamentally changing – there has been wide acknowledgment among the agricultural community that the Trump administration’s mercurial policies are taking a toll. Even if the whiplash has just a marginal impact in swing districts, it could make a difference in the midterms.

In Montana, Democrat Sam Forstag, a union leader and former smokejumper who has notched Congdon's vote, is in a neck-and-neck race against Aaron Flint, a Trump-endorsed veteran and conservative radio host. Montana hasn't elected a Democrat to the House of Representatives since 1994, but in September the nonpartisan elections handicapper the Cook Political Report moved the district from "likely Republican" to "lean Republican." This month, the race became even closer when Cook shifted it to a "toss-up."

"I'm very depressed to tell you Montana 1 is listed as a toss-up," Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson told a group of Republicans at a Flint campaign event in the city of Bozeman last week.

In an interview with USA TODAY, Flint agreed that farmers and ranchers are hurting. He even broke with Trump recently, opposing the president's foreign beef import efforts.

Still, Flint argued, livestock producers were much worse off during the Biden years. He touted his own endorsement from the Montana Stockgrowers Association, the state's most powerful ag lobby, and he promised to loosen regulations on his farm-owning constituents.

"They know that I'm going to be somebody who’s going to have their back," Flint said.

Farmers facing 'ridiculous' prices

A convergence of issues is uniquely testing the loyalty of farmers and ranchers to Republicans this election cycle.

For one thing, Trump’s penchant for tariffs has hiked supply costs while threatening the export markets that producers rely on to make a living.

Steve Sheffels, a wheat farmer and the president of the Montana Grain Growers Association, said he hasn't bought a new combine since 2013. Trump’s steel tariffs have made replacing many pieces of equipment that people like him need more expensive.

"The price of parts at the store is ridiculous," he said.

Conflicts overseas have made life even harder lately in cattle country. The war in Iran has disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for global oil markets. The regional tumult has dramatically raised the price of both fertilizer, which often requires natural gas to make, and diesel, the fuel on which America’s farms largely run.

Sheffels said a friend of his was paying about $3,500 a week just for fuel during the winter wheat harvest this year.

Trump's foreign beef fixation

It’s all happening as ranchers are already trying to recover from a yearslong period of shifting weather patterns, including severe drought, that have worsened pasture conditions and left lingering impacts.

As the overall U.S. beef and dairy cattle herd hit a 75-year low, prices went up, making groceries more broadly expensive for Americans. In hopes of making staples like steak and hamburger more affordable, Trump signed a decree in September to ease tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of foreign beef imports to be sold below market value. It followed a similar move in February, when he lifted tariffs on beef from Argentina.

Both decisions angered livestock producers and congressional Republicans alike.

Ben Peterson, a rancher in the roughly 100-person town of Judith Gap, Montana, said he likely lost about $5,000 due to the pricing pressure Trump's latest import announcement put on the cattle market. Other ranchers told USA TODAY in August they, too, were missing out on hundreds of dollars per cow at the auction barn.

Peterson, a Democrat, lives in the eastern part of the state, where Montana's other Republican congressman, Troy Downing, is cruising to reelection. He was skeptical that the recent instability would push many ranchers to vote for Democrats.

Disillusionment with Trump, though, has clearly grown among livestock producers, he said.

"They're more likely to just sit out," he said.

A last-minute scramble

With the midterms in sight, Trump and Vice President JD Vance have been barnstorming the campaign trail in red states, including with trips to Montana.

During an Oct. 14 rally in the mountain town of Kalispell, Trump stressed that he and GOP lawmakers passed legislation last year to eliminate estate taxes for family farms. He also suggested that Chinese President Xi Jinping promised he'd be "doubling up on his purchases from the farmers."

"We're never going to let our farmers get hurt," Trump said.

In recent weeks, the White House announced a flurry of new agricultural policies. Among them was an $8 billion Department of Agriculture program offering one-time payments to offset high diesel costs from this fall’s harvest. The president also penned an order to loosen rules on off-road, cheaper diesel. And top federal officials are reportedly working toward a detente in the trade war with Canada.

Walter Schweitzer, president of the Montana Farmers Union, likened some of those measures, however, to "pissing on a forest fire."

Zachary Schermele is the congressional correspondent for USA TODAY. Reach him by email at zschermele@usatoday.com and on Signal @zachschermele.02. Follow him on X at @ZachSchermele.

text:
On October 23, 2026, a federal appeals court ruled that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) may detain certain individuals without a bond hearing while their cases are pending. In a 10-7 decision, the entire Fifth Circuit held that individuals who are not lawfully admitted and who have pending immigration hearings are not constitutionally entitled to a bond hearing. The ruling applies in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi. The issue is still open and could be before the Supreme Court.

Background

In Feburary 2026, a Fifth Circuit panel upheld ICE’s reading of immigration law, which required detention without a bond hearing. Other federal judges have since found that such a policy constitutes a violation of the detainee’s right to due process. Over the past year, judges have ruled against ICE’s policy of detaining without bond in over 21,150 cases. The Fifth Circuit’s decision now renders that approach invalid, according to the New Republic.

Litigation

Three men who had been in the U.S. for at least 14 years were the subject of the case. In July 2026, a three judge panel ruled in their favor, finding that ICE could not constitutionally detain someone for more than 90 days without a bond hearing. The full Fifth Circuit then took the case en banc and reversed that decision. Reuters points out the importance of this ruling given that Texas and Louisiana have the largest populations of immigration detainees. The court held that an immigrant who is not lawfully admitted is not entitled to any constitutional rights beyond those conferred by Congress.

Next Steps

Despite that ruling, the debate about ICE detention is far from over. The Supreme Court has agreed to take a separate case this month on whether federal immigration law requires bond hearings (that case doesn’t deal with the constitutional issue that the Fifth Circuit has decided). Watch the Supreme Court for any developments on this issue.

A Chelsea family filed a federal lawsuit Wednesday against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after what they call a traumatizing ICE assault and arrest.

Hilda Ramirez Sanan said she was "violently attacked" during a September 2025 encounter near Chelsea District Court when ICE agents smashed windows and dragged her out of her car in front of her two U.S. citizen children, the lawsuit alleges.

According to the complaint, officers forcibly arrested Ramirez Sanan, who has lived lawfully in the United States for more than 20 years, without first asking about her immigration status or checking the identification in her purse.

Ramirez Sanan brings the lawsuit with her daughter, Michelle Ramirez Sanan, who was 17 at the time of the arrest, and her son, identified as J.R.S., who was 13 years old at the time and has autism.

Lawyers allege ICE officers continued their arrest despite repeated statements from Ramirez Sanan and bystanders that she has legal status. “My family lives every day with the consequences of what ICE did to our family,” said Hilda Ramirez Sanan. “I want my children to know that we will stand up to fight for ourselves and the rights of immigrants who have also suffered abuse by ICE officers.”

The complaint brings claims that include unlawful detention, physical assault and emotional harm suffered by the family, as well as negligent supervision and damage to their property.

text:
Groups that provide legal services to immigrants filed a lawsuit Wednesday seeking to stop the Trump administration’s new policy of hiding the locations of tens of thousands of detainees with final deportation orders.

The policy, adopted suddenly last month to expedite deportations, interferes with immigration lawyers’ rights by making it difficult, and sometimes impossible, to locate their clients, according to the lawsuit filed in federal court in Boston. It asks a judge to issue an order blocking the “unlawful and inhumane” change.

“No one should be denied a meaningful opportunity to defend their rights because the government has made it impossible for their lawyer to find them,” said Jacquelynne Bowman, executive director of Greater Boston Legal Services, one of the four groups listed as plaintiffs. “This arbitrary new administrative change leaves hundreds of thousands of people at risk of potentially life-altering consequences without essential legal help.”

The lawsuit challenges U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s decision, first reported by The Associated Press, to remove the locations of people facing final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System and to instruct staff not to reveal their whereabouts. As of last month, the move affected more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 detainees who were in ICE custody.

ICE and its parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, didn’t immediately respond to a message seeking comment on the lawsuit.

The agencies have not publicly confirmed the change but have said they are prioritizing people with final removal orders for deportation. They have also said they are facing a “historic number of injunctions” from courts blocking their efforts. The agencies have denied that they are disappearing detainees, saying they remain free to make phone calls.

Since 2010, lawyers and family members have used the online system to track detainees as they get moved from facility to facility through ICE’s sprawling detention network.

Approximately 1.4 million people living in the U.S. are subject to final orders of removal, which means an immigration judge has ruled they should be deported and the decision has been upheld on appeal or not appealed.

Those individuals still have several options to challenge the conditions of their detention and looming deportations, including asking to reopen proceedings, seeking relief from removal to third countries and challenging violations of their rights. Federal judges have ruled thousands of times that detainees should be released or granted bond hearings.

Since the change went into effect, lawyers have been unable to find clients and potential clients and have spent “significantly more time” tracking down others, the lawsuit says. Calls to ICE, including to its Detention and Removal Information Line, “lead to long wait times on hold, sudden hang-ups, a general lack of information or no answer at all,” it says.

As a workaround, some lawyers have tried to find their clients through an ICE program that schedules legal calls, but only a small percentage of detention centers use it, the lawsuit says. The result has been delayed or missed legal filings and fewer cases taken, according to the organizations.

The lawsuit argues the change violates the Administrative Procedure Act because it was adopted without explanation and because of the First Amendment, which protects lawyers’ ability to advise people of their legal rights and seek prospective clients.

A judge denied Monday a request to hold Laramie County Sheriff Brian Kozak in contempt of court in a lawsuit concerning immigration arrest records.

While acknowledging that Kozak and his counsel, Laramie County Attorney Mark Voss, didn’t fully comply with a court order requiring them to produce immigration arrest records, Laramie County Judge Robin Cooley wrote in her decision that there wasn’t clear evidence showing their noncompliance was willful.

A Colorado law firm requested records from the Laramie County Sheriff’s Office related to a deputy’s April immigration arrest of Mario Fabian Valenzuela-Robles, a Mexican national with three children who are U.S. citizens. The legal practice, Lichter Immigration, is representing Valenzuela-Robles in ongoing immigration proceedings, and the evidence is vital to his defense in federal court, the firm has said.

Alleging that it faced barriers to obtaining certain records, Lichter Immigration, represented by former Wyoming GOP Chairman Drake Hill, sued Kozak and his office in July. Later that month, Cooley ordered Kozak to provide additional records concerning Valenzuela-Robles’ detention.

But Kozak and Voss didn’t fully comply with that order, missing the agreed-upon deadline by two days. Some documents were in a format the plaintiffs couldn’t open or read. Kozak’s office didn’t provide a log explaining why certain documents were withheld. Because of these shortcomings, Lichter Immigration asked Cooley to hold Kozak and his office in contempt of court.

But noncompliance alone, Cooley wrote in her decision, “does not establish civil contempt.”

“Plaintiffs have not proven by clear and convincing evidence that the failure to comply was willful,” Cooley wrote.

Kozak also noted this point. “The law says you have to willfully, you know, withhold the evidence, and so of course we didn’t do that,” he said in a phone call to WyoFile.

That being said, Cooley continued, just because the defendants’ noncompliance wasn’t willful “does not make it acceptable.”

She noted that the defendants helped draft the terms of the order compelling production of records. Cooley also pointed out that Hill had asked Voss in an August letter to address concerns about the records.

The defendants’ failure to address those concerns “prolonged a dispute that should have been resolved without the necessity of further Court proceedings,” Cooley wrote.

While declining to hold Kozak in contempt, Cooley ordered the sheriff and Voss to provide within 10 days a log explaining why certain records were withheld, records in a readable format and written explanations addressing each of the alleged missing records the plaintiffs had identified.

Kozak said he had talked with Voss and expects to comply with the order in the next couple of days.

An Oshkosh middle school teacher has been detained by federal immigration authorities after being ordered to leave the country.

Wendy Mendez moved to Wisconsin from Costa Rica in 2020 with her husband and two sons. She is a Spanish teacher at Vel Phillips Middle School, and was recognized as an “employee of the year” by the Oshkosh Area School District last year.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, arrested Mendez on Oct. 14 in Milwaukee, according to a statement from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

The statement said Mendez came to the country legally “on a temporary basis” six years ago and “failed to depart” in 2021. According to federal officials, Mendez was placed into removal proceedings in February and was ordered to be removed in September for failing to show up for an immigration hearing.

But one of Mendez’s friends says Mendez missed the hearing because federal immigration officials mailed a hearing notice to an old address.

Deb Nez, the friend of Mendez, wrote on social media that the notice was sent to a three-year-old address and that U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services had Mendez’s correct address “within days” of the family moving into their home.

“This was not the first time that USCIS had made that mistake,” Nez wrote on Oct. 22.

Mendez’s story was first reported by the Advance-Titan, the independent student newspaper of the University of Wisconsin-Oshkosh.

Nez wrote that Mendez had been forced to sleep on concrete floors and had been moved to six detention centers in eight days.

The Department of Homeland Security’s statement said Mendez will “remain in custody pending her removal from the United States.”

The agency added that “being in detention is a choice,” saying the federal government is offering $3,000 and a free flight to individuals who self-deport.

“We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream,” the statement read. “If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.”

The Oshkosh Area School District sent a letter to Vel Phillips Middle School families following Mendez’s detainment, saying she would be “out of the classroom for the foreseeable future” due to “unforeseen circumstances.”

The Oct. 26 letter said Mendez is an employee in good standing and had been placed on unpaid leave. The district also said Mendez’s leave of absence was not related to school safety or her performance.

“We know this situation brings heartbreak, frustration, and worry for many in our community,” the letter reads.

In an email, a spokesperson for the Oshkosh school district said the district does not comment on confidential employee matters. But the spokesperson confirmed Mendez is in good standing with the district.

“Our primary focus remains on supporting our students and staff and keeping learning moving forward in our classrooms,” the spokesperson said.

Mendez was recognized by the Oshkosh Area School District in the 2024-25 school year as one of the district’s employees of the year. She was recognized as an interpreter.

In a video posted to the district’s YouTube page in April 2025, Oshkosh Superintendent Bryan Davis is seen walking into Mendez’s classroom to give her the award. As Davis hands her a balloon and a large mug, Mendez becomes emotional.

Oshkosh School Board member Molly Smiltneek issued a statement Monday night, expressing frustration over Mendez’s detention by ICE.

“This is not normal. This is not a personnel issue. This is not a political issue,” she said. “This is a human issue. I know there are a lot of people, kids and adults, in our community who are hurting, sad and trying to make sense of the sudden disappearance of an important person in their lives.”

“And there is a mother, a teacher, a leader, a role-model, neighbor, a human being, an employee of the year who was torn away from all she built and valued,” Smiltneek added.

On Oct. 25, Nez wrote on social media that Mendez was “safe and doing okay,” but was “recovering from the horrid experience she went through” both mentally and emotionally.

“This is not the end of the road for Wendy,” Nez wrote. “There is still a long and expensive legal battle ahead, with significant legal fees and uncertainty about what comes next.”

Contact information for Mendez’s legal representation was not immediately available.

In response to Mendez’s detention, a local nonprofit will host a “vigil for the missing” on Friday at 6 p.m. in downtown Oshkosh.

The lawsuit, filed in Tennessee, seeks details of ICE’s instructions to state and local law enforcement agencies about whether to release records requested under state laws.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C., October 28, 2026 — The American Immigration Council, the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition (TIRRC), and researcher Meghan Conley filed a lawsuit today seeking information about what ICE is telling local police and sheriffs about sharing immigration enforcement records with the public.

The lawsuit, filed in Tennessee, seeks details of ICE’s instructions to state and local law enforcement agencies about whether to release records requested under state laws. The requested records would shed light on what ICE tells state police and other local law enforcement to do when they receive public record requests regarding their collaboration with ICE.

According to the lawsuit, ICE has told local police and sheriffs they need to check with federal officials before sharing certain records with the public, even when state transparency laws say otherwise. This raises concerns that ICE may be making it harder for journalists, advocates , and the general public to find out how local police and sheriffs are working with federal immigration authorities.

In August, the plaintiffs in this lawsuit filed a FOIA request with ICE seeking records of the instructions ICE gave to state and local law enforcement. ICE did not produce the records sought.

The lawsuit comes as ICE is working with a growing number of police and sheriff departments across the country to carry out the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda, an effort that is increasingly unpopular with Americans and is inflicting enormous harm on families and communities across the country.

“As ICE works with more local police and sheriffs across the country, more people are going to have questions about what these partnerships mean for their communities. How is taxpayer money being spent? What role are local police officers playing in immigration arrests? How are people being treated in detention? The public deserves answers to these questions, and ICE shouldn’t be making it harder to get them,” said Raul Pinto, deputy legal director for transparency at the American Immigration Council.

In Tennessee, the push for answers is particularly urgent. ICE has rapidly expanded its partnerships with local law enforcement across the state, with 163 agreements in place as of September 2026. This has led to a four-fold increase in immigration arrests and detentions, the majority involving people with no criminal record.

“Families across Tennessee are living with the consequences of this horrific immigration crackdown. Longtime U.S. residents are being arrested in their neighborhoods, families are being separated, mothers pulled away from their children, and local police and sheriffs are playing a growing role in making it all happen. Tennesseans deserve to know what their local law enforcement agencies are doing and who is being affected. We can’t hold our government accountable if we can’t even get basic information about what’s happening in our communities,” said Spring Miller, Senior Legal Strategy Director at TIRCC.

text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KAKE) - Immigration Enforcement agents detained another Wichita business owner, along with her family.
This happened two weeks ago, on October 14, after they received a letter for their immigration check-in at the Woodlawn ICE offices.
Pablo Hernandez, the boyfriend of Yessica Olivas, dropped her and three other family members, Mario, Maribel, and Marisela, off at the ICE office that day.
Hernandez was told he would be allowed to pick them up for lunch at noon.
“I got there at exactly 12 o’clock on October 14,” Hernandez said. “I dropped food off and everything. I was waiting for them to come out, and nothing. It was like one, two passed, nothing.”
Hernandez said that after three hours, an ICE agent came out asking for the Olivas’ family friend, Raquel Reyes.
“An agent came out of the office and asked me to come pick up their paperwork while I was on the phone with Pablo,” Reyes said. “I went in, and we didn’t get to see them that day at all. So from there they went to Chase County.”
Reyes says Yessica, the eldest daughter and founder of Lady Burritos, a food delivery service in Wichita, built strong connections in town.
“She is a giving person,” Reyes said. “She’s a caring person. She thinks of others before herself. She has given when she has nothing, and selflessly and without question. If somebody needs help, she’s willing to do what she can do within her limits.”
A family friend of 10 years, Gisela Pena, adds that the family has been giving to people in Wichita, such as Yessica, and they didn’t deserve to be in the situation they’re in.
“Whenever they can, they help the community,” Pena said. “I can only say that this family is like so many others here. We’ve all come here chasing a dream, you know, the dream of improving our lives.”
Reyes says the Olivas family doesn’t have a criminal record.
For now, Reyes and many others have started a
GoFundMe
to help the Olivas family with legal fees and transition costs.
Reyes also says scheduled orders with Lady Burritos will most likely be completed, but the business will then be on hold until they know what happens next.
A spokesperson from the Department of Homeland Security says that in 2013, the Olivas family entered the U.S. through Columbus, New Mexico, and were released into the country by the Obama Administration.

text:
The US Supreme Court declined on Tuesday to reinstate the authority of immigration judges to temporarily postpone deportation cases, keeping in place an agreement between President Donald Trump’s administration and Republican-governed Texas that bars the once common practice.

The justices denied an emergency request by three US cities, including Baltimore, and an immigrant legal advocacy group to halt for now the deal ending the practice, known as “administrative closure”, while litigation continues in the dispute.

The supreme court’s decision, issued as a brief, one-sentence order, did not offer any explanation, as is common when it handles emergency requests. None of the justices publicly dissented from the decision.

This dangerous abuse of the judicial process threatens the rule of law and sets a troubling precedent for dismantling federal policies without meaningful public participation or judicial scrutiny

— Baltimore and the other litigants

The administration and Texas filed the agreement in a federal court in Texas on June 22, the same day that the state sued to challenge the immigration court procedure. A federal judge swiftly approved the agreement on the same day.

Baltimore and the other litigants said the federal government improperly colluded with Texas to secure the rule’s invalidation. The litigants and the lawyers representing them from the liberal legal group Democracy Forward expressed disappointment in Tuesday’s decision.

“Eliminating these protections puts vulnerable people at greater risk of deportation and undermines public safety in communities across the country,” they said.

“This dangerous abuse of the judicial process threatens the rule of law and sets a troubling precedent for dismantling federal policies without meaningful public participation or judicial scrutiny,” they added.

Representatives from the justice department and the Texas attorney-general’s office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Immigration judges relied on administrative closure for decades to clear certain deportation cases off their busy dockets, including when separate proceedings involving the same person are pending that could prevent removal, such as on a visa petition or an appeal of a criminal conviction.

Critics, including Texas and the Trump administration, have said administrative closure has allowed immigrants who lack legal status to remain indefinitely in the US, acting in effect like an amnesty.

Hundreds of thousands of cases

Administrative closure has been applied over the years in hundreds of thousands of deportation cases. Ending the practice is part of Trump’s hardline approach towards immigrants.

In 2024 Joe Biden’s administration adopted a regulation that formally codified administrative closure procedures, concluding that it lets judges efficiently manage their caseloads and promote the fair treatment of immigrants. That regulation replaced a previous rule adopted in 2020 during Trump’s first term in office that had been judicially blocked.

After Trump returned to office in 2025, the justice department office that oversees immigration courts, the executive office for immigration review, announced it would not defend the Biden rule against a legal challenge.

The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception

— The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza

In a lawsuit, Texas argued that the rule lets immigration judges “effectively grant indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country”.

Trump’s administration and the state then jointly asked US district judge Reed O’Connor in Wichita Falls, Texas, to approve an agreement declaring the Biden rule unlawful. O’Connor did so, blocking it permanently, nationwide.

Three municipalities — Baltimore; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio — and the legal services provider, Centro Legal de la Raza, sought to intervene in the case to defend the rule, but O’Connor rejected their bid. The cities say they all have substantial immigrant populations.

The New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put the agreement on hold pending an appeal of O’Connor’s decision.

The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza told the supreme court in a filing that Trump’s administration circumvented a federal law governing agency procedures by using “manufactured litigation” with “ideologically aligned” Texas to eliminate a regulation it disliked.

“The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception,” they wrote.

title: Chelsea mother claims in lawsuit that ICE officers 'violently attacked' her in front of her child
description:
A Chelsea mother and green card holder says in a new lawsuit against the Trump administration that she was “violently attacked” by masked federal immigration officers last year.
The federal lawsuit alleges the ICE officers’ conduct violated the Fourth and Fifth amendments, federal statute and ICE’s own standards of conduct.
When she cried out to the ICE officers that her brother had autism, one told her to “shut up,”’ reads the complaint.
The son, who Ramirez Sanan said has trouble communicating verbally, witnessed the entire arrest.

text:
A Chelsea mother and green card holder says in a new lawsuit against the Trump administration that she was “violently attacked” by masked federal immigration officers last year.

Hilda Ramirez Sanan sued the federal government in the U.S. District Court of Massachusetts on Tuesday after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrested her during a September 2025 encounter near Chelsea District Court. Other plaintiffs in the federal lawsuit are her U.S. citizen children— her daughter, Michelle Ramirez Sanan, 18, and her now 14-year-old son, identified in the suit as J.R.S.

Ramirez Sanan, who has lived lawfully in the country for more than 20 years, says the officers didn’t check her identification nor look at her green card.

In an interview with GBH News on Tuesday, Ramirez Sanan tearfully recounted how the incident caused long-lasting harm that upended the lives of her family members. “I want justice. It’s not just us— we’re humans, we’re not animals. We have rights. We’re human beings,” said Ramirez Sanan.

“I didn’t have any immigration issues or open case. I don’t know why they did this,“ she said. “No one listened to me. No one asked for my identification. I begged them to listen because my son was witnessing this and was being held by four ICE agents who were armed, and this has caused us such profound trauma.”

Ramirez Sanan has been unable to work due to injuries from the arrest, going to occupational therapy for her injuries to her hand, legs and feet every eight days.

The family is suing for the physical and emotional trauma experienced during the arrest, which their attorneys at Lawyers for Civil Rights and Zimmer, Citron & Clarke LLP say was illegal.

“The family is courageously bringing this suit to seek justice for themselves, and to stand up to government abuses towards immigrant communities more broadly. ICE’s attack of the family was illegal, unconstitutional, and unconscionable, and we intend to seek justice,” said Jillian Lenson, senior attorney at Lawyers for Civil Rights in an interview.

In late 2025, the family submitted an administrative claim to the Department of Homeland Security and ICE a required precursor for a federal lawsuit. In the claim, they sought a million dollars in damages.

Under the Federal Tort Claims Act, once six months have elapsed, a lawsuit may be filed in federal court. Lenson said the federal government never “resolved” the complaint from last December.

The federal lawsuit alleges the ICE officers’ conduct violated the Fourth and Fifth amendments, federal statute and ICE’s own standards of conduct.

“We are seeking damages on behalf of the family for the enduring emotional trauma and pain and suffering they’ve continued to feel since the violent attack,” said Lenson.

LCR posted a video of the interaction on its website.

Case history

On Sept. 26, 2025 Ramirez Sanan, 51, was accompanying a family member to a court hearing in Chelsea with her son in the backseat, according to the lawsuit. A group of unmarked vehicles surrounded and blocked her car two blocks from the courthouse, and eight armed and masked officers surrounded the car, the lawsuit says.

In a video of the incident, masked agents tell Ramirez Sanan, a green card holder, to get out of the car and she refuses. The agents eventually smash the car glass, pull Ramirez Sanan out and forcibly restrain her.

They also unbuckled the seat belt and pulled her then 13-year-old, who has autism, out of the car while he cried. He was asked his legal status. The vehicle, according to the complaint, had a prominently displayed disability placard hanging in the front.

When Ramirez Sanan’s eldest daughter arrived at the scene, she was physically blocked from talking to her mother and brother. She’s shown in another video being kept away.

“‘[An ICE officer] forcibly holding her hands and wrists, and physically preventing her from approaching her mother and brother. When she cried out to the ICE officers that her brother had autism, one told her to “shut up,”’ reads the complaint.

The son, who Ramirez Sanan said has trouble communicating verbally, witnessed the entire arrest. Agents grabbed him by the shoulder and kept him against the fence. They threatened to arrest him if he did not answer their questions or show them his papers.

According to the complaint, one of the agents kicked Ramirez Sanan, twisted her arms behind her back, and pushing her to the ground face-first. Ramirez Sanan said she “lost consciousness” during that time.

Ramirez Sanan said in the complaint that as she was being dragged to an unmarked vehicle, local police showed up.

“Local police intervened and requested that the ICE officers check Ms. Ramirez Sanan’s identification. Now under the watch of local law enforcement, the ICE officers reviewed Ms. Ramirez Sanan’s identification, released her from their custody, and left the scene,” said the complaint.

An ambulance then took her and her children to a hospital emergency room for medical evaluation. She has been in occupational therapy weekly for her leg and her hands for the past year, and is in the process of getting behavioral health support for her child, who she described to GBH News as “immensely impacted.”

Doctors gave Ramirez Sanan a blood test, several X-rays, and a CT scan for her head and spine to determine her injuries, the lawsuit said. The doctors assessed that she likely had a radial nerve injury and referred her to a consult with a hand surgeon, according to the complaint, and that she was potentially concussed.

JRS is now taking medication for anxiety and depression, and has had trouble walking since the incident. He’s seeing a neurologist and physical therapist.

The complaint describes changes in his mental health. “Since the attack, he has suffered migraines, frequent crying fits, and nightmares. He has woken up from his nightmares screaming, “don’t kill my mom.”

title: What the Supreme Court's Block on Immigration Judge Pauses Means for 361,000 ...
description:
More than 361,000 immigration cases — the vast majority involving Latino immigrants — currently sit off active court dockets, and attorneys warn those cases now face an accelerated path toward hearings and potential removal orders.
Decades of Practice, Eliminated in a Single Day Administrative closure developed over decades inside the immigration court system as a practical caseload tool.
Those figures span both immigration court and Board of Immigration Appeals cases.
The geographic concentration of the impact falls hardest on communities with the heaviest immigration court backlogs.
The EOIR automated case inquiry system allows individuals to check the current status of an immigration court case using their A-number at no cost.
text:
The Briefing

The U.S. Supreme Court issued an unsigned order on October 27 rejecting an emergency request to restore immigration judges' authority to temporarily close deportation cases, leaving in place a June 2026 Texas federal court judgment that eliminated the Biden administration's formal administrative closure rule.

More than 361,000 immigration cases — the vast majority involving Latino immigrants — currently sit off active court dockets, and attorneys warn those cases now face an accelerated path toward hearings and potential removal orders.

Crime victims holding U visa applications, immigrants with pending family petitions, and people appealing criminal convictions face the sharpest exposure, as the ruling removes the only procedural mechanism available to pause their deportation cases while separate legal proceedings play out.

What the Supreme Court Ruled — and What It Deliberately Left Open

Without a single dissent or a word of written reasoning, the U.S. Supreme Court on October 27 refused to block a lower court judgment that stripped immigration judges of their power to temporarily suspend deportation proceedings. The court's unsigned order rejected an emergency application filed by three cities and a legal services group asking the justices to pause that judgment while they fought to intervene in the underlying case.

Crucially, the court did not declare administrative closure unconstitutional, nor did it settle whether immigration judges retain some residual authority to close cases outside a formal regulation. The order simply left the existing Texas federal court judgment in place — a meaningful distinction for practitioners, even if the practical effect for immigrants in the system is immediate and severe.

Decades of Practice, Eliminated in a Single Day

Administrative closure developed over decades inside the immigration court system as a practical caseload tool. When a person facing deportation had a separate proceeding in progress — a pending visa petition with a U.S. citizen spouse, a U visa application filed after cooperating with police, or a criminal conviction under appeal that could affect their removability — a judge could temporarily remove that case from the active calendar. The deportation case did not close; it paused.

The Biden administration formally codified the practice in 2024 under the regulation known as the "Efficient Case and Docket Management in Immigration Proceedings" rule, giving it a regulatory foundation it had previously lacked. That foundation was eliminated on June 22, 2026, and the Supreme Court's October 27 order confirms that elimination will stand.

The Texas-DOJ Agreement That Set This in Motion

On the morning of June 22, 2026, Texas filed a lawsuit in the Northern District of Texas challenging the 2024 administrative closure rule. Within hours of that complaint being docketed, Texas and the Trump administration's Justice Department jointly moved for entry of a consent judgment — in effect settling a case that had been filed that same morning. Chief U.S. District Judge Reed O'Connor signed the final order the same day, vacating the rule in its entirety, permanently barring DOJ from enforcing it, and prohibiting any future administration from issuing similar regulations without express Congressional authorization. Both sides waived the right to appeal.

The challengers told the Supreme Court the arrangement amounted to "egregious collusion" — a coordinated maneuver to kill a federal regulation through manufactured litigation, bypassing the notice-and-comment process that the Administrative Procedure Act requires for standard rulemaking. Texas and the administration argued the opposite: that the practice had operated as an unauthorized indefinite stay for people with no legal path to remain in the country.

Who Filed the Emergency Appeal — and Why They Failed

After the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals declined to grant emergency relief and allow the coalition to formally intervene in the case, three cities — Baltimore, Columbus, Ohio, and New Haven, Connecticut — together with Centro Legal de la Raza, an immigrant legal services organization, brought an emergency application to the Supreme Court on October 9. The application was first directed to Justice Samuel Alito and subsequently referred to the full court.

In their filings, the cities argued that eliminating administrative closure would generate measurable harm at the local level: fewer undocumented crime victims willing to report offenses to police, accelerated removal of longtime residents who contribute to local tax bases, and an erosion of the due process protections the courts had recognized for decades. The Supreme Court's silent denial on October 27 ended that argument without response.

What the 361,000 Paused Cases Face Now

According to EOIR adjudication statistics generated on July 31, 2025, there were 361,614 cases classified as inactive pending — held off active immigration court dockets by administrative closure orders. The average case in that pool had been closed for approximately 16½ years; the median was roughly 11½ years. Those figures span both immigration court and Board of Immigration Appeals cases.

The DOJ maintained during litigation that the June 2026 judgment does not require immigration courts to immediately reopen every closed case. But immigration practitioners warn the distinction is narrowing quickly: cases are already being recalendared, and without any regulatory authority to request closure, there is no procedural mechanism left to resist that process.

The geographic concentration of the impact falls hardest on communities with the heaviest immigration court backlogs. TRAC data from February 2026 shows Miami-Dade County leading the country with 143,817 pending deportation cases, followed by Cook County, Illinois at 112,686, Queens County, New York at 103,791, and Los Angeles County at 98,792. A substantial portion of those cases previously had the protection of administrative closure.

Crime Victims and U Visa Applicants Face the Sharpest Risk

Congress created the U visa specifically to encourage undocumented crime victims to cooperate with law enforcement, offering a path toward legal status in exchange for assistance with investigations and prosecutions. The program's annual approval cap sits at 10,000 principal visas per fiscal year — far below the volume of applicants, producing a multi-year waiting list for people who have already been vetted by law enforcement.

Since 2021, USCIS had been issuing what are called "good faith determinations" — official acknowledgments that a U visa petition meets the baseline criteria for review — and those documents offered a measure of protection from removal while applicants waited. According to NBC News reporting, immigration attorneys and legal experts now say the Trump administration has taken the position that good faith determinations no longer shield applicants from deportation or detention. That means a person who reported a crime, received law enforcement certification, and holds a USCIS good faith determination can still be arrested and removed while their visa application remains unresolved.

The Track Record of Closed Cases — and What It Reveals

Prior research tracking outcomes for immigrants whose administratively closed cases were later returned to active dockets has found that the majority of those individuals ultimately receive authorization to remain in the United States. Advocates have long cited this data to argue that administrative closure has functioned not merely as a scheduling tool but as a reliable signal that a credible legal claim exists. The Supreme Court's refusal to intervene leaves that protection unavailable to the more than 361,000 people whose cases had depended on it.

What Families and Attorneys Should Do Immediately

For anyone whose immigration case is currently in administrative closure, the most urgent priority is confirming whether that case has been or is likely to be recalendared. Those with a pending I-130 family petition, an active U visa application, or a criminal conviction still under appeal retain potential routes forward — but only if they act before a hearing is set and a removal order is issued.

The EOIR automated case inquiry system allows individuals to check the current status of an immigration court case using their A-number at no cost. The same information is available by calling 1-800-898-7180. Consulting a qualified immigration attorney before any hearing date is scheduled remains the most effective protective step available.

Along with then–White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, she said that Trump wanted his armed supporters to march that day, and overheard a conversation where Trump said that Mike Pence “deserves it,” regarding chants of “hang Mike Pence” heard during the riot.

Faruqui told the prosecutors that if they wanted to file a superseding complaint, then a judge would first have to find probable cause that a crime had actually been committed. Instead, the government had transmitted the complaint in the middle of the night and expected the judge to sign it.

Faruqui said that he believed the government had broken precedent by seeking a superseding complaint without first receiving a judge’s signature.

“I’m concerned with your view as to what the law is,” he said. “Why today, on this one case, have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases?”

After Floris and Benavides surrendered on arrest warrants last week, Faruqui had ordered a hearing on Tuesday in order to establish probable cause for the initial complaint. Notably, the DOJ did not obtain a grand jury indictment against the ex-officials.

On Monday night, the government submitted an unsworn affidavit it claimed would support an additional obstruction charge. Faruqui refused to sign the complaint without reviewing it or finding probable cause, and proceeded to hold the hearing on just the first complaint.
