text:
The Advocates for Human Rights accepts Zabel Human Rights Award on behalf of Courageous Minnesotans

October 27, 2026

The Advocates joined Minnesota-based COPAL earlier this month to accept Human Rights First's William D. Zabel Human Rights Award on behalf of courageous Minnesotans standing up for our neighbors and U.S. democracy. Read Executive Director Michele Garnett McKenzie's full remarks below:

Good evening.

I’m Michele Garnett McKenzie, executive director of The Advocates for Human Rights, and I am deeply honored to accept the William D. Zabel Human Rights Award on behalf of the people of Minnesota.

This award recognizes something extraordinary. Not the work of a single organization or the efforts of a handful of leaders. But the collective courage of thousands of ordinary people who chose solidarity over fear.

At The Advocates for Human Rights, we believe that everyone has a part to play in defending human rights.

Minnesota proved that.

When human rights are under attack, lawyers have a part to play. Organizers have a part to play. Faith leaders, teachers, healthcare workers, business owners, students, artists, neighbors—and most of all—those who are in the crosshairs of oppression for no reason other than what they look or sound like, what they say or believe—we all have a part to play.

Human rights are protected when ordinary people decide those rights matter.

Operation Metro Surge was billed as an immigration enforcement operation. But those of us who witnessed it understood that it was something more.

Yes, it was a direct attack on refugees and immigrants in Minnesota. But it was a shot across the bow of democracy itself.

Textbook authoritarianism. Target communities you believe are vulnerable. Test whether people will look away. Whether institutions will remain silent. Whether fear will become stronger than solidarity.

What happened in Minnesota was a test. And the people of Minnesota answered.

Across the state, people refused to stand by. Led by fearless immigrant, refugee, Indigenous, and labor leaders, Minnesotans marched on a cold day in January. Checked on neighbors. Patrolled the streets. Stood guard over mosques and schools. People who had never thought of themselves as human rights defenders discovered that they were exactly that.

Over the last six months, The Advocates for Human Rights has worked with the Minnesota Truth Council to document the impact of Operation Metro Surge and Operation PARRIS. We have documented human rights violations from enforced disappearances and arbitrary detention to the denial of the right to food, health, and education. Of infiltration and surveillance. Of direct targeting of movement leaders. But also stories of extraordinary courage, resilience, and resistance.

Because authoritarianism depends on distortion and erasure, on people forgetting what happened or doubting what we experienced, documenting truth is itself an act of resistance.

Authoritarian regimes do not rely on strength alone. They rely on exhaustion.

They throw everything they have at people. They spread lies. They manufacture confusion. They create crisis after crisis. Their goal is to wear us down, distract us, divide us, and make us too afraid to act.

Authoritarianism is not inevitable.

When people remain clear-eyed about the truth, when we are relentless in demanding accountability, and when we keep our focus on the world we are trying to build, we can prevail.

Minnesota showed that courage is contagious.

Minnesota showed that solidarity is stronger than intimidation.

Minnesota showed that when people unite around human dignity, authoritarian tactics can be defeated.

The work ahead remains difficult. The forces that seek to divide us have not disappeared. The attacks on immigrant communities are escalating. The pressure on democratic institutions is real.

But this award reminds us that we are not powerless.

Thank you to Human Rights First for your courage, your documentation, and your recognition that everyone has a part to play in defending human rights.

The parents of Alex Pretti, a U.S. citizen and ICU nurse who was fatally shot by immigration officers in Minneapolis nine months ago, slammed the federal government and demanded the release of all the evidence related to their son’s death.

Michael and Susan Pretti said at a news conference Tuesday that the federal government has kept them in the dark for 275 days — even after they sent a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche over the summer “begging for basic information the law affords,” including the identities of the officers involved in the shooting.

“At every turn, they have ignored us, misled us and shielded Alex’s killers,” Michael Pretti said.

“We want our son’s killers to be brought into justice once and for all,” Susan Pretti said. “We are here begging for the Department of Justice to do what is right.”

Kiersten Pels, a spokesperson for the Department of Justice, told NBC News that communications between federal officials and victims’ families “do not typically occur” during an investigation.

“As is standard practice, communications with family members, if any, come at a later stage of a case, such as indictment, initial appearance, plea, trial, or sentencing,” Pels said in a statement. “The timing is consistent with how these types of investigations proceed.”

The Department of Homeland Security referred all questions to the FBI.

Tuesday’s news conference comes nearly a week after Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said the federal government stopped sharing information with Minnesota authorities who are investigating Pretti’s killing.

Moriarty’s office sued the Trump administration in March to compel federal officials to share key evidence pertaining to Pretti’s death and the shootings of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan man who was wounded by an ICE officer, and Renee Good, who was fatally shot by another ICE officer.

The three Minnesota shootings took place in January, after the Trump administration deployed more than 3,000 immigration officers and agents to the state as part of “Operation Metro Surge,” the DHS’s largest immigration enforcement operation.

In July, Minnesota officials said the federal government was starting to turn over evidence in the cases, including police body camera video and hard drives containing statements. Moriarty said at the time that she expected to receive “all the evidence.”

That changed this month, according to Moriarty. In a statement last week, she accused the federal government of withholding evidence related to the fatal shootings of Good and Pretti and “obstructing our investigations for however long they can.”

“Our lawsuit was filed to gain access to all of the evidence and our efforts to obtain it will continue. We have filed our motion for summary judgment to bring an end to the case and secure the evidence to which we’re entitled,” Moriarty said. “The federal government responded with a motion to dismiss; their aim is clear.”

In the motion filed by DOJ attorneys at the U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., last week, the federal government argued it has the authority to decline sharing information with state authorities if no formal legal proceedings are underway.

The Trump administration has previously suggested that state prosecutors have no jurisdiction to investigate federal officers, while Minnesota officials have said the federal government can’t be trusted to investigate itself.

“This is not normal. This is not justice. It is morally wrong,” Michael Pretti said at the news conference. He decried the lack of cooperation between federal and local authorities in investigating his son’s killing as “just baffling, disappointing and reprehensible.”

Steven L. Schleicher, a lawyer for the Prettis who was also at the news conference, said his clients are entitled to see any evidence about the shooting under the Crime Victims’ Rights Act.

“How is it possible that the Department of Justice is not sharing evidence?” Schleicher said. “What are they hiding?”

During his confirmation hearing in July, Blanche was asked about his commitment to sharing information on the ICE-involved shootings in Minnesota with state officials. He said he expected the investigations into those cases to be run as usual, adding that “the definition of full cooperation can be disputed.”

Videos showing Alex Pretti’s killing haunt his family every day, his parents said. At the same time, according to them, those images were crucial in contradicting the Trump administration’s narrative of the shooting.

“The federal government went on TV and lied about Alex. They tried to slander his memory to cover up their crime,” Susan Pretti said. “Not only was it wrong, it was shameful, unfair, unacceptable. We want to clear our son’s name.”

Joins coalition of 20 AGs in lawsuit to block Treasury Department’s gutting of bipartisan Corporate Transparency Act, which requires businesses to disclose who owns and controls them so criminals can’t hide dirty money

Trump Administration issued new rule exempting nearly every business from reporting, making it nearly impossible to catch and prosecute money launderers, tax cheats, and fraudsters

AG Ellison: “This. Corruption. Has. To. Stop”

October 27, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) — Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison today joined a coalition of 21 states filing in a lawsuit to stop the Trump administration from gutting a federal law that helps police and prosecutors catch money launderers, tax cheats, and fraudsters.

The law, the Corporate Transparency Act, requires businesses to tell the federal government who actually owns and controls them. That matters because criminals often hide their money in shell companies — businesses that exist on paper but don’t do much of anything — so their names never show up. Now the United States Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, known as FinCEN, has exempted 99.9% of businesses from the law, making it nearly useless.

“Let’s review: the Treasury Department that answers to Donald Trump, the most nakedly corrupt president in American history — who has 34 personal convictions for fraud, has pardoned or commuted the sentences of scores of convicted fraudsters, and is gleefully using the White House to enrich himself to the tune of billions of dollars through shady deals with foreign governments and bitcoin companies — has gutted a bipartisan federal law designed to track dirty money and keep corporations honest. Raise your hand if you’re surprised,” Attorney General Ellison said. “FinCEN now stands for the Financial Crimes Empowerment Network. I’m filing this lawsuit because This. Corruption. Has. To. Stop.”

Congress passed the Corporate Transparency Act with bipartisan support in 2021. It created a Treasury database of business owners that law enforcement can use to trace dirty money, track down stolen assets, and uncover bribes and political payoffs.

In August 2026, the Trump Administration issued a rule exempting nearly every business from reporting. Then FinCEN went further, announcing it would delete the ownership information already in the database, records that likely include evidence of unsolved crimes. The states argue that would break multiple federal laws.

In the lawsuit, Attorney General Ellison and the coalition that FinCEN has:

Violated the Corporate Transparency Act and Administrative Procedure Act;

Skipped required legal steps before changing the rule;

Acted arbitrarily and without a reasonable explanation; and

Failed to properly consult the Secretary of Homeland Security and the U.S. Attorney General before exempting nearly all businesses.

Attorney General Ellison and the coalition ask the court to throw out FinCEN’s rule and require the agency to keep collecting and maintaining the ownership database for law enforcement.

Leads coalition of 17 AGs in amicus brief asking federal court to hear appeal; second time this year AG Ellison and coalition have supported TPS for Somali Americans

October 27, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) — For the second time this year, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison has led a coalition of 17 attorneys general in filing an amicus brief in support of a lawsuit to block Department of Homeland Security’s termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Somali immigrants. The TPS program is a crucial humanitarian lifeline that Congress established in the 1990 to protect immigrants from being returned to countries like Somalia that have been deemed unsafe, allowing them to work and build a life in the United States. Approximately 3,850 immigrants from Somalia have been living in the United States with TPS or have had pending applications for TPS, many of them in Minnesota.

“The Trump Administration’s insistence on terminating Temporary Protected Status for Somali nationals isn’t only cruel, it’s harmful to communities across Minnesota and in every state where Somalis live, work, grow the economy, pay taxes, and give back,” Attorney General Ellison said. “I led this coalition of attorneys general supporting the plaintiffs who want to block the revocation of TPS for Somalis because we recognize the contributions of our Somali neighbors that strengthen our states and our people and do not want our states to be harmed if the revocation is allowed to stand.”

This is the second amicus brief that Attorney General Ellison led this year of attorneys general defending Somali TPS, following the first one he led in April 2026. The brief filed yesterday in African Communities Together v. Mullin supports the plaintiffs’ request that the appeals court reverse a lower court decision not to grant emergency relief and block the Department of Homeland Security’s revocation of TPS for Somali nationals.

The coalition states are home to at least 53,000 Somali immigrants, with Minnesota alone home to at least 37,500. These numbers include TPS holders, whom the coalition states have taken public steps to support because Somali immigrants, including TPS holders, make vital contributions to the communities in which they live: they are valued neighbors, homeowners, coworkers, teachers, students, entrepreneurs, caregivers, construction workers, union members, and parents. Stripping TPS holders of legal status would harm the residents, economies, and public health and safety of Minnesota and the coalition states.

In the brief, Attorney General Ellison and the coalition highlight the harms Minnesota and the coalition states and their residents — including the U.S. citizen children of Somali nationals with TPS — will experience with the revocation of TPS for Somalis, arguing that it would harm their states’ economies, residents, and public health and safety.

Somali immigrants make a significant, positive impact on Minnesota’s economy: their annual economic impact is roughly $8.6 billion and they pay an estimated $228 million annually in state and local taxes. They also contribute to critical industries: as of 2019, over 15 percent of all Somali immigrants in Minnesota worked in home health care, and Somali workers made up 11 percent of the state’s workers in animal food processing. Somali immigrants are also known for their entrepreneurship, starting businesses that create jobs, circulate dollars locally, and revitalize communities. The Minnesota Department of Economic Development has recognized that “[w]ithout foreign-born workers,” of which Somalis are the second-largest group in Minnesota, “many businesses in Minnesota would not have the workers they need to operate, let alone grow and thrive.” Allowing the revocation of Somalia’s TPS designation to stand endangers these economic contributions to communities in every corner of Minnesota.

Creating new undocumented citizens by revoking TPS for Somali nationals would have ripple effects throughout educational and public-health systems. Operation Metro Surge, the purpose of which President Trump claimed was to root out fraud in Somali communities in Minnesota, led to high rates of absenteeism throughout public schools in Minneapolis, including of U.S. citizen children of Somali immigrants — many of whom themselves are U.S. citizens.

Stripping legal status from Somali immigrants also risks serious negative consequences for public health. Everyone benefits when residents are vaccinated or seek testing and treatment for infectious diseases. But undocumented immigrants are often reluctant to seek medical treatment due to fear of detention and deportation. Newly undocumented former TPS holders may also not seek treatment for their U.S. citizen children. Children of undocumented immigrants frequently miss preventive annual exams and are often sicker when seeking emergency room care. In Minneapolis, 40 percent of respondents to a recent survey who needed to go to urgent care or the hospital during Operation Metro Surge reported they stayed home because of fears about ICE agents, and 30 percent of respondents who had a regularly scheduled vaccine during the operation missed the vaccine out of the same fears.

The impacts on the mental health and well-being of revoking TPS for Somali nationals on their U.S. citizen children would also be severe. Children of undocumented parents in the United States frequently experience persistent anxiety from fear that a family member may be deported. During Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota, immigration officers targeted individuals they believed appeared to be Somali regardless of citizenship or immigration status, demonstrating that these fears were unfortunately well founded.

Mental health consequences are even more severe when these fears are realized and families are forcibly separated. Parental deportation is deeply traumatic for children and is linked to extreme psychological distress, anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, externalizing behaviors such as aggression, and difficulties sleeping.

In the brief, Attorney General Ellison and the coalition note that revoking Somalia’s TPS designation would present current TPS holders, particularly those with U.S. citizen children, with an agonizing choice:

return to Somalia alone, leaving their children behind;

taking their U.S. citizen children with them to a dangerous country that the children do not know; or

staying in the United States without authorization and living with significant fear and uncertainty, knowing they cannot work legally and could be forcibly removed to Somalia at any time.

History of TPS for Somali nationals

Somalia was first designated for TPS in 1991 by Acting Attorney General William Barr due to “extraordinary and temporary conditions.” Civil war has raged in Somalia for the ensuing 35 years, resulting in hundreds of thousands of deaths, children being forced into combat, extrajudicial killings, sexual and gender-based violence, and other human-rights abuses. Given the ongoing violence and suffering, Somalia’s TPS designation had been continually in place until now.

In November 2025, President Trump posted on social media that he was “hereby terminating, effective immediately, the Temporary Protected Status (TPS Program) for Somalis in Minnesota...” Since then, President Trump has repeatedly launched racist attacks against Somali immigrants, calling them “garbage” and “stupid people” with “low IQs” “from a crooked country, disgusting country, one of the worst countries in the world.” In January 2026, Kristi then-Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem announced she was terminating Somalia’s TPS designation in part even though she did not claim that Somalia as a whole is safe and despite the fact that the U.S. State Department has issued its highest travel advisory for Somalia, warning travelers, “Do not travel to Somalia for any reason,” because of “unrest, crime, kidnapping, terrorism,” and more.

Following a June 2026 decision of the U.S. Supreme Court, DHS revoked TPS for immigrants from Somalia on August 14, 2026.

Today, Representative Rick Larsen (WA-02) wrote to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) regarding Larsen’s visit to ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) suboffice in Ferndale on October 9th:

“I support HSI’s mission to investigate and apprehend individuals involved in cross-border criminal activity, including human and drug trafficking,” said Rep. Larsen. “However, I am concerned by reports that HSI personnel, including those in Northwest Washington, have been reassigned to conduct civil immigration enforcement. HSI agents should be focused on investigating serious criminal activity, not diverted to support the President’s mass deportation agenda."

Rep. Larsen is conducting robust, close oversight of Trump’s immigration enforcement in Northwest Washington. In addition to ICE’s HSI facility, Rep. Larsen visited ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) facility in Ferndale in July 2026 and the privately-run ICE detention facility in Tacoma in June 2025.

“This is not case-closed on oversight of ICE activity in our region,” said Rep. Larsen. “I will keep pushing to get answers and accountability for my community. My office stands ready to help family members locate their loved ones in ICE custody and access legal services – call 425-252-3188 or go to larsen.house.gov/helping-you/visas-and-immigration.htm.”

Rep. Larsen’s full letter to Secretary Mullin and Acting Director Venturella is available here and below.

October 27, 2026

Dear Secretary Mullin and Acting Director Venturella:

Thank you for the opportunity to visit the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Blaine field office in Ferndale, Washington on October 9, 2026.

I support HSI’s mission to investigate and apprehend individuals involved in cross-border criminal activity, including drug smuggling, human trafficking and child exploitation. However, I am concerned by reports that HSI personnel, including those in Northwest Washington, have been reassigned to conduct civil immigration enforcement alongside ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO).

According to an August 20, 2026 report by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Office of Inspector General (OIG), HSI agents devoted 800 percent more hours to immigration enforcement in Fiscal Year (FY) 2025 than in FY 2024. During the same period, hours spent investigating fentanyl-related crimes fell by 31 percent, while fentanyl seizures by HSI agents declined by 39 percent.1 HSI agents should be focused on investigating serious criminal activity, not diverted to support ERO’s civil immigration enforcement operations as part of the President’s mass deportation agenda.

To better understand whether HSI’s operations in Northwest Washington have been affected by the diversion of HSI staff to civil immigration enforcement, please provide the following information no later than Friday, November 20, 2026:

1. Since January 20, 2025, how many HSI agents assigned to the Blaine field office have been reassigned, detailed or otherwise assigned to support ERO operations? For each reassignment, please provide the number of personnel involved, the date the reassignment began and the duration.

2. Since the start of FY 2023 on October 1, 2022, how many agent hours at HSI Blaine have been dedicated to supporting the ERO mission of civil immigration enforcement? Please provide this data by year for FY 2023 through FY 2026.

3. Since the start of FY 2023, how many agent hours at HSI Blaine have been dedicated to investigating fentanyl-related criminal activity? Please provide this data by year for FY 2023 through FY 2026.

4. Since the start of FY 2023, how many fentanyl seizures have agents at HSI Blaine carried out? Please provide this data by year for FY 2023 through FY 2026.

5. Since January 20, 2025, have HSI officers received any directives, orders or guidance to expand or limit their work with ERO? If so, please provide copies of any relevant directives, orders or guidance and their dates of issuance.

6. Has the HSI Blaine facility been used to detain individuals arrested by ERO? If so, please provide exact dates and details of these detentions.

Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter. I look forward to your response.

text:
The Senate has ordered a comprehensive investigation into travel agencies suspected of facilitating the trafficking and exploitation of Nigerians in Libya, following the adoption of a joint committee report on the abuse of Nigerian migrants in the North African country.

The report, considered at plenary on Tuesday, 27th October 2027, was presented by Sen. Anthony Yaro (APC: Gombe) on behalf of the Joint Committees on Diaspora and Non-Governmental Organisations; Judiciary, Human Rights and Legal Matters; Foreign Affairs; and Special Duties, arising from a motion on the urgent need to protect Nigerians from trafficking, slavery and human rights abuses in Libya.

Adopting the report’s recommendations, the Senate directed the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP) to lead the investigation in collaboration with the Nigeria Police Force, the Nigeria Immigration Service, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission and the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The agencies are to interrogate the directors, officers and agents of the identified travel agencies, with the inquiry covering recruitment networks, financial transactions and travel arrangements linked to the trafficking and exploitation of Nigerians abroad.

The Senate further urged a review and stronger enforcement of the Trafficking in Persons (Prohibition) Enforcement and Administration Act, 2015 and the Child Rights Act, 2003, and called for increased funding for NAPTIP and other relevant agencies to support investigations, prosecutions and victim assistance.

On victim support, the Senate resolved that the Federal Government should establish a National Reintegration and Protection Programme for returning victims and vulnerable Nigerians, to be coordinated by the National Commission for Refugees, Migrants and Internally Displaced Persons in collaboration with NAPTIP. It also urged the Federal Government to intensify diplomatic engagement with Libya through bilateral and multilateral channels, both to combat trafficking and to promote safe and legal migration pathways.

However, theconsideration of the report prompted a wider debate on domestic security, with senators calling for stricter tenancy laws requiring landlords to verify the identities of their tenants, including through the National Identification Number, and proposing legislation to regulate short-let apartments on the ground that unverified rentals could enable criminals to avoid detection.

Senate President Godswill Akpabio (APC: Akwa Ibom) said landlords who rent to unidentified persons “could inadvertently provide cover for criminal activities,” and proposed a “Know-Your-Tenant” policy that would hold landlords accountable for tenant information. He called for tougher deterrent measures, citing the anti-kidnapping legislation he signed as Governor of Akwa Ibom State.

Sen. Aminu Tambuwal (ADC:Sokoto) proposed tenant registration, rent control, security checks and proof of landlord ownership, and urged the National Assembly to encourage state legislatures to adopt similar measures. Sen. Babangida Hussaini (APC: Jigawa) pointed to Lagos State’s existing tenancy law as a possible model, while Sen. Adams Oshiomhole (APC:Edo) emphasised the organised and international features of trafficking and the need to address demand in destination countries.

Sen. Neda Imasuen (APC: Edo) struck a dissenting note, arguing that Nigeria’s difficulty lies not in a shortage of legislation but in the failure to enforce the laws already on the statute books.

text:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court refused Tuesday to immediately block an immigration-related agreement between the Justice Department and the state of Texas affecting the rules for deportation proceedings that opponents have described as “egregious collusion” between the Republican-led state and the Trump administration.

Three cities and an immigrant advocacy group had asked the justices to halt the deal and clear a path to reinstate a Biden administration policy that had given immigration judges discretion to postpone deportation proceedings in certain cases.

The cities — Baltimore; New Haven, Conn.; and Columbus, Ohio — have significant immigrant communities and back the Biden-era policy, saying it was an important procedure that has existed in some form for decades and has implications for hundreds of thousands of cases.

The Supreme Court’s one-sentence order did not include any reasoning, which is often the case when the justices respond to emergency requests. There were no noted dissents.

At issue was the rule known as “administrative closure,” which gives immigration judges discretion to suspend deportation proceedings in some situations, such as when an individual is seeking humanitarian protections or other legal status to remain in the country. The cities told the court that the administrative closure process was intended to “promote efficiency or protect due process rights.”

Between 2013 and 2017, the number of removal cases closed using the rule increased from nearly 172,000 to more than 268,000, according to the Trump administration.

During the first Trump administration, the attorney general found that immigration judges lacked the authority “to indefinitely suspend immigration proceedings through administrative closure.” In 2024, the Justice Department issued a new rule that once again gave immigration judges the discretion to halt some deportation proceedings.

As part of President Donald Trump’s mass-deportation agenda, the administration has overhauled immigration courts and pressured judges to deport more people. Unlike the independent federal judiciary, immigration courts are part of the Justice Department.

In April 2025, the acting director of the Executive Office for Immigration Review, the unit at the Justice Department that runs the immigration courts, issued a memo saying it “could not — and will not — defend” the 2024 rule reinstating the administrative closure process. But the office said immigration judges should continue to follow it “unless they have a legal basis for not doing so.”

Ken Paxton, the Republican attorney general in Texas and an ally of Trump, sued the federal government in June over the 2024 rule, which he argued operated as de facto amnesty because it allowed immigration judges to delay deportation proceedings, in some cases for years. The continued presence of immigrants lacking permanent legal status, the state said, caused “fiscal, public safety, and sovereign harms.”

The two sides were ideologically aligned but formally on opposite sides in a lawsuit. On the same day the lawsuit was filed, the two sides told a judge they had agreed to settle it, ending the matter with a binding agreement removing the immigration judges’ discretion. America First Legal, a group co-founded by Stephen Miller, a senior White House adviser and the architect of much of Trump’s immigration policy, has helped represent Texas.

The lawsuit was filed in Wichita Falls, Texas, a go-to destination for the Justice Department. At the time, Judge Reed O’Connor, who was nominated by President George W. Bush, heard every case brought in that division.

O’Connor quickly signed off on the settlement with a brief order and later ruled that the cities and advocates did not have legal grounds, known as standing, to sue. The 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals refused to block the agreement, and opponents then asked the Supreme Court to intervene.

In court filings, city officials and Centro Legal, which provides legal services to immigrants, said the proposed agreement was an abuse of the court system because the federal government and the state of Texas were on the same side. The move, they said, allowed the administration to undo an agency action without going through the proper process.

Paxton’s office told the justices in a filing that there had been a live, legitimate controversy between the state and the administration because the rule was still in effect when Texas sued.

The cities said they would be harmed by the settlement in part because of the potential loss of tax revenue from residents who might be deported and because crime victims living in the country illegally might be discouraged from cooperating with law enforcement in the face of reopened deportation hearings.

In response, D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, said the challengers did not have legal grounds to intervene because they were not regulated by the rule, which applies to immigrants in removal proceedings and not to the cities. He pushed back on the assertion that the deal struck with Texas would be immune from a legal challenge. Undocumented immigrations, he said, could potentially bring lawsuits targeting the elimination of the rule.

title: Judge hears arguments in Rokita–Marté ICE detainer fight, decision not expected before Nov. 12
description:
A decision on the last unresolved issue in Indiana attorney general Todd Rokita’s lawsuit against Monroe County sheriff Ruben Marté is not expected before Nov. 12.
That’s how things stand after more than two hours of oral arguments Tuesday (Oct. 27) in Monroe County circuit court.
The consent decree bars blanket restrictions on deputies communicating or cooperating with federal immigration authorities, but leaves the detainer prohibition unresolved.

text:
A decision on the last unresolved issue in Indiana attorney general Todd Rokita’s lawsuit against Monroe County sheriff Ruben Marté is not expected before Nov. 12. That’s how things stand after more than two hours of oral arguments Tuesday (Oct. 27) in Monroe County circuit court.

Special judge Luke Rudisill heard competing requests for summary judgment, which is a decision based just on the law and an agreed set of facts. At stake is whether Marté can prohibit sheriff’s deputies from keeping people jailed solely on federal immigration detainers that are not accompanied by criminal judicial warrants.

Rudisill gave the two sides until Thursday, Nov. 12, to submit proposed orders.

The judge was active during the hearing, at times interrupting attorneys to clarify their positions. Many of his questions circled back to one issue: When federal immigration officers say they have grounds to detain someone, can a county jailer rely on that determination to keep the person in custody?

That question involves what’s known as the collective knowledge doctrine, which allows law enforcement officers, under certain circumstances, to rely on information known to other officers.

The lawsuit, filed in July 2024, has narrowed considerably. An August consent decree resolved many of the attorney general’s objections to the sheriff’s policy, known as MCSO-012. The consent decree bars blanket restrictions on deputies communicating or cooperating with federal immigration authorities, but leaves the detainer prohibition unresolved.

The issue before Rudisill on Tuesday was Section 4 of Indiana Code 5-2-18.2. It prohibits local governments from restricting the enforcement of federal immigration laws to less than what federal law permits, whether the enforcement is carried out by federal, state or local officers, as long as the enforcement actions do not violate federal or state law.

Rokita argues that holding someone on an detainer from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is lawful, so Marté cannot categorically prevent deputies from doing it. Marté argues that keeping a person jailed after the grounds for local custody end, without a criminal judicial warrant, would violate the Fourth Amendment and Indiana’s Constitution. Section 4, he says, cannot require him to permit unconstitutional detentions.

That question is distinct from a related dispute already before the Indiana Court of Appeals. A law adopted this spring, Senate Enrolled Act 76, added Section 9, which requires jail authorities to comply with requests in ICE detainers. Such requests typically ask local jails to hold people for up to 48 hours after their scheduled release, so immigration officers can take custody.

On June 30, Rudisill issued a preliminary injunction barring the state from enforcing Section 9, and its detainer-compliance requirement against Marté and his office, while litigation continues. The order was not a final ruling on constitutionality.

Rokita appealed the preliminary injunction before the case was finished, which is called an interlocutory appeal. On Aug. 28, the appellate court denied Rokita’s request to suspend the injunction during the appeal, but did not decide the appeal itself. The Aug. 28 appellate order reflects that narrower ruling in the appeals case, which is numbered 26A-PL-1737.

Courtroom arguments about earlier decisions

Tuesday’s hearing lasted about two hours and 25 minutes. Blake Lanning, an attorney from Rokita’s office, presented the state’s position. Marté was represented by Alexandra Lichtenstein, of Georgetown University Law Center’s Institute for Constitutional Advocacy and Protection, and Monroe County attorney Justin Roddye. Lichtenstein made the sheriff’s presentation.

Before presenting, both attorneys moved from tables along the sides of the courtroom to a center table, where they remained seated while addressing the judge. It made for less rhetorical flourish and more measured, at times tedious argumentation, revolving mostly around previous cases, and what those courts actually held. That’s opposed to what subsequent courts said about the holdings, or what the courts might have mentioned in their rulings that was not actually a part of the holding.

Rudisill was no passive listener. He interrupted both sides throughout their presentations with questions meant to distill the myriad details into a few key issues.

One was whether a federal administrative immigration warrant, which is issued by an immigration official, not a judge, gives enough grounds for a local officer to prolong the detention of somebody already in jail. A related question was whether the constitutional analysis changes because removability from the country under immigration law is a civil matter, not a criminal one.

Rudisill also asked the two sides to scrutinize a potential distinction between federal immigration officers and local officers. Does the federal government’s authority to make civil immigration arrests extend to county officers acting at ICE’s request? Does it make a difference whether local officers are operating under a formal 287(g) agreement, through which local personnel receive federal immigration-enforcement authority and training?

The judge’s most sustained inquiries concerned the collective knowledge doctrine. In ordinary policing, an officer can sometimes make an arrest based on information another officer possesses, even without personally knowing all the facts establishing probable cause. The question during Tuesday’s hearing was whether that principle works across the boundary between federal civil immigration enforcement and local law enforcement.

A Monroe County jailer receiving an ICE detainer generally does not independently investigate ICE’s basis for detention. If the federal officer’s knowledge can legally be attributed to the jailer, that supports Rokita. If the doctrine cannot apply here, or ICE supplies insufficient information, that supports Marté’s constitutional objection.

Rudisill pressed the lawyers on whether decisions involving criminal arrests establish a rule for civil immigration detention. Another key question was whether it matters that an ICE officer’s determination is not reviewed by an independent judge.

What happens at the Monroe County jail?

The constitutional dispute between Rokita and Marté does not mean the jail has stopped dealing with ICE. In a response to a B Square public records request followed by a phone interview, jail commander Kyle Gibbons described a routine that involves notifications and, in some cases, arrests by immigration officers at the jail.

The request did not result in production of any records. The sheriff’s office withheld some requested records, citing federal confidentiality rules, and said it had no responsive records for other categories.

But Gibbons described for The B Square how the Monroe County jail interacts with ICE. Detainer requests arrive by email or fax. Gibbons said fingerprint checks can also alert federal authorities that someone is in custody. The jail acknowledges receipt of retainer requests and notifies ICE when a prisoner is scheduled for release. But that does not mean Monroe County jail holds anyone past their scheduled release time.

Under Rudisill’s preliminary injunction, the sheriff’s office says it does not hold anyone past the time they otherwise must be released, just to await the arrival of ICE.

When federal immigration officers or an affiliated law-enforcement agency arrive for a release, the jail uses its secure sally port, which is the controlled vehicle-entry area. Gibbons described how county staff release the prisoner when local authority to hold the person ends, and after that immigration authorities then make their own arrest.

Gibbons said the sally-port arrangement avoids attempted arrests in public areas that could lead to attempted flight, pursuits or injuries.

From January 2026 through the date of the response to the records request, Gibbons said 18 people at the jail had been flagged through some form of immigration-related notice or paperwork. Of those, six were released and then detained by ICE or an affiliated agency. The 18 did not all represent formal ICE detainer requests, and the jail does not track which particular outside agency makes an arrest. So it’s not recorded exactly who made the six arrests.

That practice illustrates a key distinction in the lawsuit. The sheriff’s office says it complies with requirements to notify ICE about scheduled releases, but maintains that it cannot be required to keep people in custody beyond their scheduled release times, just on ICE’s say-so.

At the close of Tuesday’s hearing, Rudisill took both motions for summary judgment on the Section 4 issue under advisement.

With proposed orders due Nov. 12, the trial court’s next ruling will address the legality of the sheriff’s remaining detainer restriction. It will not resolve the separate Section 9 dispute, which remains in front of the Indiana Court of Appeals on an interlocutory appeal.

text:
ICE’s domestic air network has exploded to over 18,000 flights since Trump took office, with zero transparency or accountability into operations and costs

Repeated transfers can disrupt access to counsel, medical care, and pressure individuals to self-deport, with some detainees being transferred 15+ times

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator John Hickenlooper demanded answers from the Department of Homeland Security, sending a letter questioning the substantial increase in domestic transfer flights that move detainees in Immigration and Custom Enforcement (ICE) custody between ICE detention centers and deportation staging facilities.

In his letter, Hickenlooper highlighted the number of so-called “shuttle” flights carrying detainees between immigration detention centers and deportation staging facilities has increased substantially since President Trump took office, with over 18,000 domestic shuttle flights reportedly conducted since January 2025. The frequency with which individual detainees are transferred has also increased. A 2026 investigation identified detainees transferred nine, twelve, and thirteen times. In another reported case, between May and July 2025, a 20-year-old man with no criminal record was transferred 15 times between facilities in Florida, California, Arizona, Hawaii, and Louisiana. This expanded network and frequency creates more confusion and chaos for detainees – a majority of which have never been convicted of a violent crime – that can disrupt access to legal counsel, cut off communication with family and community members, and delay medical care.

“We are concerned by the scale and frequency of these transfers, the costs to taxpayers, and the impact repeated transfers can have on detainees’ access to legal counsel, medical care, and other essential services,” wrote Hickenlooper. “Repeated transfers have significant consequences for detainees and their families. Transfers often disrupt communication with counsel, delay attorneys’ and families’ abilities to locate detainees (particularly due to lags and policy changes pertaining to ICE’s Online Detainee Locator System), and interfere with continuity of medical care. Detainees have also reported difficulties accessing commissary funds following transfers.”

By analyzing millions of flight records, reviewing federal detention data, examining court filings and documenting specific flights, investigative reporters led by local Colorado station 9News/KUSA-TV found a vast domestic transportation system that ICE uses to move detainees from one part of the country to another, often multiple times, before those detainees are deported or released.

According to Human Rights First, 8,721 domestic transfer flights were recorded in 2025, compared to 3,975 in 2024. In July 2026, 1,363 flights were recorded – a 75 percent increase from July 2025. In August 2026, 1,267 flights were recorded across 56 U.S. cities. Between January and July 2025, 12 percent of detainees were transferred four or more times.

In addition, Hickenlooper demanded transparency into the costs of these more than 18,000 domestic shuttle flights to the American taxpayer. Just six multi-leg flights chartered by DHS to transport detainees to and from Guantanamo Bay in 2026 cost $979,000, according to a 2026 Department of Defense Inspector General report.

Watch Hickenlooper’s interview with 9News HERE.

Hickenlooper requested written responses to the following questions:

Domestic transfer flights: How many domestic transfer flights did ICE conduct between January 1, 2025, and September 1, 2026? Please provide a monthly breakdown, including the departure and arrival cities for each leg of the transfer and the cost of each leg of these flights.

Purpose of transfers: What percentage of domestic transfer flights were to removal staging facilities, and what percentage were to other detention facilities?

Facility capacity: For domestic transfer flights to other detention facilities, how many transfers originated from facilities operating below 85 percent of capacity? Please provide the number of transfers by originating facility alongside the monthly average daily population of the facility at the time of the transfer.

Frequency of transfers: How many individuals in ICE custody were placed on domestic transfer flights more than once during this period? Please provide the number and percentage of detainees transferred one, two, three, four, or more times.

Continuity of services: What policies and procedures does ICE use to ensure that transferred detainees maintain uninterrupted access to counsel, medical care, prescribed medications, and commissary funds?

Access to counsel: If an individual transferred to a different ICE facility has a pending virtual attorney visit scheduled, how does ICE ensure that the meeting can take place? Additionally, how does ICE ensure that detainees who are transferred don’t have to re-register their attorney for legal calls upon arrival at new facilities?

Medical care: What is ICE’s policy when a receiving facility does not include a detainee’s current medication in its formulary? Under that circumstance, what options is the detainee provided in terms of medical care?

Ground transportation: Between January 1, 2025 and September 1, 2026, how much has ICE spent on moving detainees between ICE facilities via ground transportation?

Transfers by AOR: For each ICE Area of Responsibility (AOR), please provide monthly counts of transfers out of the AOR involving individuals without a final order of removal. Please disaggregate these figures by air and ground transportation and include the estimated cost associated with these transfers.

Hickenlooper has been outspoken in the face of ICE’s lawlessness and demanded a top-to-bottom overhaul of the agency to stop ICE from terrorizing our communities. Hickenlooper also voted against the DHS funding bill because it failed to overhaul ICE. He has consistently pushed for more oversight andtransparency for federal immigration enforcement efforts, and has worked to help families desperately searching for loved ones arrested by ICE. In January, Hickenlooper spoke on the Senate floor to denounce the horrifying killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good, condemn the reports that families in Eagle County found “death cards” left in the cars of family members taken by ICE agents, and to demand the overhaul of ICE. He’s shown up at ICE facilities previously to conduct congressional oversight visits and raise concerns about ICE disregarding due process. He helped launch an investigation into ICE’s unlawful obstruction of congressional oversight, introduced legislation to ban ICE from wearing masks, and pushed to cut back the excessive funding that MAGA Republicans gave to ICE.

text:
Speaker Robert Rivas and Assembly leaders are condemning Trump and ICE agents for the violent assault on a young student with special needs in California.

On October 21, ICE agents attacked and injured Santa Maria High School student Erik Zepeda — a U.S. citizen — while walking to school. Erik, 20, is enrolled in an educational program for young adults with disabilities.

According to public officials, ICE agents tackled and detained Erik several blocks from his school, restrained him in their vehicle, and drove around the neighborhood. After determining there was no basis for arrest, the agents dropped him off at a random location and fled.

After the attack, Erik made his way to Santa Maria High School, where educators immediately called an ambulance to take him to the hospital. Officials say Erik suffered a broken wrist that required surgery, as well as a black eye, bruises, and lacerations. Beyond his physical injuries, he endured the trauma of being forcibly detained by ICE agents on his way to class.

“Erik is a U.S. citizen who was simply walking to school, and ICE agents broke his wrist. This is not immigration enforcement or public safety. It’s reckless, indiscriminate violence, and it’s indefensible,” Speaker of the Assembly Robert Rivas said. “Our Assembly will continue to hold the Trump administration and ICE accountable.”

“The Trump Administration’s masked secret police have hit a new low — harming a young man with special needs who was on his way to school. The Trump Administration must hear us when we say: Our community stands with Erik and rejects the lawless, dangerous enforcement campaign that put Erik in harm’s way. The case of Erik, a California-born American citizen, is a startling reminder of the disregard for the rule of law and common decency that we are seeing from the agents deployed on our streets. This cannot continue,” said Assemblymember Gregg Hart, who represents Santa Maria.

“I condemn this disgusting, racially motivated attack by ICE on one of our students,” said Assemblymember Juan Carrillo, incoming Chair of the California Latino Legislative Caucus. “School officials and families are rightly concerned because every time ICE lies and tells the public it was a case of a mistaken identity, someone innocent is always harmed, and no one is held accountable for these attacks. This special-needs student, with limited speech capabilities, has no immediate family based on news reports, to comfort them through this. Would any of you want your own children to go through this kind of traumatic experience alone? Of course not.”

“Californians keep living in fear because of ICE’s lawless violence. Shame on ICE and the companies raking in billions from attacking our communities, including a disabled US citizen in Santa Maria on their way to school,” said Latino Caucus vice-chair Assemblymember Liz Ortega.

Speaker Rivas and the Latino Caucus leaders have previously condemned Trump’s escalated ICE arrests and voter-suppression actions in California.

On Saturday evening, community members gathered for a rally to condemn Erik’s detention and the violent tactics by ICE agents that resulted in his injuries. A representative from Assemblymember Hart’s office spoke at the rally, alongside local officials and nonprofit partners.

It is an incredibly busy time to be an immigration attorney, but even amid the many demands on their time, our members continue to step up and make a difference. As we celebrate this year’s Pro Bono Week, we wanted to share two different examples of the amazing pro bono work our members do, and the lives they change.

Anna Relias from Chicago, IL shares:

“Can I share an ongoing pro bono commitment that has not (yet) resulted in a win? I am fighting tooth and nail in federal litigation for a detained client. After a Magistrate Judge recommended release on a habeas in WDLA, the district court judge accepted the government objection that he lacked jurisdiction on my procedural due process claim and denied my habeas but did not rule on other claims including substantive due process violations, regulatory, statutory and procedural violations by ICE, 4th amendment violations and prolonged detention. I am motioning the court to reconsider and will consider appellate options. I won't give up.”

That’s the kind of case that demonstrates the clear need for zealous advocacy on behalf of a client, even in the face of significant pressures and challenges. Keep up the fight, Anna!

Richard Link from Rochester, NY, sharesonecase he’ll always remember:

“When I was starting my practice, I attended a CLE by a nonprofit organization that urged attendees to accept a detained removal case pro bono in exchange. I did, and it was the best learning experience possible. As a solo, I handled a bond hearing, 42A cancellation individual hearing, BIA appeal, and circuit court appeal arising from the case. I met many colleagues who helped me with practical advice. This experience was essential in being able to provide representation to paying clients. If you are starting out or moving into a different type of immigration practice, pro bono cases are your opportunity to build valuable skills.”

The AILA community is a space wherementorship and the sharing of skills and knowledge are so prevalent. Knowing that another practitioner will help you think through options and overcome challenges is invaluable; even before graduation AILA law student members can find ways to engage and learn through pro bono!

This Pro Bono Week, we invite you to explore all the resources AILA offers, and if you can make the time, find a case or client you can take on. You’ll change your client’s life and your own!

Looking for ways to make pro bono service work within a busy practice? Join AILA’s Pro Bono Committee for the Why Say “Yes” to Pro Bono: Creating Sustainable Pathways to Service roundtable tomorrow, October 28, at 1pm (ET) to discuss practical strategies for making pro bono a sustainable and rewarding part of your practice.

text:
The Supreme Court ruled Tuesday that immigration judges can’t postpone deportation cases, giving President Trump another tool in his mass deportation agenda.

The court denied an emergency request to reinstate administrative closure, the practice that allows judges to temporarily delay deportation cases, after the Trump administration made an agreement with the state of Texas to end it in June. The request came from three cities—Baltimore; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio—and from nonprofit legal aid organization Centro ⁠Legal de la Raza.

The court’s denial was one sentence long without any explanation, a standard practice for emergency requests, and there were no reported dissents.

The agreement to end administrative closure was made in federal court in Texas on the same day the state sued to challenge the practice. A judge also approved the agreement the same day, which the plaintiffs cited in their lawsuit as proof the White House colluded with Texas to get rid of the rule.

“The need for interim relief is ​underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception,” the cities and organization wrote.

Administrative closure used to be common, with immigration judges using the tool to clear packed dockets, especially when a person had proceedings that could prevent their deportation such as a visa petition or appeal of a criminal conviction. Conservative politicians in places like Texas argue that the practice allows immigrants without legal status to stay in the country indefinitely.

The Biden administration tried to make the practice permanent in 2024, but after Trump returned to the White House, the Department of Justice announced it would no longer defend administrative closure. Tuesday’s ruling follows Friday’s federal appeals court decision that immigrants aren’t entitled to bond hearings. In less than a week, the Trump administration has successfully eroded immigration law in order to deport more people.

U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz got into a screaming match with Cuban Foreign Affairs Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla on Tuesday, after Parrilla approached Waltz’s podium mid-speech and called him a liar.

This comes as the U.N. prepares to vote on whether to condemn the U.S. embargo on Cuba, the longest-running economic war and trade embargo in modern history. Parrilla has accused the U.S. of pressuring other countries into voting against a condemnation of the embargo, even as the most recent fuel blockade has led to the collapse of the once-revered Cuban medical system, doubling the infant mortality rate and putting millions of Cubans at risk. Waltz spent the entirety of his speech Tuesday calling Cuba’s government corrupt, accusing its leaders of having a private island and Rolex collections, and blaming them for their country’s current situation—even as the U.S continues to block fuel from reaching the island.

Parrilla interrupted Waltz’s speech by calling for a point of order, arguing that the rules of the General Assembly had been violated, referencing Rule 71, which holds that “a representative may rise to a point of order, and the point of order shall be immediately decided by the President in accordance with the rules of procedure.”

Waltz disagreed, saying that Parrilla just didn’t “like” the points he was making. “He doesn’t like the hard truths,” he said as Parrilla began to approach the podium, still demanding that his point of order be recognized. “You can come and intimidate all you want, I ask you to back away from this podium!”

Waltz then turned back to General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman.

“Mr. President, this individual needs to back away from this podium, he’s not going to intimidate me in the United States of America like he tries to do to political prisoners! I’m the representative of the United States of America, back up!”

“You are a liar!” Parrilla retorted.

“Back away! … Do you understand who you’re dealing with?” Waltz threatened while Parrilla continued to call him a liar. “This is the United States of America. Back up.” The meeting was then suspended.

While President Obama loosened many of the embargo’s restrictions during his tenure, President Trump doubled down on them—especially in his second term when Cuban American Marco Rubio became Secretary of State. The fuel blockade has induced food and water shortages, daily blackouts, a mass exodus from the country, and a medicine shortage that has forced Cubans to buy lifesaving drugs off the black market. Even ventilators keeping premature babies alive aren’t working. The U.S. has continued to insist that these sanctions are targeting Cuba’s Communist government, but they are obviously having direct negative impacts on the Cuban people. Even still, Waltz’s outburst indicates that the Trump administration has no intention of loosening the economic “noose” on Cuba anytime soon.

Alaskans are apparently too “busy” to comprehend what “incumbent” means, according to Vice President JD Vance.

Vance was asked Tuesday to explain the rationale behind a fast-tracked Justice Department lawsuit working to preemptively block the Last Frontier’s Senate election results in the case of a Democratic win, but instead he offended the intelligence of voting Alaskans.

At issue is a general election ballot that will feature two men named Dan Sullivan. There’s Senator Dan Sullivan, the Republican nominee who will be prominently noted as the “incumbent,” and Dan J. Sullivan Jr., an independent candidate who remains unaffiliated with any official party.

“Why shouldn’t Alaskans find it insulting that the administration is suggesting they can’t read the word ‘incumbent’ on their ballot and know to vote for Senator Sullivan?” a reporter asked Vance at Joint Base Andrews Tuesday morning.

Vance’s explanation wasn’t particularly satisfying.

“I think the question presumes quite a bit. I mean, look, a lot of Alaskans are going to go and look at the ballot and realize exactly what you said, that this is all a big fraud,” Vance said, claiming the reporter said something that he did not.

But the vice president’s answer only went downhill from there as he suggested that Alaskans are so overwhelmed by the burden of daily labor that they don’t have the time to properly read election ballots.

“But people are busy. People have lives. People have jobs. And when you put a person on the ballot, explicitly to try and confuse voters, I think that’s electoral fraud,” Vance added.

The second Sullivan initially filed to run as a Republican in the Senate primary in May, days before the filing deadline. State Republicans have since argued that Sullivan worked with Democrats to cook up the scheme, accusing him of attempting to snatch votes away from the two-term senator in a flagrant bid to aid Mary Peltola, a former U.S. representative and the Democratic nominee.

But the unaffiliated politico has rejected the allegations.

“I entered this race because I am unhappy with the 12 year record of the current Senator and I feel we need a change,” Sullivan wrote in a social media post at the time. “It’s that simple.”

Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith got spooked at a rally in her home state of Mississippi with President Trump Monday.

Hyde-Smith, who is up for reelection next week, was supposed to speak after Trump introduced her but upon reaching the podium, she said one sentence and then bolted.

“Is this not the best president of our lifetime?” Hyde-Smith told the crowd, before stepping down. Trump quickly attempted to spin her abrupt departure.

“Thank you, Cindy. I love that, you know? Sometimes they get up and they talk for 10 minutes,” Trump said.

Despite the rally being held in a Southern, staunchly Republican state, Trump was interrupted at least three times by hecklers during his own speech, including one who shouted, “Shove that ballroom up your fat ass!” While Trump dismissed the protester as being “paid $250 by [George] Soros,” it seems Hyde-Smith was scared to be on the stage with Trump for too long.

Trump’s historic unpopularity is bringing the entire Republican Party down, putting safe states like Mississippi in play. Anti-Trump protesters would have been unheard of in the Magnolia State in previous years, but the president’s policies have caused a backlash even in deep red states.

Hyde-Smith’s reelection campaign wasn’t going well before this rally. In February, in response to people upset over high beef prices, she said, “You know you have so many proteins to choose from.” That was quickly seized upon by her Democratic opponent, Scott Colom, who put out an attack ad where a man grilling burgers said, “Pick another protein? I’d rather pick another senator instead.” Colom trails Hyde-Smith by only three points in the latest poll.

FBI Director Kash Patel has been accused of threatening staff charged with redacting the government’s files on Jeffrey Epstein, and using their mistakes as an excuse to fire them.

In a complaint made in March 2025 and obtained and published Tuesday by The PunchUp, a whistleblower who worked for the FBI’s Information Management Division described the chaotic, high-pressure process of readacting the Epstein files for release.

“The director has threatened to fire [FBI staff] if the job is not done by his made up deadline, and has already tried to slim down the FBI,” the whistleblower wrote. “What better way than to fire us during this ever changing process, or as scapegoats for the DOJ’s lack of proper procedures.”

The complaint came as the Department of Justice shed thousands of employees.

John Sullivan, former section chief in the intelligence division, told The New York Times in January that Patel had berated employees on the redaction team during a conference call, telling them to work faster and that he’d fire anyone who didn’t meet his deadlines—a claim that is now reinforced by the whistleblower’s accusation.

The whistleblower also warned that reviewers were not removing personal information that could be used to identify bureau employees, and that details they’d be instructed to leave unredacted could expose survivors’ identities. The whistleblower raised concerns that the DOJ would publish the material without further checks and blame the FBI for any mistakes.

“I am concerned that the rush deadline on the project, for no [discernible] reason, will lead to mistakes that could destroy people’s lives,” they wrote.

Catherine Sheehan Bruno, assistant FBI director and chief ethics and compliance officer, responded to the complaint on March 24, 2025, saying she was obliged to report the allegations. The following day, an FBI lawyer confirmed that the employee was willing to be identified to the inspector general. Then the FBI closed its own case. It’s unclear whether the inspector general took the matter any further or whether anyone charged with reviewing the Epstein files was subsequently fired.

In the end, there were thousands of redaction errors in the DOJ’s massive release of Epstein-related documents, which allegedly exposed the names of at least 100 survivors. Nearly 40 nude photos of women, possibly underage, were mistakenly released unredacted, while an innocuous photo of President Donald Trump somehow was redacted.

text:
Private prison company CoreCivic confirmed that someone in its custody died on Oct. 24 in one of the housing units.

Written by Kate Morrissey, Edited by Lauren J. Mapp

Author's note: This is a breaking news story and may be updated as more information becomes available.

A person in the custody of Immigration and Customs Enforcement died Saturday at Otay Mesa Detention Center.

Private prison company CoreCivic, which operates the detention facility, confirmed the death via email to Daylight San Diego on Monday.

According to the company, which did not provide a named spokesperson, a staff member found a detainee unresponsive in one of the housing units a little after 11:30 a.m. The company said that staff attempted life-saving measures on the person and called emergency medical services for help. It said emergency medical professionals pronounced the person dead at the facility.

The company did not provide information about the person's identity, gender or nationality, and it directed all other questions to ICE. ICE did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As of Monday evening, ICE had not yet published information about the death in its news releases, where it typically reports information about those who died in its custody. The most recent death listed on the site happened at a facility in Georgia on Friday.
