text:
This update covers developments relating to the freedoms of expression, association and peaceful assembly in the United States of America from 1st May to 30th June 2026.

Context

Deaths rise as US expands immigration detention system amid broader assault on migrants’ rights

On 25th June 2026, Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights released a report titled “Dying in Detention: Rising Deaths in an Expanding US Immigration Detention System”. The report highlights that 52 people died in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) custody between 20th January 2025 and 4th June 2026 (the first 500 days of President Trump’s second term), and that this mortality rate is at its highest level in over a decade, even higher than during the Covid-19 pandemic.

The report finds lack of transparency and public accountability for deaths, evidence of inadequate or delayed health care, and poor conditions of detention, raising concerns of violations of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), the UN Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (Mandela Rules), ICE’s own standards, and also, possibly, the Convention Against Torture (CAT).

Just the day before, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California struck down the Trump administration’s courthouse arrest policy as unlawful, vacating it nationwide, as well as a policy that eliminated the 12-hour limit on detention in temporary holding cells.

Agencies cannot simply abandon longstanding practices without justifying the change. The government agencies failed to do so here, and the court rightfully vacated their policies. This ruling serves as a powerful deterrent to future administrations who will think twice before weaponising the courthouse and detention conditions, knowing that such overreach cannot survive judicial scrutiny. - Duff Beach, Coblentz Patch Duffy & Bass LLP.

According to a Reuters analysis of ICE data, immigration detention facilities recorded an annual death rate equivalent to one death per 3,848 detainees between 2009 and 2024, based on their average daily detained population. Since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025, the annual death rate has more than doubled, reaching approximately one death per 1,630 detainees, according to preliminary data through early June 2026.

Supreme Court allows Alabama to use a map that intentionally discriminates against Black voters

On 2nd June 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for Alabama to use a congressional map that had been previously struck by a lower court as racially discriminatory. The Court left the lower court’s ruling on hold while the appeal continues. Deuel Ross, Director of Litigation at the Legal Defence Fund, stated that “The Supreme Court’s decision gives cover to Alabama and others to deliberately and openly discriminate against Black voters without fear of any consequence. The Court’s shameless decision to reinstate a racially discriminatory map defies any thoughtful or consistent application of the law. We will continue to throw all of our resources into the fight to ensure that Alabama voters have the fair representation that they deserve in Congress.”

This decision followed the April 2026 Supreme Court ruling in the case of Louisiana v. Callais, which struck down Louisiana’s congressional map that included two districts that allowed Black voters to elect a candidate of their choice, thus opening the door for states to enact discriminatory maps that dilute the vote for voters of colour.

Association

FBI searches raise concerns over intimidation of voter registration activism

On 11th June 2026, a hundred agents from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) raided the Cleveland office of the Ohio Organizing Collaborative (OCC), - an organisation that builds grassroots community power in the state and works on voter registration - in connection with a federal investigation into potential fraud violations. Agents questioned staff, seized computers, phones and documents, and went to the homes of employees, volunteers, and board members across Ohio seeking interviews and information, in some cases with subpoenas and requests for information and electronic devices.

OOC Board Member Prentiss Haney accused agents of using “intimidation tactics” and said the operation had frightened staff members and their families. “Demanding and accusing people of voter fraud as if it was a witch hunt […], and scaring them with the children, following them in their cars to school and to work. I mean this was a full-out assault. I mean, we haven't seen anything like this since Selma. And so this was completely […] politically motivated.”

According to Signal Ohio, an independent, community-led, nonprofit newsroom, the federal investigation concerned, at least in part, voter registration forms submitted by canvassers working for Black Fork Strategies, a company owned by OOC founder Kirk Noden. However, election officials said they had found no evidence that the registrations resulted in fraudulent voting, while federal authorities have not publicly disclosed the full basis or scope of the investigation.

In response, civil society organisations, including the Brennan Center for Justice, have criticised the scale of the operation aiming “to intimidate voters and those who helped them exercise the franchise.” It also warned that law enforcement action targeting people involved in voter registration could have a chilling effect on citizen participation, especially ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. OOC allies also launched the #HandsOffOhio campaign.

In recent months, federal authorities have also scrutinised election administration in at least eight states, seeking or seizing election records and other materials. These included records related to the 2020 election in Arizona, Georgia, and Wisconsin, as well as ballots and other records from the 2024 election in Michigan. The Department of Justice has also sought detailed voter registration data from states across the country, including Minnesota, saying it intended in part to compare voter rolls with federal databases to identify possible non-US citizens registered to vote. Reuters reported that only 129 people had been prosecuted for non-citizen voting since Congress criminalised it in 1996, with most cases involving voter confusion or miscommunication with election officials rather than fraud.

Departments of Treasury, Justice, and State target Cuba-solidarity networks

Between 23rd-26th May 2026, openly conservative news outlets and commentators reported that the Departments of the Treasury and Justice were investigating 145 civil society organisations and activist networks engaged in Cuba solidarity efforts for their alleged violations of the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) and sanctions restrictions. Their information indicated that prominent progressive activists, including Medea Benjamin, CodePink Co-Founder and Twitch streamer, Hasan Piker, were allegedly sent administrative subpoenas seeking more information about their involvement in the March 2026 Nuestra América Convoy, an effort to deliver humanitarian aid to Cuba.

CodePink and Piker initially denied having received any such subpoena, though CodePink later acknowledged receiving an inquiry via email. The reporting further indicated that the investigation “closely mirrors” the framework laid out in National Security Presidential Memorandum 7 (NSPM-7). As previously raised by the CIVICUS Monitor, NSPM-7 directed federal agencies and law enforcement bodies to investigate and target civil society organisations, their funders, and activists, under the pretext of preventing political violence, but rather establishing a roadmap for the suppression of dissent, and which, months after its publication, continues to be followed to the letter, evidencing a pattern of investigations into numerous civil society organisations.

On 4th June 2026, the Department of State imposed sanctions on 10 entities and individuals linked to the Cuban regime, including the Cuban Institute of Friendship with the Peoples (known as ICAP, for its acronym in Spanish), with which various U.S. nonprofits, including CodePink, would have allegedly worked regarding the aforementioned convoy. On 17th June 2026, Florida Senator Rick Scott doubled down and called on the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) to strip CodePink of its tax-exempt status.

People’s World noted that “[t]he factual basis for the investigations comes entirely from Fox News reporting” and that this “weaponising [of] federal law enforcement against the left [is] not to address genuine security threats, but to silence political opposition and intimidate movements that challenge the bipartisan foreign policy consensus”, “serv[ing] a chilling function regardless of whether charges are ever filed”.

The situation raises multiple concerns. Investigations of this nature force civil society organisations to focus their resources (human, financial, etc.) on protecting and/or defending themselves, rather than on carrying out their existential missions. Findings of violations of sanctions programmes administered by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) may result in substantial civil and, in some cases, criminal penalties.

The revocation of a civil society organisation’s tax-exempt status could force them to have to cease operations altogether. Looking to the future, the most recent sanctions further complicate matters for U.S. nonprofits whose mission is to provide humanitarian assistance around the world, of heightened relevance after the dismantling of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), as previously reported by the CIVICUS Monitor.

Moreover, the right-wing media appears to be doing the government’s bidding for them; not only by conducting the foundational research into civil society organisations leading to the government investigation, but also by seemingly acting like a government spokesperson in expressly linking said investigations to NSPM-7 and amplifying the coverage in this regard. Each of these factors, on their own—and more so in the aggregate—constitute severe obstacles for the operations of civil society organisations, they serve to intimidate, harass, and generate a chilling effect on civil society organisations and their members and, ultimately, to promote an environment not conducive for the full exercise of the right to freedom of association.

Increasingly politicised scrutiny of federal spending for nonprofits

On 5th May 2026, the Committee on Ways and Means of the U.S. House of Representatives reiterated its 4th September 2025 request for information and documentation concerning the funding sources and fiscal sponsorships of three U.S. nonprofit organisations (BreakThrough News, Tricontinental, and The People’s Forum) who would have received funding from Neville Roy Singham, a wealthy American expatriate alleged to have close ties to the Chinese Communist Party (CCP).

On 29th June 2026, Fox News reported that the Department of Justice had launched a federal grand jury investigation into possible financial crimes by Singham, the organisations he would have funded (which include CodePink, one of whose co-founders is married to Singham) and/or their leaders, a move supported by the Chairman of the US House Committee on Ways and Means.

On 13th May 2026, the Office of Management Budget (OMB) circulated a memo to all federal agencies requesting that they submit information on all monetary agreements and awards of federal funding provided to 49 listed nonprofit organisations “to better understand the scope of funding.” The groups targeted by this memo carry out work primarily on immigration, humanitarian aid, and civil rights.

Compounding this increasingly politicised scrutiny over nonprofit organisations, on 29th May 2026, the OMB published a proposal for significant revisions to the Guidance for Federal Financial Assistance, which governs federal grants, agreements, and federal assistance at large. The summary indicates that the OMB proposes these revisions to ensure “that American tax dollars are not wasted or misused, […] that basic American principles of equality and equal opportunity are upheld throughout all stages of the award making process and that unlawful discrimination is no longer permitted.”

An analysis by The Dispatch highlights, among other proposed changes, the sidelining of merit-based reviews for grant applications, declaring technical peer review as advisory, limiting the ability of grant recipients to challenge terminations, and requiring senior appointees to conduct pre-issuance reviews in alignment with the President’s policy priorities and reject proposals related to racial preferences, illegal immigration, those where the recipient denies the “sex binary in humans,” and others that “compromise public safety or promote anti-American values.”

A former federal programme officer noted that this is “not a reform of grants management” but “a complete political control apparatus layered over every stage of the federal […] funding lifecycle.” Diane Yentel, President and CEO of the National Council of Nonprofits (which issued a summary of the proposed harmful provisions and a corresponding call to action), expressed concern over the implications of overhauling this guidance: “The sweeping changes included in the more than 400-page proposal may profoundly impact nonprofits that partner with the federal government to deliver essential services, including housing, health, education, food, shelter, disaster recovery, and more, in communities nationwide.” Her colleague, Sarah Saadian, added that this was “an attempt by the White House to achieve what they haven’t been able to achieve in courts” and warned that “many nonprofits […] may simply decide it is not worth the risk to seek funding.” Comments on the proposal were due in mid-July 2026.

The escalation of congressional investigations into federal grand jury investigations signals a worrisome turn that could result in the potential criminalisation of nonprofit leaders. The increased scrutiny over nonprofit public and private funding further pushes a narrative framing their critical work as lacking government oversight, despite the burdensome requirements from multiple agencies already in place.

Sanctions hinder awareness-raising, solidarity, research, and activism on Palestine

On 19th May 2026, the federal government imposed sanctions on four activists participating in a flotilla seeking to deliver humanitarian assistance and bring attention to the siege and blockade of Gaza. On that day, Israel intercepted the 50-boat flotilla organised by the Global Sumud Flotilla and Freedom Flotilla Coalition. Without producing any evidence, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) called them a “pro-Hamas flotilla” organised by a group previously designated as Specially Designated Global Terrorists (SDGTs) for its work on Palestine issues.

On 20th May 2026, UN Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories, Francesca Albanese, was removed from OFAC’s list of Specially Designated Nationals. This followed her family’s legal challenge to sanctions imposed on Albanese, by way of the International Criminal Court (ICC) sanctions regime of 9th July 2025 (previously reported on by the CIVICUS Monitor), in which they argued that the sanctions restricted their First Amendment and property rights. The court had granted a temporary injunction against the sanctions, paving the way for her delisting. One week later, she was re-added to the list after a District of Columbia Appeals Court issued an order to stop the preceding, favourable order. The Trump administration has also filed an appeal against this order.

On 24th June 2026, three ICC judges filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration in response to the 2025 ICC sanctions regime. The complaint argues that the sanctions violate US obligations under international law, as well as the judges’ property rights, and are further arbitrary, capricious, and an abuse of discretion violative of the Administrative Procedures Act. They also allege that the US fails to consider their impact on US-supported prosecutions for international crimes and attempts to punish and influence their judicial decisions. The government’s position has been to publicly refer to the ICC’s involvement in “an unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security and foreign policy of the [US]” and, on 30th July 2026, it filed its opposition and motion to dismiss.

The blanket conflation of advocacy for Palestine with terrorism can have severe financial and legal implications for civil society actors and organisations. The sanctions, together with rhetoric against the ICC and other international bodies, interfere with the work of civil society organisations, precluding them from freely engaging with judges, prosecutors, and other international officials in documenting and calling for accountability by states committing human rights violations, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. Moreover, the effects of the sanctions transcend the targeted individuals, even affecting their family members in fulfilling their most basic needs. They also violate the individual’s freedom of expression and provoke a broader chilling effect on civil society organisations and anyone wishing to speak up. CIVICUS has highlighted the harmful impacts of sanctions as a tool for repression against civil society.

White House publishes concerning counterterrorism priorities encompassing “violent left-wing extremists”

On 6th May 2026, the White House released its 2026 United States Counterterrorism Strategy, outlining national security threats to the US and how the government seeks to address them. The document explicitly indicates that “a new type of domestic terrorism has emerged, driven by violent extremists who have adopted ideologies antithetical to freedom and the American way of life” (p. 4) and that the strategy will prioritise “the rapid identification and neutralisation of violent secular political groups whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist.” (p. 7)

An analysis by the Charity & Security Network (C&SN) notes that “[b]road and vague terms like ‘anti-American’ are not defined, leaving their interpretation to the discretion of law enforcement and granting the administration power that can be easily weaponised to target political opponents. In addition, the inclusion of ‘radically pro-transgender’ political groups marks a dangerous escalation in targeting of organisations working on issues of gender, sexuality, and reproductive justice.”

The strategy builds on previous worrisome policies and directives put out by the administration that characterise advocacy and organising around progressive or “left-wing” issues as terrorism, such as NSPM-7, the sanctions against the International Criminal Court, and terrorism designations (see above). But it goes further in including “left-wing” groups as part of its formal, comprehensive strategy and referring to their “neutralisation” (language typically reserved for conflict settings), thus continuing to push a dangerous narrative aimed at instilling fear based on an alleged internal enemy of their own creation (widely known authoritarian strategy).

As noted by the C&SN, while the document “does not carry any specific regulatory weight, [it] does demonstrate the Administration’s continued effort to paint perceived political enemies as terrorist threats,” further contributing to a chilling and challenging environment for civil society organisations, and the erosion of civic space.

Attack on leading civil rights organisation expands and escalates

On 20th May and 9th June 2026, the Judiciary Committee of the US House of Representatives facilitated a two-part hearing titled “The Southern Poverty Law Center: Manufacturing Hate”. According to a Charity & Security Network report, both hearings followed similar patterns in which, on one hand, Republican members and majority witnesses referred to the organisation’s alleged fraud on donors and purported deviations between its past and present work, and on the other, Democratic members and the minority witnesses pushed back against the alleged fraud narrative and defended the organisation’s civil rights track record.

Some Congress members have raised concerns and demanded an investigation into what they characterise as the “politically motivated prosecution” of the Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC), while others have focused on the funding restrictions imposed on the SPLC, wondering “whether financial institutions are beginning to deny services to IRS approved non-profit organisations based on political pressure, ideological disagreement, or fear of retaliation from the Trump Administration”. Civil society organisations and leaders have turned out in droves to condemn the hearings supporting the Administration’s smear campaign and to defend the SPLC and the sector itself from government attacks.

These legislative hearings follow the grand jury indictment against the SPLC in April, as previously reported by the CIVICUS Monitor, evidencing the multi-pronged nature of the government’s strategy. We will continue to advance the fundamental principle that all young people deserve equal opportunity to thrive and succeed.”

The Human Rights Campaign clarified that this ruling “does not serve to create a nationwide blanket ban on transgender athletes [as it] primarily addressed the lawfulness of anti-transgender discrimination within the context of sports” and added that “[s]till, this ruling falls in line with other rulings from conservative justices on the Supreme Court that have rolled back rights and freedoms for many marginalised communities, including LGBTQ+ people, asylum seekers, immigrants, and BIPOC voters disproportionately impacted by the gutting of voting rights protections.”

Department of the Army. This ruling allows the Winnebago Tribe to proceed with its lawsuit against the US Army, pending before the US District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, seeking the repatriation of the remains of Samuel Gilbert and Edward Hensley, two Winnebago boys who died at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School more than 125 years ago.

text:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday cleared the way for the Trump administration to restrict a Biden-era policy allowing immigration judges to temporarily close thousands of deportation cases.

According to The Washington Post, the justices rejected an appeal by three cities and an immigrant rights group that sought to preserve the policy. It gives immigration judges discretion to remove certain cases from their active schedules without dismissing them.

The practice, known as administrative closure, allows judges to manage overwhelming caseloads while giving some migrants, including crime victims and neglected children, time to pursue legal options to remain in the United States.

Critics call the procedure a form of backdoor amnesty.

The practice has existed in various forms for decades. Approximately 360,000 migrants have received administrative closure since 1990, according to government statistics.

The Biden administration formally established the policy in 2024 after the first Trump administration attempted to prohibit its use.

When Trump returned to office in 2025, his administration stopped defending the rule. Texas challenged it in federal court, and a judge issued a permanent injunction blocking the policy.

Baltimore, Columbus, Ohio, and New Haven, Connecticut, along with an immigrant rights group, unsuccessfully sought to intervene before appealing to the Supreme Court.

The justices offered no explanation for rejecting the appeal.

Although administratively closed cases are not automatically reopened, they remain pending and could be returned to active deportation proceedings.

text:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to revive a Biden-era rule allowing immigration judges to close deportation proceedings for people who are in the process of obtaining lawful status.

The one-line order comes almost two weeks after three cities and a California legal aid group petitioned the justices to restore the rule, arguing that the Justice Department and Texas colluded to eliminate it outside of the established rulemaking process.

At issue is a June judgment halting the rule nationwide. A federal judge in Texas entered it on the same day the state filed a lawsuit against the Justice Department. The Trump administration and Texas jointly asked the court to bar the immigration court system from ever enacting a similar policy.

In an application to the justices, Baltimore; Columbus, Ohio; New Haven, Connecticut; and Centro Legal de la Raza argued that the judgment erased certain important procedures, “over the course of a single day, without meaningful judicial review, public participation” or rulemaking requirements.

Trending

The blocked rule had given immigration judges discretion to spare victims of crimes or neglected children from facing deportation proceedings while undergoing a process to gain immigration relief from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the application says.

The Supreme Court decided to let the judgment stand while the legal case plays out. The Justice Department and Texas argued in filings last week that the cities and Centro Legal de la Raza lacked the right to intervene.

“A stay would revive a rule the district court declared unlawful, renew the fiscal and sovereign injuries Texas alleged, and unsettle a final judgment accepted by the actual parties,” Texas’ court filing last week states. “It would also restore a binding regulation that the Federal Government would have to administer unless and until lawfully displaced, even though responsible officials concluded that the Rule cannot be defended in good faith.”

The parents of Alex Pretti, a Minneapolis intensive-care nurse who was shot and killed by federal immigration agents in January, spoke publicly for the first time on Tuesday.

They accused the Department of Justice (DOJ) of denying them information about the investigation, as well as ignoring them.

"We are here begging for the Department of Justice to do what is right," Susan Pretti, Alex's mother, said.

Susan Pretti, along with her husband, Michael, said officials have failed to give them updates about the shooting. They said they decided to speak out to demand transparency, accountability, and respect, after sending the DOJ an unanswered letter in July.

"Our son was murdered," Michael said. "We all saw it and the lack of cooperation is just baffling. It's disappointing."

Michael said he will no longer stay silent. He said the deadly shooting was unjustified, as well as called out U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and Dan Rosen, who is the U.S. Attorney for the District of Minnesota.

"Look in your heart and do what is right. Share the evidence now so prosecutors can follow the facts and hold these men accountable," Michael said of the agents who shot his son.

Pretti, 37, was killed on January 24 during President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement -- Operation Metro Surge -- in Minneapolis. The DOJ later announced a civil rights investigation into the shooting.

In the letter, according to CNN, the family said while they met with Rosen, he refused to share information with them. The family wants federal officials to identify the agents who fired their guns, confirm whether the FBI investigation remains active, and return property they says is no longer needed as evidence.

"It is impossible to convey how the government’s refusal to engage in transparent communication with the Pretti family has compounded their heartbreak," the letter noted, per CNN. "Further, with each such refusal, U.S. Attorney Rosen even refused to explain the basis for his position, instead stating only that 'I can’t tell you for all kinds of reasons,' without providing a single one."

State officials have separately said the federal government stopped providing materials needed for their own inquiry.

"We are working on this case every single day. My office is working in a collaborative way with the local county attorney. We're working together to make sure that the truth and justice prevails in Alex Pretti's case," Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, a Democrat who is leading a lawsuit against the DOJ, told CNN on Tuesday.

"We are in litigation with the federal government right now to secure the rest of the remaining file, which they could give us this morning if they were inclined to do so," he added. "But it looks like we're going to need a court order. I'm sorry that it comes to that."

The DOJ has said victim-family communications may take place at later stages of a case.

No criminal charges have been announced in Pretti’s death.

"We're hoping that the federal government will stop fighting this," Steve Schleicher, an attorney who is representing Susan and Michael Pretti, said.

text:
An Oshkosh middle school teacher has been detained by federal immigration authorities after being ordered to leave the country.

Wendy Mendez moved to Wisconsin from Costa Rica in 2020 with her husband and two sons. She is a Spanish teacher at Vel Phillips Middle School, and was recognized as an “employee of the year” by the Oshkosh Area School District last year.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, arrested Mendez on Oct. 14 in Milwaukee, according to a statement from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

The statement said Mendez came to the country legally “on a temporary basis” six years ago and “failed to depart” in 2021. According to federal officials, Mendez was placed into removal proceedings in February and was ordered to be removed in September for failing to show up for an immigration hearing.

But one of Mendez’s friends says Mendez missed the hearing because federal immigration officials mailed a hearing notice to an old address.

Deb Nez, the friend of Mendez, wrote on social media that the notice was sent to a three-year-old address and that U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services had Mendez’s correct address “within days” of the family moving into their home.

“This was not the first time that USCIS had made that mistake,” Nez wrote on Oct. 22.

Mendez’s story was first reported by the Advance-Titan, the independent student newspaper of the University of Wisconsin-Oshkosh.

Nez wrote that Mendez had been forced to sleep on concrete floors and had been moved to six detention centers in eight days.

The Department of Homeland Security’s statement said Mendez will “remain in custody pending her removal from the United States.”

The agency added that “being in detention is a choice,” saying the federal government is offering $3,000 and a free flight to individuals who self-deport.

“We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream,” the statement read. “If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.”

The Oshkosh Area School District sent a letter to Vel Phillips Middle School families following Mendez’s detainment, saying she would be “out of the classroom for the foreseeable future” due to “unforeseen circumstances.”

The Oct. 26 letter said Mendez is an employee in good standing and had been placed on unpaid leave. The district also said Mendez’s leave of absence was not related to school safety or her performance.

“We know this situation brings heartbreak, frustration, and worry for many in our community,” the letter reads.

In an email, a spokesperson for the Oshkosh school district said the district does not comment on confidential employee matters. But the spokesperson confirmed Mendez is in good standing with the district.

“Our primary focus remains on supporting our students and staff and keeping learning moving forward in our classrooms,” the spokesperson said.

Mendez was recognized by the Oshkosh Area School District in the 2024-25 school year as one of the district’s employees of the year. She was recognized as an interpreter.

In a video posted to the district’s YouTube page in April 2025, Oshkosh Superintendent Bryan Davis is seen walking into Mendez’s classroom to give her the award. As Davis hands her a balloon and a large mug, Mendez becomes emotional.

Oshkosh School Board member Molly Smiltneek issued a statement Monday night, expressing frustration over Mendez’s detention by ICE.

“This is not normal. This is not a personnel issue. This is not a political issue,” she said. “This is a human issue. I know there are a lot of people, kids and adults, in our community who are hurting, sad and trying to make sense of the sudden disappearance of an important person in their lives.”

“And there is a mother, a teacher, a leader, a role-model, neighbor, a human being, an employee of the year who was torn away from all she built and valued,” Smiltneek added.

On Oct. 25, Nez wrote on social media that Mendez was “safe and doing okay,” but was “recovering from the horrid experience she went through” both mentally and emotionally.

“This is not the end of the road for Wendy,” Nez wrote. “There is still a long and expensive legal battle ahead, with significant legal fees and uncertainty about what comes next.”

Contact information for Mendez’s legal representation was not immediately available.

text:
Representative Randy Fine, a Florida Republican, said anyone who lied on immigration paperwork to become a U.S. citizen should be denaturalized and deported after being asked whether that standard should apply to first lady Melania Trump and billionaire Elon Musk.

Fine made the remarks during a Monday night interview with NewsNation's Nichole Berlie, who asked whether scrutiny of U.S. Representative Ilhan Omar's citizenship should extend to high-profile immigrants with ties to the Trump administration.

"Anyone who was not honest in their immigration paperwork," Fine said, adding that he did not know the circumstances of Melania Trump or Musk's immigration proceedings and was unaware of any allegations against either of them.

"I believe anyone who lied on their paperwork to become a citizen should be denaturalized and should be deported," he said.

Melania Trump was born in Slovenia and became a U.S. citizen in 2006, according to the White House. Musk was born in South Africa and became a U.S. citizen through naturalization in 2002, according to his biography written by Walter Isaacson.

Newsweek has reached out to the White House and Musk's representatives for comment outside of normal business hours.

Fine also called for the reevaluation of everyone who became a naturalized U.S. citizen since 1990, saying he believed citizenship fraud was widespread in Minnesota and citing allegations involving Omar, a Minnesota Democrat.

"So yeah, I think Ilhan Omar needs to be the first. She certainly should not be the last," Fine said.

The comments come amid an ongoing federal investigation into Omar's immigration and naturalization paperwork. Federal agents searched her Washington, D.C.-area home on October 12. The Department of Justice (DOJ) previously told Newsweek that the search was part of an "ongoing federal criminal investigation." Omar has not been charged in connection with the probe.

Federal authorities have also issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of Omar's relatives, according to the Associated Press. The scope of the investigation remains unclear.

Omar has said she fears returning to her home following the raid, citing death threats and concerns about her publicly available address.

"Obviously, I can't continue to live there," she told MS NOW on October 21. "So have to figure out where to move to."

During the interview, Omar recounted waking around 6 a.m. October 12 to Homeland Security Investigations agents pounding on the front and back doors of her home while she, her husband and their 20-year-old son were inside. She described the search as chaotic, saying her family scrambled to get dressed and go downstairs as they tried to understand what was happening.

President Donald Trump called on Omar to resign from Congress on Thursday, alleging she had used a different name to get elected and take the congressional oath.

"It was just revealed just a little while ago that … her name is not Ilhan Omar, the one she used to get elected and sworn into Congress," Trump told supporters at a rally in Iowa. "She used a fake name to be sworn in. I assume she must immediately have to resign from Congress."

The investigation has also renewed attention on longstanding unproven accusations that Omar married her now-former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, who critics have alleged was her brother, to facilitate his entry into the United States. Omar has repeatedly denied the allegation. In an interview with MS NOW's Chris Hayes last week, she called the claims "insane" and, when asked whether she was related to Elmi, said, "Not to my knowledge."

Omar arrived in the United States as a refugee from Somalia and became a naturalized citizen in 2000. She has accused Trump of using the investigation to intimidate her and his other political opponents. Trump has repeatedly attacked Omar's background and questioned her citizenship.

Newsweek has reached out to Omar's campaign and the DOJ for comment.

The Trump administration faces a proposed class action seeking to halt policies that have frozen green card applications for thousands of refugees already admitted to the United States and subjected some to renewed scrutiny of their original refugee claims.

The lawsuit, filed Monday by six refugee organizations and four individual refugees in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, challenges three Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) policies: an indefinite hold on certain refugees' applications for lawful permanent residence, a program to re-vet refugees admitted during the Biden administration, and a new rule reducing the time refugees have to respond to proposed termination of their refugee status from 30 days to 10.

The plaintiffs argue that the three policies violate federal immigration and administrative law and constitutional due-process protections. The plaintiffs simultaneously asked the court for emergency relief, including an immediate administrative stay of the new 10-day termination rule. They said at least one refugee had already received a termination notice under the new system and could lose refugee status while the court considers the wider challenge.

Newsweek contacted USCIS and its parent agency, DHS, for comment via email outside office hours.

What the Plaintiffs Are Seeking

The plaintiffs want the court to block the three policies while the case proceeds and ultimately set them aside. They are also asking the court to certify a nationwide class consisting of people admitted to the United States as refugees who had not adjusted to lawful permanent resident status as of October 14, 2026, or afterward. They say the group numbers in the tens of thousands. The court has not yet certified the class.

The four individual plaintiffs are:

Lida A., a 27-year-old Afghan refugee living in Massachusetts who worked for a U.S.-funded organization before fleeing after the Taliban takeover.

Abdi B., a 39-year-old Ethiopian refugee living in Minnesota who was detained during Operation PARRIS in January and transferred to Texas before a federal court ordered his release.

Julio C., a 26-year-old Colombian refugee living in Texas who relies on Medicaid for HIV medication.

Firas D., a 23-year-old Iraqi refugee living in Texas who was arrested in Iraq because of his sexual orientation.

All four have applied for permanent residence and are awaiting decisions, according to court filings.

The six organizations also serving as plaintiffs in the lawsuit are Partnership for the Advancement of New Americans, Jewish Family Service of Western Massachusetts, International Institute of New England, African Communities Together, HIAS and Refugee Council USA.

The case challenges a November 21, 2025, USCIS policy memorandum that placed pending green card applications from refugees admitted between January 20, 2021, and February 20, 2025, on hold and called for a review and potential re-interviews of refugees admitted during that period. The memorandum said the measures were intended to reassess whether those refugees met the refugee definition when admitted and cited national security and public safety concerns. The plaintiffs argue the agency has not substantiated broader concerns about refugees vetted and admitted during the period.

"The Trump-Vance administration is trapping refugees in cruel legal limbo by blocking their path to permanent residency while simultaneously making it easier to strip them of their lawful status and the protections they are eligible for," Skye Perryman, the president and CEO of Democracy Forward, told Newsweek. "These inhumane and unlawful policies violate fundamental due process protections, and we are going to court to stop them."

Changes to US Refugee Policy Under Trump

DHS has estimated that about 113,000 refugees have pending adjustment applications, according to the plaintiffs' filings. USCIS data cited in the original complaint show the agency adjudicated 121 refugee adjustment applications between January and March this year, compared with 17,569 during the same period in 2025. The 121 figure includes cases outside the population covered by the November hold.

Before that change, the average processing time for refugee adjustment applications was 7.8 months in the third quarter of 2025, according to court filings.

Under federal law, refugees must have been physically present in the United States for at least one year to qualify for lawful permanent residence and must undergo an examination to determine their admissibility. The plaintiffs argue that the government can examine admissibility during that process but does not have authority to impose a categorical, indefinite hold or require an entire group of already-admitted refugees to .

The policies are part of wider changes to refugee policy during President Donald Trump's second administration. On his first day back in office, Trump signed an executive order suspending entry through the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program and decisions on refugee applications. A separate executive order called for additional identification safeguards for refugees and stateless people seeking admission.

The administration subsequently established a program for white South Africans. Trump's fiscal 2026 refugee determination initially set an , with admissions "primarily" allocated to Afrikaners. A May 2026 determination increased the maximum by 10,000.

How Operation PARRIS Unfolded

The policies challenged in the Massachusetts lawsuit primarily concern refugees who have already been admitted to the United States.

In January, USCIS launched Operation PARRIS (Post-Admission Refugee Reverification and Integrity Strengthening) in Minnesota, initially focusing on 5,600 refugees without green cards and subjecting cases to new background checks and verification. Court filings say some refugees were arrested and transported to Texas for interviews about their original refugee applications. A Minnesota judge subsequently blocked detention based on refugees' unadjusted status, and a Massachusetts federal court in March stayed a later nationwide refugee detention policy as separate litigation proceeded.

On October 14, DHS issued an interim final rule cutting the period for responding to a Notice of Intent to Terminate refugee status from 30 days to 10 days, changing a procedure that had been in place for about 45 years.

DHS said the change was intended to "restore integrity to the immigration system, mitigate risks to national security and public safety, and prevent fraud and exploitation." The rule took effect immediately while DHS opened a 30-day public comment period.

DHS estimates that about 186,000 refugee cases admitted from fiscal 2015 through fiscal 2025 remain unadjusted and could be subject to the termination rule.

According to the plaintiffs, USCIS issued at least one notice under the new rule on October 15, the day after it took effect. It was delivered to the refugee on October 19. The plaintiffs argue that 10 days may not provide enough time to obtain counsel, interpreters and records needed to respond. They note that the median USCIS processing time for a simple Freedom of Information Act request was 27 days in 2025.

The high court turned down a request from Democratic-led cities who say the rule was used to help crime victims and neglected juveniles and should be revived.
Texas and the Trump administration agreed to a court order blocking the regulation after the state sued.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court declined to intervene Tuesday in a dispute over a Biden-era immigration regulation that allowed immigration judges to pause some deportation proceedings.

The high court turned down a request from Democratic-led cities who say the rule was used to help crime victims and neglected juveniles and should be revived.

Texas and the Trump administration agreed to a court order blocking the regulation after the state sued. Texas alleged that the practice called administrative closure was dramatically expanded under former President Joe Biden and effectively allowed people to stay in the country indefinitely.

The cities of Baltimore, Columbus, Ohio and New Haven, Connecticut, along with the legal group Centro Legal de la Raza, had asked to join the case to defend the regulation. They filed an emergency appeal before the Supreme Court after a judge refused to allow them to intervene.

Represented by the group Democracy Forward, they argued that Texas and the Trump administration had worked together to allow the regulation to be permanently blocked in court, bypassing a public rulemaking process.

The Justice Department had urged the justices to deny the appeal, saying the cities had no legal standing to challenge the settlement and they had not shown they'd suffer immediate legal harm.

text:
In the wake of a video purportedly showing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents detaining a Lyft driver outside the main terminal of the Nashville International Airport before sunrise on Oct. 22, community members and local immigrant advocates quickly identified him.

People commenting on the video, recorded by the man’s stunned passenger and posted by Music City MigraWatch, recognized him as a Venezuelan man who went by Samuel and also worked as a barber. Nashville Noticias reported that he was 32 years old, his legal name was Salin Ramos, and cited a message from his partner who said Ramos was working to support his parents and children back in Venezuela.

“He is well-known there for being a good person,” she reportedly told the Spanish-language news outlet. “He just told me that he was picked up by immigration and asked me to take good care of the girls.”

On Monday, however, ICE spokesperson Melissa Egan said in an emailed statement that “ICE arrested Salin Dahel Ramos Alvarez, a Known or Suspected Terrorist Gang Member of Tren de Aragua (TdA), Oct. 22 during a targeted enforcement operation.” The statement goes on to say that he was detained by U.S. Border Patrol on Aug. 29, 2023, after entering the country illegally near El Paso, Texas and was “released by the Biden administration.” According to Egan, an immigration judge ordered his removal from the U.S. on Nov. 28, 2023.

ICE’s statement did not cite any evidence of ties between Ramos Alvarez and Tren de Aragua or reference any criminal record. He does not appear to have any criminal history in Nashville.

Egan’s statement also said that “Ramos Alvarez informed ICE officers he was not a Lyft driver but had been paid by an acquaintance to drive them to the airport.”

But the woman he drove to the airport — who spoke to the Banner the following day and asked to be identified only by her first name, Megan — did book her ride for that morning earlier in the week through the Lyft app. She also said she did not know Ramos Alvarez.

She shared screenshots with the Banner showing that although the driver was listed under a different name, the vehicle and license plate matched the car she rode in. She recalled that he arrived early to pick her up, which she appreciated. When they got to the airport, she said, he got out of the car to help her with her bags. Immediately, the two agents approached.

“It was so early in the morning that I wasn’t paying attention to my surroundings like I normally would, so I don’t know if they were following us from my house,” she told the Banner. “I don’t know where these agents came from.”

She said she looked at Ramos Alvarez and asked if he was OK before asking the agents where they were taking him.

“Nashville,” one told her. “Do you want to go with him?”

Megan said she took the comment as a clear warning to stay out of it or risk being detained herself.

After quickly getting the rest of her belongings out of the still-idling car, she said she went through security and walked to her gate in shock. Once there, she said, it occurred to her that her ride was probably still active in the Lyft app. It was and it showed the vehicle had been driven to the Nashville ICE field office on Brick Church Park Drive. She said she later reported the incident to Lyft out of concern for the driver and was told they would be looking into what happened.

The detention comes as the airport’s participation in Flock’s nationwide automated license plate reader network is under scrutiny. The Banner reported in August on the airport’s cameras and how the footage they capture is used by law enforcement agencies across the country. WKRN reported earlier this month that internal audit logs showed agencies searching surveillance data on behalf of ICE.

Asked whether officials were concerned that the driver’s detention would make people fear ICE agents at the airport, an airport spokesperson said the airport “does not participate in, assist with, or oversee ICE enforcement actions” and directed further questions to ICE.

title: ICE in SDF: Records detail immigration arrests at Louisville airport
description:

In Louisville, airport officials aren’t tracking how many people ICE has arrested on their property.
The airport is a public facility, she said, and ICE agents do not need airport officials’ permission to be on-site or make an arrest.
In Nashville, where ICE arrested a flight attendant in July, airport officials said their public safety department doesn’t help federal agents make immigration arrests and directed KyCIR to ICE when asked if the airport collects records detailing ICE arrests inside the facility.

text:
In July, ICE agents in Louisville detained a 31-year-old Ugandan woman with sickle-cell anemia heading to a medical convention in Los Angeles.

In August, agents nabbed a 26-year-old student from Senegal, the center for Kentucky State University’s basketball team, as she was on the way to a tournament in New York.

Later that same month, court records show, ICE agents picked up a 40-year-old Chinese man who lives in California with his wife and two daughters and works as a network engineer. And on Aug. 23, agents arrested a 26-year-old man, who has dual citizenship in Brazil and Portugal, on his way to Florida.

All the arrests happened at the Louisville Muhammad Ali International Airport – the details laid out in court records reviewed by the Kentucky Center for Investigative Reporting. They’re part of a recent trend in ICE arrests at airports across the country under President Donald Trump’s aggressive campaign to oust millions of immigrants.

The exact number of immigrants ICE has arrested in airports nationwide is not known due to limited publicly available data.

In Louisville, airport officials aren’t tracking how many people ICE has arrested on their property.

Natalie Chaudoin, a spokesperson for the Louisville Regional Airport Authority, said officials do not compile reports on arrests made in the airport by outside agencies, like ICE.

The airport is a public facility, she said, and ICE agents do not need airport officials’ permission to be on-site or make an arrest. Officials at other airports in the region said the same.

The Kentucky Center for Investigative Reporting asked officials at all five of Kentucky’s public use commercial service airports, as well as the Nashville International Airport, about ICE operations on their property.

In Nashville, where ICE arrested a flight attendant in July, airport officials said their public safety department doesn’t help federal agents make immigration arrests and directed KyCIR to ICE when asked if the airport collects records detailing ICE arrests inside the facility.

In Lexington, Blue Grass Airport officials said they “work closely” with “many federal partners” and don’t “oversee their day-to-day activities,” but did not say if they assist ICE with arrests inside the airport. Spokesperson Amy Caudill also said they don’t “routinely collect reports” on arrests from outside state or federal agencies.

At the Barkley Regional Airport in Paducah, airport authority executive director Dennis Rouleau said ICE hasn’t shown up, and he doesn’t expect the agency to.

“Primarily because our workforce is relatively small and there are larger areas where their resources could be used more effectively,” he said in an email. “If ICE did need to come here, my staff and I would cooperate with them as we would with any other law enforcement agency.”

And in Louisville, airport officials said their agency’s public safety officers do not help ICE make arrests. They might, if asked, “provide escort services in the secure area of the terminal,” Chaudoin, the spokesperson, said. ICE has an agreement with the U.S. Transportation Security Administration that allows agents to access the secure area of the airport terminal, she said.

Officials at the Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport and the Owensboro-Daviess County Regional Airport did not respond by KyCIR’s publication deadline.

Louisville’s airport management doesn’t share data with ICE, including traveler information, Chaudoin said. She noted that they don’t “maintain or monitor the passenger manifests, the official record of each person onboard a flight, as that information is owned by the airline.”

Caudill, the Lexington airport’s spokesperson, likewise said they “do not maintain access” to traveler records, like airline or rental car information.

'Consequences far beyond immigration'

So how does ICE get data about Louisville travelers? In some cases, from the TSA.

Federal court records reviewed by KyCIR show at least two of those four recent immigration arrests at Louisville’s airport were connected to information that TSA shared with ICE.

Before ICE agents arrested Sarafinah Bukirwa, the Ugandan woman with sickle cell anemia, they received a “PERC [Pacific Enforcement Response Center] and TSA tip” that she had an expired visa and would be flying out of Louisville on that day, according to federal documents within her court file. Bukirwa’s family soon went public about her arrest.

And the arrest of the Chinese man at Louisville’s airport was part of an operation dubbed “TSA Secure Flights,” according to federal records. KyCIR is not naming the man because he could not be reached for comment.

TSA’s Secure Flight program was established nearly 20 years ago as a counterterrorism effort to check if incoming passengers are on government watch lists. The news agency Reuters reported in April that TSA gave ICE records on more than 31,000 people, collected through that program. Reuters reported these tips were connected to subsequent ICE arrests of more than 800 travelers, although it was unclear how many of those arrests were done at airports.

The two agencies, TSA and ICE, struck a deal in May 2025 to exchange data, with limitations, “to enhance national security, transportation security, law enforcement, and immigration and border management,” according to a contract obtained by American Oversight, a Washington D.C.-based nonpartisan watchdog group. The nonprofit sued ICE and TSA for access to the contract, and released it online in July.

The records don’t make clear what data TSA agreed to give ICE. The federal government redacted two sections that detail the “data elements” TSA could share. Whatever the information is, the contract says ICE will store what it gets from TSA in a data repository of its own.

The exchange of information between the agencies is part of a “dangerous precedent” set by the Trump administration, with “consequences far beyond immigration,” said Chioma Chukwu, American Oversight’s executive director, in a July statement.

“Americans provide their personal information to board a plane safely, not to become part of an immigration enforcement system or a government surveillance network,” Chukwu said. “Once the government begins expanding how it uses Americans’ personal information, it raises profound concerns about privacy, civil liberties, and public trust.”

Questions arise when different government systems work together in ways they haven’t before, and in ways that are at odds with their original stated intent, said Amber Duke, executive director of the ACLU of Kentucky.

The TSA plays an important role in keeping airports safe, she said, but the “cross-collaboration between TSA and ICE” stokes fears and questions.

”No one can quite untangle how it works,” she said. ”That continues to keep people in the shadows.”

She also said there is, “justifiably,” fear within immigrant communities about how they or their vulnerable family members might end up on ICE’s radar. And, she said, recent arrests in cities like Louisville show “our airports have become immigration enforcement checkpoints, even for domestic travel.”

A focus on visas

In an email to ICE’s media team, KyCIR requested a comment for this story and asked how many people federal immigration agents have arrested at the Louisville airport during Trump’s second term. ICE did not respond.

The ICE arrests at Louisville’s airport this summer that KyCIR identified occurred after an apparent shift in ICE tactics. The New York Times reported in July that immigration agents had recently started targeting people with expired visas at airports, whereas last year the focus was on detaining travelers who were subject to deportation orders.

Of those four people arrested at Louisville’s airport, court records say Bukirwa and the man from China had overstayed their visas, although both had pending asylum cases when ICE detained them. The other man, born in Brazil, who KyCIR is not naming because he could not be reached for comment, overstayed after entering the U.S. on a visa waiver program and also had an open asylum application when ICE stopped him.

Aminata “Amina” Seck, the basketball player whose legal team later went public about her arrest, was subject to a deportation order, although an immigration judge rescinded it after ICE jailed her.

None of these four people had criminal records, according to court documents.

After their arrest, they all were held in Kentucky jails that earn a fee to detain immigrants for ICE.

Both Bukirwa and Seck won their release from the Grayson County jail through the court cases they filed. The two men are both still in the Oldham County jail while their court cases remain unresolved.

text:
The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to restore a Biden-era regulation that allows immigration judges to suspend some deportation proceedings. In a brief, unsigned order, the court turned down a request from three cities and a group that provides legal services to immigrants to pause an agreement between Texas and the U.S. Department of Justice that threw out the rule.

There were no noted dissents.

The regulation at the center of the dispute, which provides what is known as “administrative closure,” was adopted by the Executive Office for Immigration Review, part of the Department of Justice, in 2024. Under it, immigration judges may suspend some deportation proceedings – for example, to allow a crime victim or witness to seek relief, such as asylum, from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which is a separate agency.

In June of this year, Texas went to federal court in Wichita Falls, where its case was assigned to Chief U.S. District Judge Reed O’Connor – the only federal judge in that area. Calling the administrative-closure rule “one part of the Biden-Harris Administration’s campaign to undermine our immigration laws,” it alleged that the EOIR does not have the authority to adopt the administrative-closure rule. Instead, it wrote, federal law requires an immigration judge, at the end of a proceeding, to “decide whether an alien is removable from the United States.”

Just a few hours after the case was filed, the DOJ and Texas asked O’Connor to enter a final judgment for the state. The DOJ also asked him both to throw out the rule altogether and to issue an order making clear that the EOIR could not adopt a similar rule in the future. O’Connor granted those requests on the same day.

On Aug. 7, three cities with large immigrant populations – Baltimore, Maryland; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio – and Centro Legal de la Raza, which provides legal services to immigrants, filed an emergency motion to join the case so that they could defend the administrative-closure rule on appeal, when neither Texas nor the federal government intended to do so. O’Connor denied their request on the ground that they lacked a legal right to sue, known as standing. In particular, he rejected the cities’ contention that the elimination of the rule would cost them money because their taxpayers are likely to be deported.

The challengers then went to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit, which rejected their request to block the consent judgment between Texas and the Department of Justice and thereby reinstate the administrative-closure rule while their appeal continued.

On Oct. 9, the challengers came to the Supreme Court, calling the consent agreement the product of “egregious collusion” and asking the justices to step in. Their attorney, Joshua Salzman of Democracy Forward, argued that permitting the consent agreement to stand could have widespread implications. “If a judgment procured through such open collusion is allowed to remain in effect,” he wrote, “any agency can avoid the strictures of the” federal law governing administrative agencies “by advertising its unwillingness to defend a disfavored regulation and by immediately acquiescing to nationwide relief.”

Urging the Supreme Court to leave the agreement in place, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer contended that the challengers’ request to pause O’Connor’s ruling “attempts to improperly leverage a clear-cut dispute over” the challengers’ efforts to join the case “into a far-reaching attack on the merits of” the court’s approval of the agreement. For its part, Texas told the justices that putting O’Connor’s ruling on hold “would revive a rule the district court declared unlawful, renew the fiscal and sovereign injuries Texas alleged, and unsettle a final judgment accepted by the actual parties.”

Four days after the case was fully briefed, the court denied the challengers’ request without comment.

text:
By RYAN J. FOLEY

IOWA CITY, Iowa (AP) — For nearly a year, immigration authorities have detained and sought to deport a mentally ill man whose mother, lawyers and public records say was born in the United States and not Jamaica as he claims, a review by The Associated Press found.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement has no authority to detain U.S. citizens, but has long done so, usually for hours or days, when officers mistake identities or can’t immediately verify citizenship. Immigration lawyers say a nearly 10-month improper detention would be rare but not unprecedented.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, disputes that the man is a U.S. citizen and alleges, without providing evidence, that the birth certificate he submitted to obtain a U.S. passport that he held for 15 years was fraudulent. But AP’s review found documents that support claims by his mother and legal team that he was born in Florida and therefore not subject to ICE’s authority.

The findings suggest that a cursory investigation, lax oversight, and possibly a refusal to admit a mistake may have ensnared a U.S. citizen for nearly all of 2026 as the Trump administration rushes to deport large numbers of people suspected of being in the country illegally.

Detainee insists he was born in Jamaica

Still locked up at ICE’s so-called Speedway Slammer in Indiana is Phillip James, a 39-year-old who also goes by the name Felibi Siagha-Coke, legal filings show. His lawyers are appealing an immigration judge’s ruling that he be deported to Jamaica, and a federal judge has indicated he could soon rule on a petition to free him from custody.

In seeking to detain and deport him, immigration authorities relied on James’ word that he was born in Jamaica and entered the U.S. illegally in 2009, the AP review found. But Jamaican officials have denied any record that he was born or has citizenship there, and James has been unable to provide proof, public records show.

James’ insistence that he was born in Jamaica is a grand delusion, a symptom of paranoid schizophrenia with which he has been diagnosed, according to reports filed in court by medical experts who have recently assessed him. In particular, he claims that he is the illegitimate son of a former Jamaican prime minister and the descendant of a royal family in Lebanon, where he also claims citizenship despite a lack of evidence.

One psychologist concluded James was not “a reliable historian due to the serious nature of his mental illness, including a deeply entrenched delusional belief system.”

Expert says case shows how ICE mishandles citizenship disputes

Northwestern University professor Jacqueline Stevens, who has studied ICE’s wrongful detention of citizens for two decades, said she is not surprised ICE would seek to deport James based on his claims of being foreign-born. She said she was familiar with other cases where mental illness and disabilities have played a role in similar injustices.

“What’s going on in these cases is that evidence that’s consistent with deportation is treated as accurate and evidence that is inconsistent is treated as fraudulent,” she said. “This case is not a one-off. This is a feature, not a bug, of how ICE handles claims of U.S. citizenship.”

The Department of Homeland Security denied that ICE detains U.S. citizens, and says detainees facing removal proceedings receive due process.

text:
EL PASO, Texas – An illegal alien from Mexico was sentenced in a federal court in El Paso to 110 months in prison for conspiracy to transport aliens resulting in serious bodily injury, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons for the Western District of Texas.

According to court documents, Manuel Alejandro Melendez-Cereceres aka “Monstro,” 42, was a member of an alien smuggling organization. In his role, Melendez-Cereceres recruited and coordinated drivers and vehicles to transport smuggled aliens either to harboring locations or to exchange points where the aliens would be picked up by an additional driver and transported further into the United States.

On May 15, 2025, U.S. Border Patrol agents in Tornillo interdicted a smuggling event and apprehended a foot guide. During the smuggling event led by the guide, one of the illegal aliens being smuggled fell from a fence and suffered serious bodily injuries which led to surgery for a right hip socket fracture, a right hip joint fracture, a sacral fracture and a right heel bone fracture. Through a search of the foot guide’s cell phone, agents discovered communications between the guide and Melendez-Cereceres.

Melendez-Cereceres was arrested at his residence in June 2025 and indicted for four counts related to alien smuggling. On June 11, 2026, he pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to transport aliens resulting in serious bodily injury. In addition to the nine-year federal prison sentence, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone also ordered a money judgement in the amount of $672,101.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations and the U.S. Border Patrol investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Mathew Engelbaum prosecuted the case.

The case is supported and prosecuted by Joint Task Force Alpha (JTFA), the Department’s lead effort in combating high-impact human smuggling and trafficking committed by cartels and Transnational Criminal Organizations (TCOs). A highly successful partnership between the Department of Justice and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), JTFA investigates and prosecutes human smuggling and trafficking and related immigration crimes that impact public safety and border security. JTFA’s mission is to target the leaders and organizers of Cartels and TCOs involved in human smuggling and trafficking throughout the Americas. The Attorney General has elevated and expanded JTFA to target the most prolific and dangerous human smuggling and trafficking groups operating not only in Mexico and the Northern Triangle countries of Guatemala, El Salvador, and Honduras, but also in Canada, the Caribbean and the maritime border, and elsewhere. Led by the Criminal Division’s Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section and supported by the Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, the Office of International Affairs, and the Office of Enforcement Operations, among others, JTFA has dedicated Assistant U.S. Attorney prosecutors from the Southern District of California; District of Arizona; District of New Mexico; Western and Southern Districts of Texas; Southern District of Florida; Northern District of New York; and District of Vermont. JTFA also partners with other U.S. Attorney’s Offices throughout the country and supports high-priority cases in any district. All JTFA cases rely on substantial law enforcement resources from DHS, including HSI and Customs and Border Protection, Border Patrol and Office of Field Operations as well as FBI and other law enforcement agencies. To date, JTFA’s work has resulted in more than 483 domestic and international arrests of leaders, organizers, and significant facilitators of alien smuggling and/or trafficking; more than 436 U.S. convictions; and more than 371 significant jail sentences imposed, and forfeitures of substantial assets.

This case is part of Operation Take Back America a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel the invasion of illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect our communities from the perpetrators of violent crime.

Oct 27 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court declined on Tuesday to reinstate the authority of immigration judges to temporarily postpone deportation cases, keeping in place an agreement between President Donald Trump’s administration and Republican-governed Texas that bars the once-common practice.

The justices denied an emergency request by three US cities including Baltimore and an immigrant legal advocacy group to halt for now the deal ending the practice, known as “administrative closure,” while litigation continues in the dispute.

Advertisement

The Supreme Court’s decision, issued as a brief, one-sentence order, did not offer any explanation, as is common when it handles emergency requests. None of the justices publicly dissented from decision.

The administration and Texas filed the agreement in a federal court in Texas on June 22, the same day that the state sued to challenge the immigration court procedure. A federal judge swiftly approved the agreement on the same day. Baltimore and the other litigants said the federal government improperly colluded with Texas to secure the rule’s invalidation.

Immigration judges relied on administrative closure for decades to clear certain deportation cases off their busy dockets, including when separate proceedings involving the same person are pending that could prevent removal, such as on a visa petition or an appeal of a criminal conviction.

Advertisement

Critics including Texas and the Trump administration have said administrative closure has allowed immigrants who lack legal status to remain indefinitely in the United States, acting in effect like an amnesty.

Administrative closure has been applied over the years in hundreds of thousands of deportation cases. Ending the practice is part of Trump’s hardline approach toward immigrants.

In 2024, Biden’s administration adopted a regulation that formally codified administrative closure procedures, concluding that it lets judges efficiently manage their caseloads and promote the fair treatment of immigrants. That regulation replaced a prior rule adopted in 2020 during Trump’s first term in office that had been judicially blocked.

Advertisement

After Trump returned to office in 2025, the Justice Department office that oversees immigration courts, the Executive Office for Immigration Review, announced it would not defend the Biden rule against a legal challenge.

In a lawsuit, Texas argued that the rule lets immigration judges “effectively grant indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country.”

Trump’s administration and the state then jointly asked US District Judge Reed O’Connor in Wichita Falls, Texas, to approve an agreement declaring the Biden rule unlawful. O’Connor did so, blocking it permanently, nationwide.

Advertisement

Three municipalities — Baltimore, New Haven, Connecticut, and Columbus, Ohio — and the legal services provider, Centro Legal de la Raza, sought to intervene in the case to defend the rule, but O’Connor rejected their bid. The cities say they all have substantial immigrant populations.

The New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put the agreement on hold pending an appeal of O’Connor’s decision.

The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza told the Supreme Court in a filing that Trump’s administration circumvented a federal law governing agency procedures by using “manufactured litigation” with “ideologically aligned” Texas to eliminate a regulation it disliked.

Advertisement

“The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception,” they wrote.

(Reporting by Andrew Chung in New York; editing by Will Dunham)

Like some other incidents that occurred as a result of the Trump administration's ongoing immigration crackdown, the footage from Pretti's shooting differed from the version of events provided by the Department of Homeland Security.[br /][br /]Kristi Noem, then-DHS secretary, initially described Pretti as a "terrorist" who "attacked" officers after "brandishing" a weapon, though the video disputed those claims. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller referred to Pretti as an "assassin" who tried to murder federal agents.[br /][br /]"No one from the federal government called us on that horrible day, but they did go on TV to tell lies about Alex," Michael Pretti said Tuesday.[br /][br /]Video footage shows, minutes before the fatal encounter with Pretti, immigration agents patrolling a Minneapolis street and interacting with bystanders. A witness, Nilson Barahona, told CNN agents were trying to apprehend someone who fled into a donut shop that locked its doors, leaving the group of federal officers on the sidewalk and street. One of the officers can be heard in the footage shouting: "Gun! Gun! Gun!" as Pretti is on his knees and bent forward. An agent removed Pretti's gun from his waistband and can be seen exiting the skirmish. At about the same time, one agent drew his service weapon.[br /][br /]About a second after the agent holding Pretti's weapon moved away, the officer who drew his own weapon appeared to fire several shots at Pretti before another agent drew his weapon and a shot rang out. text:
OSHKOSH (WLUK) – Wendy Mendez, a teacher at Vel Phillips Middle School, was arrested by ICE and is in the process of being deported after not showing up for an immigration hearing.

According to ICE, Mendez is an illegal alien from Costa Rica. She was taken into custody on Oct. 14.

ICE told FOX 11:

On August 10, 2020, Mendez legally entered the United States on a temporary basis, but in violation of our laws, failed to depart by February 9, 2021. On February 18, 2026, she was placed into removal proceedings, and on September 9, was ordered removed by an immigration judge for failing to show up for her removal proceedings. The Oshkosh Area School District confirmed Mendez works for the district.

The district wrote:

Under district policy and applicable privacy regulations, the Oshkosh Area School District does not comment on confidential personnel or individual employee matters. According to a Facebook post by Deb Nez, who states she is Mendez’s friend, a mailing error about the hearing led to the arrest.

“They had no knowledge of that because the court sent the notice to their previous address from more that 3 years ago. USCIS had their new address within days of them moving to the new house. This was not the first time that USCIS had made that mistake. FOX 11 has yet to independently confirm the details in Nez’s post.

Being in detention is a choice. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.
